INTRODUCTION
 
 
I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry,  having   been authorised  by the
Committee, hereby present this  Eighty-Seventh  Report on  Implementation Status of Financial Assistance - cum-restructuring
Package and Revival of Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL)
2.         The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee-I for Ministry of Steel to examine the  Implementation Status
of Financial Assistance - cum-restructuring Package and Revival of Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL) .The Sub-Committee visited
Kolkata from 17th to 20th July 01, and interacted with the  management  of  Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL).  
3.         The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 14th March 2002, heard  the   Secretary, Ministry of Steel and official concerned 
to Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL) .   The Report  has been prepared  on the  basis of   on the spot  study by the Sub-Committee -I for
Ministry of Steel and Mines  and  interaction with the    Secretary , Ministry of Steel and officials  of Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL).
4.         The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 8th August, 2002 considered and adopted  the  Report. 
5          The Committee at its  meeting  held on    9th August, 2002 considered and adopted the Report.
6.         The Report was presented   to the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha  on 20th August, 2002 by the then Chairman , Shri T.N.
Chaturvedi.
 
NEW DELHI
December… 2002
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
 Chairman
Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
Report
            The Refractory Industry in India is more than century old and the growth of this industry is closely inter-linked with the
development and growth of steel industry as more than 75 per cent of the total refractories produced in the country are consumed by
steel industries. Refractories contribute around 5 per cent   towards the total cost of steel making.  Under the changing scenario of
globalisation and liberalization, steel makers are facing stiff competition in the market, therefore, Steel Industry is  left with no  other
alternative than to produce the best  quality at the least cost.  The Steel Industry has started to demand  superior grade refractories
required for blast furnace, secondary refining and continuous casting units of steel industries which has posed challenges to the
refractory industry.  The emphasis by the industry in the recent years has been towards import substitution and production of special
items like magnesia carbon, slide gate refractories. 
1.1       Bharat Refractories Limited (BRL) was originally incorporated as a subsidiary company of Bokaro Steel Ltd. as the
production unit of (BHRP) which was earlier acquired by Government of India in 1972 and placed under the management of Bokaro
Steel Limited. Consequent upon restructuring of the Public Sector and steel industries on 1
st May 1978, Ranchi Road Refractories
Plant (RRRPL) at Ramgarh, which was under the control of erstwhile Hindustan Steel Limited and Bhilai Refractories Plant was also
transferred to BRL.  India Firebricks and Insulation Co. (IFICO) which was taken over by Steel Authority of India Ltd., with effect
from December, 1976, was also transferred as a subsidiary of BRL with effect from the date of restructurings.  At present, Bharat
Refractories Ltd (BRL) has four units, namely;
(a)    Bhandaridah Refractories Plant, Bhandaridah;
(b)   Ranchi Road Refractories Plant, Ramgarh;
(c)    Bhilai Refractories plant at Bhilai; and
(d)   IFICO Refractories Plant at Ramgarh.
1.2 The company is engaged in the manufacture and supply of various kinds of refractories not only to the integrated steel plants, but
also to the mini and medium steel plants.
1.3       The Committee notes the stages involved in the   formation of Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL)  and hopes   that BRL
management would leave no stone unturned in assessing the   strength of all the four units of BRL and chalk out a short and long
term strategic course of action for early turnaround of company as a whole.  The Committee recommends that BRL management
work to ensure that all four units of BRL are making efforts towards the common mission for achieving common organizational goal
and are contributing to the physical and financial performance of the company.  None of them should    prove a burden on the
company.
2.0
              Capital Structure

2.3       The company  has to pay pending statutory dues to its employees. The company is not able to generate sufficient funds to
meet its gross salaries and  wages liabilities. It has defaulted  in terms of payment of statutory liabilities, which stand at Rs.58 crore
as on 31"June, 2001.
2.4       The Sub-Committee was informed that BRL management has taken   step to improve the   financial ratio of the company
which includes  reduction of manpower and improving the productivity and steps taken to produce only value added items for Steel
industry in particular.
 
2.5.      The Committee is constrained   to express  its concern over the deteriorating   balance  sheet of BRL.  The Committee in its
34
th  and  50 th Reports has  been recommending to the Government  that it should  provide sufficient working capital BRL at the 
earliest so that  it could reduce its  loss, loans and  liability and readjust itself for profit make track . The Committee, in this regard, 
recommends that the BRL management and the Ministry of  Steel  should examine  and assess the capital structure of BRL, from
time to time, and suggest  measures  for capital restructuring ,in such a way, that BRL  achieves the break -even point and economy
of  scales ensuring maximum   Return on Investment (ROI).
 
 
3.0       Sickness of BRL and IFICO.
3.1       The Sub-Committee was informed  that  BRL and  India Fire Bricks  and Insulation Company  (IFICO)  were sick due to
under mentioned  reasons  and came under the purview  of Sick Industrial  Companies (Special Provision) Act,  1985 and was
referred to BIFR in 1992:-
 
(a)
         Obsolescence of machinery technological indiscipline and underutilization of capacity.
(b)         Managerial inefficiency and low  man-power   utilization.
(c)         Shortage of working capital  resulting into delay  in the procurement  of raw-material ..
(d)         Erratic power supply.
(e)         Changing   demand pattern of  refractories  etc.
3.2.      The Committee notes the reasons for BRL  and IFICO  becoming sick and coming under the purview of BIFR in  1992.  The
Committee observes that due attention for  revival of BRL was not considered at the appropriate time  and that  is the reason why
BRL continued  to make losses year  after year.  What  other result might be expected, from a loss making company which continued
to operate with  obsolescent machinery;    under utilisation  of  installed capacity;     low labour- productivity and shortage of capital ,
than falling  in the  net of BIFR.  BRL missed the ( the first  opportunity for revival), the Committee concludes.
4.0       IDBI's Revival Scheme
4.1       IDBI was appointed  the  operating agency to formulate revival scheme which was  approved by BIFR in January, 1997.  The
revival package consisted of financial relief granted by Government of India, which are enumerated a below:
i
                Waiver of interest per cent  on loans amounting to Rs.61.64 crore;
ii               Conversion of 50 per cent  plan loan (Rs.39.76) into equity and the remaining 50 per cent  of loan R.39.76 crore) into
fresh loan bearing interest @ 12 per cent  p.a. with interest holiday for 3 years, and moratorium on loan repayment for 4
years;
iii             Conversion of non-plan loan amounting to Rs. 12.05   crore into 7 per cent  non-cumulative preference shares
redeemable in ten years; and

iv             Merger of IFICO  with  the holding company i.e. BRL.
4.2       The Sub-Committee was given an understanding that as per IDBI's  recommendation report the State Bank of India was
appointed  to assess the working capital requirement  of the company and accordingly to extend credit  facilities as per the  prescribed
lending rate.   The revival scheme envisaged working capital requirement  to the tune of Rs.21.00 crore and  on this estimation, the
profitability of the company was projected but  since SBI under estimated the  company working capital    requirement at Rs.14.00
crore  .
4.3       Highlighting the problematic aspects of IDBI's scheme the management stated that IDBI's schemes could not succeed because
of following reasons:-
1.                 The Revival scheme with effective date of implementation as 1.4.95 was finally approved in January 1997, after two
years with the result that the targets envisaged in the revival scheme could not be achieved.
2.                 Underestimation of the working capital by SBI and non-disbursement of even Rs.14.00 crore hindered the
procurement of raw materials and dispatch of finished products.
3.                 As all units except BRP were sick at the time of takeover, Amalgamation and modernisation required substantial
investment to cater to the changes in demand pattern of refractories due to change in technology in steel industry.  A
mere Rs.31.00 crore would hardly help the company in achieving the desired level of production envisaged in the
revival plan.
4.
                 Since the company was regularly incurring losses right from its inception, the payment of interest and repayment of
loan was never made by it.  The continued cash loss eroded its liquidity base of the company and resulted into huge  
outstanding creditors and suppliers, thus, affecting the credit worthiness and smooth flow of raw -materials and other
inputs.
5.                 The revival scheme stipulated 12 per cent  interest p.a. for loan by the Government.  However, the  loan presently
received by the company is   carrying   interest @ 15 per cent p.a. with penal interest of 2.75 per cent
4.4       The Committee  observes  that since IDBI's revival package had  no cash assistance to BRL as working capital  on the
assumption that with its revised capital base and net worth position,  BRL   would be in  a position to raise working capital and
sustain higher levels of production during 1995-96 and onwards, the  non-availability of working  capital to BRL  blocked the
chances of increasing its production as well as improving its product  mix  for better   sales realisation . The Committee understands
that it is because of the slow down in the steel industry .The demand for refractories had not been of the level expected. It is but
natural that, in the above scenario, the company was unable to generate internal resources so as to meet its plan and non-plan
expenditure.  BRL ended 1997-98 with a cash loss of Rs.14.33 crore and   the same adverse trend persisted during   1998-99.
4.5       The Committee understands that the general recession in steel industry in addition to BRL’s inherent problems i.e. under
utilisation of installed capacity, interruption in power supply, problems in the procurement of raw-material due to lack of working
capital followed by non -implementation of IDBI's   revival scheme led to the continued dwindling in physical and financial
performance of the company.
5.0       Second Revival Package for BRL
5.1       The management explained that   the Continued cash loss incurred by BRL, capital liquidity position, huge accumulation of
outstanding dues coupled with resentment of workers due to non-revision of wages had severely affected production and sale
realisation.  Due to paucity of funds and inadequate assistance from Government, most of the plant and machinery outlived their
effective life and required immediate replacement.  Taking into consideration all these factors the Ministry of steel formulated the
second revival package for BRL. This revival package included: -
i
                Grant of non-plan   loan Rs.400 crore for meeting revised wage bill during 1998-99,
ii               Grant of non--plan interest   free loan of Rs.16.00 crore during 1998-99 for meeting the working capital interest
holiday on existing loan as on 31.3.99 till 2007-2008;
iii             Moratorium on loan repaying for existing loans for another four years i.e. till 2003-2004;
iv             and Government of India  guarantee for  enhancing the  working capital limit  to Rs.24.00 crore. 
5.2       The second revisal package   for BRL was approved by the CCEA in its meeting held on 21.1.99.  Necessary non-plan
provision of Rs.20.50 crore was made   in RE 1998-99.
5.3       Contrary to all hopes the Second revival packages for BRL failed because of the following inherent problems of the company
were not attended to: -
i                Low labour productivity due to excess manpower
ii               High cost of production due to high operating cost and increase in the price of input but decline in the price of
refractory items.
iii             Under utilisation of production capacity due to obsolete machinery, inadequate working capital and low work orders
from steel industry due to decline in demand of conventional refractory items.
iv      Continued monthly loss as a result- of quoting selling price at contribution margin by the company due to stiff
competition.

7.0       Problems being faced by Refectories industry 
7.1       The Sub-Committee was given an understanding that the growth of Refractory Industry is closely inter-linked with the
development and growth of steel industry as more than 75 per cent of the total refractories produced in the country are consumed by
steel industries while 15 per cent are used by Cement & Glass Industries and rest goes for Non-ferrous metal and petrol-chemical
sectors.  Refractories contribute around 5 per cent   towards the total cost of steel making.    During the last several years, the demand
of superior grade refractories required for BOF, secondary refining and continuous casting units of steel industries posed challenges
to the refractory producers.  The emphasis by the industry in the recent years is towards import substitution    and production of
special items like magnesia carbon, slide gate refractories, submerged nozzles, shrouds.  Monoblock stoppers, low –cement castables,
dense silica bricks for tall coke ovens, etc. The choice of refractories for steel making depends on various factors like achieving
reduced fuel consumption, increased furnace capacity, increased furnace life and availability and improved product quality.  The
future of refractory industry lies in continued development of improved bonding in basic and high alumina materials, advances in tar  
pitch bonding and impregnation and development of resion bonding. Monolithics special those incorporating low cement, carbon/.
Graphite emerged and relatively high performance materials.  Besides there is greater emphasis for greater energy efficiency. The
changing attitude of present day consumers is laying more importance on the availability of furnace, cleanliness of steel, ultimate cost
benefit, even if the initial investment were high.  This may be reckoned from the fact that during the last three decades, the
improvement in refractories quality has led to about 50 to 60 per cent decrease in specific consumption of refractories, whereas the
turnover of refractory units has been steadily rising.
 
7.2       The Committee is of the view that, since 75 per cent of the total refractories produced in the country      are consumed by steel
industries and steel industry is demanding superior grade of refractories, the Ministry of steel should facilitate the refractories
industry in general and BRL in particular to     undertake adequate research work for production of such superior grade of refractories
which suits the requirement of steel industry.  The Committee   recommends that research work in refractories industry may take into
consideration the requirement of steel industry which inter-alia include reduction in fuel consumption, incurred furnace capacity,
incurred furnace   life and availability and improved product quality.
 
7.3       The major factors that have led to decline in refractory consumption are increased stringency on the quality of refractory
products and improvement of quality along with improved operational parameters. The operating data of SAIL and their perspective
planning as indicated below for the next decade are indicators of the trend in steel sector.

7.4.      The Sub-Committee wanted to know whether it is a fact that technological improvement in steel making has affected the
entire refractories industry and unhealthy competition has led to price war, if so, the measures that could be undertaken to improve
the physical and financial performance of refractories industry in general and BRL in particular. The BRL management informed the
Sub-Committee that improvement in Steel making Technology alongwith development of superior quality refractories has reduced
the consumption of refractories per ton of steel in the country, which has particularly created a price war situation. Impact of this
during last three years resulted in price reduction to the tune of 20 / 25 per cent every year leading to a situation as on date when
some of the products are priced at almost raw materials cost.
7.5       The Committee observes that technological improvement in steel making has not only led to the increasing demand   of
superior quality refractories and reduction in total consumption of refractories but also generated a price war situation   and unfair
trade price due to excessive competition among refractories producers.  The Committee is of the view that improvement in steel
making technology is a welcome and necessary   development for betterment   of steel industry while reduction in total consumption
of refractories is an unavoidable development and it may be hoped that with the sign of recovery in steel industry the demand of
refractories would increase.  So far as the situation of price was due to excessive competition   is concerned, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Steel should take up the matter to ensure that healthy competition should prevail in the Refractories
Industry and competition should not result into unfair trade   prices.  The price of the refractories product be allowed to be determined
by the free market forces of demand and supply.

manufacturing cost and selling price.  The price of finished products has been drastically reduced whereas there is an increasing trend
in the price structure of input materials.   The trend of the price structure of input materials vis-à-vis the finished product is indicated

7.7       The BRL management stated that the imbalances between manufacturing cost and selling price of refractories can be removed
in the following ways:
 
i
                Age old machinery   and equipment need to be replaced to reduce the idle time and increase in productivity.
 
ii
               Reduction in   manpower by VRS to increase the productivity per man/year.
 
iii
             Reduction of Customs Duty on imported input materials for hi-tech refractories required at present.
7.8       Because of huge capacity of production in the country and lesser requirement as also import of substantial quantity  of
refractories, the profitability rate/margin  of profit in general for BRL is negative.
 
7.9.      The Committee understands the problems being faced by refractories industry arising due to imbalance between
manufacturing cost and selling price.  The Committee observes that the price of the finished products has been drastically reduced
(ranging from 30 to 44 per cent) whereas there is a trend in increase in the price structure of input materials (ranging from 5 to 17 per
cent).  This is the double loss to the refractory industry and under the   said circumstances any industry is bound to be affected. 
Therefore, the Committee is of the view that refractories industry in general and BRL management   in particular should chalk out a
two pronged strategy i.e. one to arrest the fall in the selling price of refractories and   to reverse the trend and other strategy is
required to minimise the cost of production so that the `margin of profit' for refractories industry may increase.  The Committee
further recommends   that   the Ministry of Steel should act as a facilitator and guide the BRL management to undertake measures for
maximisation of profit.
 
7.10 Cost Component of BRL Products Vis- a-Vis Unit In Private Sectors
7.10.1  Apprising the Sub-Committee of cost component of BRL products vis-a--vis unit in Private sectors and steps undertaken to
reduce the same and out-come of efforts undertaken the management stated that the main difference of cost component between BRL
products vis- a-vis Private sectors products are due to over-head cost mainly Salary & wages and other benefits. This cost is about 30

10.2.2.Refractories for continuous casting system (RCC)
A feasibility   Report  for Refractories for continuous casting system (RCC) has been prepared by the M/s MECON,
appointed  as consultant.  The technical know-how  for the production of continuous casting refractory  has already been  obtained 
by the company from M/s Shinagawa Refractores  Ltd., Japan.  With the   technological changes in steel sector leading to the
reduction of consumption of  conventional refractories and demand for the refractories for  continuous casting system ways and
means would however have necessarily to be found for setting  up of the project for the  survival  of the company. The company
proposes to set up the project through joint venture utilising the existing facilities at IFICO. Refractories Plant . In view of the same,
a  provision of Rs.10.90 crore has been made in the BE 2001-2002  with a budgetary support of Rs.0.50 crore.
10.2.3  The Sub-Committee wanted to know the  current status of BRL plan to set up a continuous Casting Refractories Plant in joint
venture  and the original estimated cost and current cost for setting un the same ,the management stated that BRL floated open tender
and one Party namely MONNET ISPAT LTD. offered their proposal to become joint venture partner and this has been forwarded to
the Ministry. The proposal is for 60 : 40 percent equity participation by Monnet &BRL and for signing MOU on this basis. BRL
asked permission of Ministry of Steel which is awaited. The BRL management  informed the Sub-Committee that the  original cost of
the project was about Rs. 23 crores as done by MECON in 1992 but later on in 2000- 2001 the cost escalated upto 38 crores when a
separate Company in joint venture was thought.  Replying to the Sub-Committee's query regarding the proportion   of the 
Government equity and the sources to raise the required fund the BRL management stated that BRL's equity part of 40 per cent
would be adjusted by the cost of land and Technology transfer cost alongwith some fund from plan loan to be sanctioned by Govt of
India in 10th 5 year plan .
 
10.2.4  BRL is not  in a position to generate sufficient  internal  resources to meet the cost  of the project.  BRL proposed  to make the
project for a joint venture.  In order to obtain a joint venture partner, BRL floated open  tender  and only one party viz., Monnet Ispat
Limited responded for the same for 60:40 equity participation  by  Monnet and BRL.   The  proposal is under consideration   of the  
Government Chairman-cum-Managing Director, BRL have also  discussed   with Managing  Director, Ferro scrap Nigam Ltd.  for 
their participation in the project which is under scrutiny stage at Ferrro scrap Nigam Ltd.  which is also a public sector undertaking
under the Ministry of Steel.
10.2.5  The   Committee is of the considered view that setting up of Continuous Casting System (RCC)  is long  overdue .The  
Standing  Committee on Industry has  recommended   in its earlier reports for setting up of refractories for  Continuous   Casting 
System at the earliest for ensured survival of the company.  The RCC has got the merit of positive  feasibility report as prepared by
M/s  MECON and the technical know-how as obtained from M/s  Shinagow Refractories  Ltd.,  Japan.  The   technological changes
in steel  making process leaves little scope for demand of conventional refractories and  opens the  avenues    for refractories  for
Continuous Casting System.  All   these factors   necessitate    the setting up of RCC, sooner the better, since  original   estimated
cost  i.e. Rs.23 crore has  already overrun  to the tune of Rs.38.00 crore .  The only   deterring  factor  earlier was the lack of fund for
the project as BRL was  not in a position to generate  sufficient internal   resources to meet the cost of the project.    However, this 
problem seems to be solved  as  M/s Monnet  Ispat Ltd. has offered the  proposal to become a  joint venture partner with BRL  with
the  equity  ratio of  60 : 40 and , not only that , BRL's  equity of 40 per cent  would be  adjusted by  the cost of land and technology
transfer cost alongwith  Government fund from plan loan during the 10
th Five Year Plan.  Would the Ministry of Steel further   allow
the  time and cost  overrun  on the project and  leaving the BRL to  dither  to a point of no return?  The Committee raises the query to
be solved   by the Ministry of Steel in its Action Taken Note of the present  Report.  The Committee is  , otherwise ,  of the view 
that  the  having been given the latest revival package  for BRL, setting up of RCC should not be  delayed further.

13.0     Tax Structure
13.1     Pertaining to the Sub-Committee's query as  to what extent the existing tax structure is beneficial in the interest of refractories
industry  and the steps  which could be undertaken for rationalization of tax structure,  the BRL management stated that most of the
raw materials required for manufacturing of high tech refractory items are not available in the country as such import of huge
quantity of these materials is a must. There has been some rationalization of tax structure during the budget of 2001- 2002 while
custom duties of three items namely D-B-M, Fused Magnesite & Sea Water Magnesia was reduced to 15 per cent. Thereby giving
some relief to Refractory industries. However, there are various other raw materials like B-F-A, W-F-A, Tabular Alumina graphite &
fume Silica required for high Tech products needs the same relief to enable Indian products cost effective & competitive in price
compared to foreign suppliers.
 
13.2     During the budget presentation for 2001-02 relief on  Sea Water Magnesia, Fused Magnesia and Dead Burnt Magnesia  was
considered  by the Government of India and the same has been reduced to  15 per cent   plus 4 per cent surcharge. During the budget  
presentation of 2002-03 , the duty on  Brown fused Alumina, Sintered Alumina, Silicon Carbon,  Graphite etc., was  reduced to 30
per cent .  However, the  refractory bricks  imported from outside is charged 25 per cent   custom duty,   Reduction of custom duty an
input material  to 50 per cent of the finished bricks import duty would be suitable for refractories industry.

time to time, and suggest  measures  for capital restructuring ,in such a way, that BRL  achieves the break -even point and economy
of  scales ensuring maximum   Return on Investment (ROI).
 
( Para : 2.5)
 
Sickness of BRL and IFICO.
 
            The Committee notes the reasons for BRL  and IFICO  becoming sick and coming under the purview of BIFR in  1992.  The
Committee observes that due attention for  revival of BRL was not considered at the appropriate time  and that  is the reasons why
BRL continued  to make losses year  after year.  What  other result might be expected, from a loss making company which continued
to operate with  obsolescent machinery;    under utilisation  of  installed capacity;     low labour- productivity and shortage of capital ,
than falling  in the  net of BIFR.  BRL missed the ( the first  opportunity for revival), the Committee concludes.
 ( Para : 3.2)
 
IDBI's Revival Scheme
            The Committee  observes  that since IDBI's revival package had  no cash assistance to BRL as working capital  on the
assumption that with its revised capital base and net worth position,  BRL   would be in  a position to raise working capital and
sustain higher levels of production during 1995-96 and onwards, the  non-availability of working  capital to BRL  blocked the
chances of increasing its production as well as improving its product  mix  for better   sales realisation . The Committee  understand
that it is because of the slow down in the steel industry .The demand for refractories had  not been of the  level expected. It is but
natural that ,  in the above scenario, the company was  unable to generate  internal resources so as to meet its  plan and non-plan
expenditure.  BRL ended 1997-98 with a cash loss of Rs.14.33 crore and   the same adverse trend persisted  during   1998-99.
( Para : 4.4)
 
            The Committee understands that the general  recession in  steel industry  in addition to BRL's  inherent problems i.e. under
utilisation of  installed capacity, interruption in power supply, problems in  the procurement of  raw-material due to lack of working
capital followed by non -implementation of IDBI's   revival scheme led to the continued  dwindling  in physical and  financial 
performance of the company.
( Para : 4.5)
 
Second Revival  Package for  BRL
The Committee  is constrained to express its anguish over the fact that  the Second Revival  Package for BRL had not 
envisaged the true picture of BRL and ,  henceforth , the Second  revival package  could  not  redress to the actual problems being
faced by  BRL.  Like IDBI's    revival  package, the Second Revival Package for BRL  failed, the committee is perturbed to note.
 
( Para : 5.4)
Physical and Financial Performance of BRL
            The Committee   notes the physical production of BRL and observes  that since  refractory  industry is linked  with the
development and  growth of  Steel Industry and since  steel industry was itself running through   rough whether  it  is but natural that
production performance of BRL is  just good.  However, the   steel industry is now coming out of wood, therefore, the Committee 
hopes  that BRL would, accordingly, streamline the production.
( Para : 6.2)
            The Committee is constrained to express its concern over the financial performance of BRL and observes that   unless and 
until the revival package for BRL is implemented  successfully financial performance would not improve. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that BRL  management would  make all out   efforts to implement the revival package  without time over-run.
( Para : 6.4)
Problems being faced by Refectories industry

            The Committee is of the view that, since 75 per cent of  the  total refractories produced in the country   are consumed by steel
industries and steel industry is  demanding  superior grade of refractories, the Ministry of steel should facilitate the refractories
industry in general and BRL in particular to     undertake adequate  research work for  production of such superior grade of 
refractories which  suits the requirement of  steel industry.  The Committee   recommends that research work in  refractories  industry
may take into  consideration  the requirement of steel industry which inter-alia  include reduction in fuel  consumption, incurred
furnace  capacity, incurred furnace   life and availability  and improved product quality.
( Para : 7.2)
            The Committee observes that  technological  improvement in steel making has  not only led to the  increasing demand   of
superior quality refractories  and reduction in total consumption  of refractories but generated  a price war situation   and unfair trade 
price due to excessive competition  among refractories producers.  The  Committee is of the view that improvement  in steel making 
technology is a welcome and necessary   development for betterment   of steel industry while  reduction in total consumption of
refractories is an unavoidable development and it may be hoped that  with the sign of recovery in steel industry the demand of
refractories would increase.  So far as the situation of price was due to  excessive competition   is concerned, the  Committee 
recommends that the Ministry  of Steel should take up the matter  to ensure that  healthy  competition should prevail in the
Refractories Industry  and competition should not result  into unfair trade   prices.  The price of the  refractories product be  allowed
to be determined  by the free market  forces  of demand and  supply.
 ( Para : 7.5)
            The Committee understands the problems  being faced by refractories industry  arising due to imbalance between
manufacturing  cost and selling price.  The Committee observes that the price of the finished  products has been  drastically reduced
(ranging from  30 to 44 per cent ) whereas there is a  trend in increase in  the price structure of input materials ( ranging from 5 to 17
per cent ).  This is the  double loss  to the refractory  industry  and under the   said  circumstances any  industry is bound to  be
affected.  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that refractories industry in general and BRL  management   in particular should 
chalk out a two pronged strategy  i.e. one  to arrest  the  fall in the selling price of refractories and   to reverse the trend  and other
strategy is required to  minimise the cost of production so that  the `margin of profit' for refractories industry may increase.  The
Committee further recommends   that   the Ministry of Steel should act as a facilitator and guide the BRL management to undertake
measures for maximisation of profit.
(Para: 7.9)
The Committee hopes that with the rationalisation of manpower labour cost in BRL would come down and would
become competitive vis-a-vis units in private s
(Para: 7.10.2)
 
Work Order Position
 
The Committee recommends that the BRL management should continue  with the production of  value added item  and may  also
undertake measures for product- mix  or for diversification of products as required  by  SAIL , RINL  and other modern steel plants.
(Para: 8.2)
 
            The Committee recommends that BRL management may make inroads  in the steel units in private sector i.e. Jindal, TISCO,
Llyods, Essar, etc. for selling the  refractories product.
(Para: 8.3)
The Committee appreciates the  initiatives  taken by the  Secretary, Ministry  of Steel for procurement of work-order for BRL.  The
Committee   hopes that the Ministry of Steel  would  continue to   assist/help  BRL management in the  procurement   of work
orders.  The Committee   desires that the   Ministry of Steel  , in  its  Action Taken Note on  the present report, would furnish the
details of steps taken in this regard.   In the form of actual volume of work-order procured for BRL.
 (Para: 8.6)
Position of inventories.
            It is but natural that a company which lacks sufficient working capital and there is a low demand of its   products,  would have
little   inventories, and Bharat Refractories Ltd. is no  exception to this rule,  the Committee observes.  However, the Committee feels
that   the BRL management should keep a constant   watch on the inventories and dispose of the    inventory as and when the same
accumulates because even small   inventory, since the volume of production   is confined to the availability of capital and market
demand, would further block the scarce resources of working capital and thereby creating a  `Vicious - circle'  of insufficient
working  capital, low production and no inventories .  Sufficient working, high volume of production and low inventory should be the
motto of the company.
(Para :9.2)
            Justification for requirements of funds
New schemes
The   Committee is of the considered view that setting up  of  Continuous Casting  System (RCC)  is long  overdue .The   Standing 
Committee on Industry has  recommended   in its earlier reports for setting up of refractories for  Continuous   Casting  System at the

earliest for ensured survival of the company.  The RCC has got the merit of positive  feasibility report as prepared by M/s  MECON
and the technical know-how as obtained from M/s  Shinagow Refractories  Ltd.,  Japan.  The   technological changes in steel  making
process leaves little scope for demand of conventional refractories and  opens the  avenues    for refractories  for Continuous Casting
System.  All   these factors   necessitate    the setting up of RCC, sooner the better, since  original   estimated cost  i.e. Rs.23 crore
has  already overrun  to the tune of Rs.38.00 crore .  The only   deterring  factor  earlier was the lack of fund for the project as BRL
was  not in a position to generate  sufficient internal   resources to meet the cost of the project.    However, this  problem seems to be
solved  as  M/s Monnet  Ispat Ltd. has offered the  proposal to become a  joint venture partner with BRL  with the  equity  ratio of  60
: 40 and , not only that , BRL's  equity of 40 per cent  would be  adjusted by  the cost of land and technology transfer cost alongwith 
Government fund from plan loan during the 10
th Five Year Plan.  Would the Ministry of Steel further   allow the  time and cost 
overrun  on the project and  leaving the BRL to  dither  to a point of no return?  The Committee raises the query to be solved   by the
Ministry of Steel in its Action Taken Note of the present  Report.  The Committee is  , otherwise ,  of the view  that  the  having been
given the latest revival package  for BRL, setting up of RCC should not be  delayed further.
 ( Para : 10.2.5)
Additions, Modifications & Replacements (AMR)
 
The Committee is of the opinion that modification replacement in existing machineries and addition of new equipment is    
essential    to keep the production process going smoothly   and   effectively.  The Committee feels that since BRL is continuously
making loss and   is not in a position to generate internal revenue, therefore, it is   but natural   that budgetary support   from the
Government is required to carry on the AMR schemes.  The Committee hopes that once BRL is put on the revival track and start
making profit, it would not require budgetary support, any longer.
 (Para : 10.3.3)
 SWOT (Strength, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threat) analysis of BRL
 
The Committee is of the view that BRL   management should keep on reviewing  the SWOT-analysis of the company.  The
Committee further recommends that BRL  management  should take  advantage of its strength  and  avail all opportunities  which 
come its way .  The Committee hopes that with the sanction of revival package by the Government   BRL would  be able to 
overcome  most  of its weaknesses i.e. surplus manpower and  obsolete  technology and non-availability of  working capital etc.  The
Committee   further   hopes that once  the revival package is implemented, properly and in time,  the Company would be able  to
combat all the threats.  As regards the  irregular supply of power by Jharkhand  State  Electricity Board,   the Committee recommends
that the  Ministry of Steel  assist the  BRL management  in taking up the matter with the state government.
(Para: 11.2)
Management By Objectives  ( MBO )
The Committee is happy to note that BRL management is guided by the principle of management by objectives in   letter and
spirit.  The Committee, however, recommends that BRL management should re-orient its objectives as per changing industrial
scenario and make its efforts to achieve the corporate objectives and mission.  The Committee further recommends   that BRL
management may chalk out `Key Areas for Intensive Action' for better performance of the company.
 (Para: 12.3)
Tax Structure
The Committee is pleased to note that Government is giving due consideration to the matter of rationalised tax structure, in
its Annual General Budget.  In General Budget 2001-02 as well as 2002-03 some tax concession have been   given to refractory
industries.   However, the Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry of Steel should keep on studying tax-structure suitable for
refractories Industry and accordingly approaches the Ministry of Finance for suitable action.
 (Para: 13.3)
Foreign collaboration
The Committee is of the view   that the transfer of technical know-how (technology) and its absorption/adaptation in the
system is   vital for carrying out production activities   in the cost effective manner and products of quality production.  In this
context, the Committee is happy to note that BRL   has entered into   collaboration for technical know-how with Central Glass &
Ceramic Research Institute, Kolkata, SAIL, Kawasaki, Refractories   Company, Japan, Singapore Refractory Co., and Plibrico.
Franch and Technology taken from this organisation have effectively been adopted in BRL.  However, the Committee desires that
impact of the `transfer of technology & its absorption in BRL must be reflected in the improved physical and financial performance
of BRL.
 (Para: 14.3)
Manpower in BRL and  VRS
            The Committee opines that proper human resource management is key to the success of any company.  The first step   in this
regard is optimisation of manpower i.e. a rational labour order, besides appropriation of  `right man at right place in right time’.  In
this regard the Committee   appreciates the recommendation of viability study as conducted by MECON Ltd. for right sizsing  of
manpower in BRL.  The Committee hopes that BRL would feel no paucity of fund, keeping in view the fact that the revival proposal

The Committee hopes that with the approval of the latest revival package for BRL, the BRL management would leave no

REPORT

Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL) commonly known as Visakhapatnam Steel
Plant (VSP), is the first shore-based integrated Steel Plant set up in India at a distance from
the major raw material sources, viz. metallurgical coal and iron ore . Being shore-based it
has the advantage of easier import of input materials like coking coal, lime-stone ete., and
casier export of finished products. The location is also expected to help industrialistion of
the region. VSP has been set up with several latest technologies for the first time in the
country, such as 100 percent continuous casting of liquid steel, dry quenching of coke
with auxiliary power gencration facilities, 100 percent Cast House Slag Granulation in
Blast Furnace and Torpedo Ladle for transporting liquid hot metal.

2.0 RINL INDEPENDENT FROM SAIL

21 RINL was originally conceived as a unit of Steel Authority of India (SAIL) to
augment its long product capacity and service its southem market, The facility was envisaged
with sourcing of raw material from National Mineral Development Corporation ( NMDC),
which was also a part of SAIL at that time, and a jetty was also envisaged for its imports and
exports. The announcement of VSP as part of SAIL was done in April 1970, the foundation
stone was laid in January,1971, the Indo-Soviet agreement was concluded in June, 1979 and
the revised DPR was prepared in 1980. In 1982, Government of India decided to carve a
separate holding company for VSP, and RINL was formed as a separate PSU under Ministry
of Steel in February ,1982.

2:2 RINL has been operating as a separate PSU primarily for the following reasons :

i to have healthy competition with the public sector
ii to improve efficiency of its operations in a competitive eavironment
iii to be accountable for its own financial performance, ete.

23 The Committee notes the contention of RINL management that RIN has been
Operating as a separate and independent PSU (independent of SAIL) for imbibing
competitive resilience in plant, injecting operational efficiency and having the benefits of
being accountable for its own financial performance.

24 The Committee, however, recommends that the Government may like to examine and
explore the possibility of merger of SAIL and RINL and take concrete step in this regard, if
the move consolidates long stcel making capacity in the country.

2.5 In the Committee's meeting held on 4% April 2002 (on Demands -for Grants 2002-

11.0 RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT

11.1. Research & Development plays a vital role in VSP, both for reducing the production
costs as well as for in developing new products. Some of the measures taken up to reduce the
cost are given below :

(i) Usage of nut coke and BF coke in Blast furnace

(ii) Usage of LD slag and metallurgical waste at Sinter Plant

(iii) Usage of Coke Dust as partial replacement of coke breeze at sinter plant

(iv) Usage of used silica bricks to replace quartzite lump at Blast Furnace

(v) Recycling of pitch at Coke ovens

(vi) Manufacture of Gas/air recuperators of reheating furnaces at engineering shops

11.2 With the use of developed 4-hole 17.5 degree lance the lining life of converter
increased to 1601 heats in one campaign and subsequently to more than 2000 heats. A
thermo chemical model of heat balance was developed for feed back monitoring of various
parameters with an aim to reduce coke rate in Blast furnace through optimization of these



parameters. The coke rate of 524 kg/thm in the 2001-02 is lowest so far. Based on the process
development specific consumption of hot metal was reduced during capital repair of Blast
Furnace-II_All these measures led to a saving of Rs.186 crore for the year 2001-02 helping the
company to improve its financial performance process parameters were developed and special
steel are being produced on regular basis. During 2001-02, thirteen new grades, two new
sections and seven new products were developed to enhance the product mix of RINL.

11.3 The Committee is pleased to note that R&D projects have been successfully
undertaken by RINL, in reducing the cost of production and developing new products. the

16.0 MARKETING POLICY

16.1. Arising out of financial crisis of South East Asia and dumping of steel from
Russia and China in the second half of 1997, the steel market was Seriously affected
all over the world and the prices started falling, and the effect was felt in India also.
Steel availability was more than the supply backed by the threat of imported steel.
Cut-throat competition started getting into Indian market even among the main
producers. With the result, RINL market share was on a continuous down slide and
the immediate task was to address the important issues and formulate a marketing
strategy. The first and foremost is to bring in four main producers of long products
viz., TISCO, 1800, SAIL and RINL together so that cut-throat competition amongst
them can be avoided.

16,2 The other issues which immediately needed attention are:

(1) Strengthening of the marketing set up

(0). Strategies to increase the market share

(ii) Closer and continuous interaction with customers

(iv) Motivate the marketing field officers to the tacks ahead.
(v) Review of decision making

(vi) Empowering the field officers.

functioning of marketing  Re-deploying capable officers from other departments

decisions were taken in a participative forum. The Practical difficulties, shortcomings and
infirmities of the system were Periodically discussed and modifications/changes, if any, were

survive and others were destined to wither away.

20.2 Furthermore, with the South East Asian crisis, Soviet disintegration and increased
dumping of steel by China/CIS countries at cheaper rates had affected the domestic as well as
intemational markets and all major producers were compelled to reduce their production
volumes and steel prices, Added to it, the plight of the long product producers like RINL in

ship breaking industry on one hand and Tecessionary trends all over the world on the other.

23.6 In the meeting of the Sub-Commuttee held on 12" September, 2001 on the subject of
“Key Concern Areas of Steel Industries and promotion of steel consumption in various sectors
of economy ", the issue of inflated freight charge was discussed in detailed. Participating in
discussion Shn R.N. Malhotra, Chairman, Railway Board expressed his views 1-

"On the ‘questions of concessions, I would like to say that we are prepared to
consider any request from any manufacturer for certain concessions which will help them and
Which in tum would help the Railways But Sir, by reducing our revenue, we can not help
anyone, If they are prepared to give us an undertaking that if we reduce the freight on the
KK Line by a certain percentage, they will be able to give us so much of extra traffic, we can

23.7. Interjecting in the discussion, the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed his opinion
in following words:-

+ the question that has been raised with regard to the KK Line related to movement of
iron ore from Bailadilla, which is used by the Vizag Steel Plant. It has a very long history.
It is not really a question of incremental traffic. The operative issue here is that 65 per cent
additional freight charge was put at a certain point of time because that line was specifically
created for the movement of iron ore from point A to point B, with an understanding that if
the level of freight crossed six million tonnes, this additionality would be removed. The
situation today is that, as against the 65 per cent enhanced rate that was being charged, the
current enhanced rate is 30 per cent, and the traffic generated on that line, today, s 12 tonnes.
We can not have a persistent kind of an incremental situation going on. We understand that at
a point of time, the line was constructed for captive use, and additional charges were levied in
order to make it viable for the Railways. Once a certain threshold of traffic generation has
been achieved, the incremental rate should not apply. That was the original understanding.
One cannot have a situation wherein because there ts an incremental rate, in order to reduce
it, you must have incremental traffic. The fact that rate was brought down from 65 per cent
to 35 per cent and now to 30 per centis, itself, a recognition of the understanding on which

v7



this 65 per cent was charged. Now, as _] that understanding, that additionality factor
should now go. This is the issue that has to be examined.

23.8 Responding to the argument of Secretary, the Chairman, Railway Board, added :-

" The Additionality which was charged earlier was for several reasons. The first
reason was that because it was a hilly area, with sharp edges and curves, the construction cost
of rails was very high. The second reason was that we had put surcharge on movement of
any traffic on that line because of the fact that in place of one locomotive, which is normally
required on a plain terrain, we had to put three locomotive in place . So, the cost of operation
also was very high. Also, the electricity bill for the operational of this line is five times
higher than what it would cost in the case of a line on the plain. Now, how do we recover
that cost? We cannot go on reducing our revenue, unless there is a commitment on the part
of the steel plants that they will be able to sell so much of extra stee! and thus give us that
much of extra traffic.”

23.9 The Secretary, Ministry of Steel further added :-

" The K.K. Line is an issue where there is difference in Perception between the
Railway Board and the Steel Ministry . It will be useful to have a re-look and see whether
there is any justification for reducing this further additionality, In fact, quite recently, the
NMDC, which is a profit-making PSU under this Ministry, had offered to take over the line
on a captive basis and bear the cost, because they are of the view that the cost additionality
that is being charged, is unjustified Unfortunately, that was not acceptable to the Railways.
But the basic issue is that the movement of freight is the business of the Ministry of Railways
and not of the NMDC or the Steel Industry. 1 feel that this matter has to be dealt with in an
impartial manner. It may be useful to get the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, the NMDC and the
Railways to jointly look at this issue and, in fact give a joint working paper on this.”

27.0 MAKING ANTI-DUMPING MECHANISM MORE EFFECTIVE

27.1 The anti-dumping mechanism is to be more effective to protect the Indian Steel
industry. As soon as the anti-dumping allegation arises, the required assessment of injury to
domestic industry is to be ascertained within the shortest possible time so that the industry is
protected against the onslaught of dumped material. The present mechanism takes longer time
to ascertain the injury to domestic industry thereby depriving the remedial action to be taken,

27.2 The Commnuttee understands that dumping of defective and secondary steel is
unflinching damage to the domestic steel industry, Western countries are quick to protect
their domestic steel industry by adopting various anti-dumping measures. The Commuttee,
although , appreciate the role of the Ministry of Steel, in Protecting the domestic industry
from the onslaught of dumping of steel, however it recommends that the Ministry of Steel
may explore the possibility of reducing the time in ascertaining the assessment of injury to
domestic industry, in case of dumping of steel takes place.

28.0 FUTURE OUTLOOK OF INDIAN STEEL INDUSTRY VIS-A-VIS
EMERGING GLOBAL STEEL SCENARIO.

28.1. While the West was restructuring steel industry by trimming their capacity to demand
forecast, East was growing by leaps and bounds and India also was looking towards the
Eastern pattern of growth. During the late 1970's Indian expectation was to achieve by 2000
AD, a steel making capacity of around 100 Mt, it was adjusted to 50 Mt in the 1980's and
Subsequently re-adjusted again to 37 Mt in. the early 90's, The current projections remain at
around 49 Mt by 2006.

28.2 This situation is alarming for a country of our size and population where the steel
consumption is not even 30 Kg/Capita/year against the consumption of over 400
Kg/Capita/year in the developed countries. If we apply the similar thinking of China as in the
late 1970's and 1980's and try to catch up with the world standard of living, then India should
have looked for a consumption of at least 100 Mt of steel per year, This level of consumption
for a country of 100 crore population will mean consumption level of only 100
Ky/Capita/year against the world average of 141 Kg/capita/year, and even the China’s
consumption level of over 100 Kg/capita/year. The surplus availability of steel at the present
level of consumption indicates a serious weakness in the Indian economy which needs to be
addressed immediately if the future development of the country is to be kept in mind,

28.3 Though the efforts on infrastructure development gave some breathing space for steel
industry, the exports have started falling down due to increased competition and lower prices,
With the result that steel makers have to look at the domestic market to find ways and means
to improve the demand. The export prices which were at one time giving good margins are
now at a level where the producers are able to meet only the production costs. Thus it can be
seen that Indian Stee! is currently going through a tough time and its ambitious growth plans

21



to some extent have Tun aground. Only the measures to revitalize it and | Prices over the
next few years with adequate protection can solve the problems of this industry.

28.4. The Committee is glad to observe the current improvement in domestic and global
Scenario and, at the same time, it hopes that RINL management would make every effort
for capitalising on the favourable conditions. Efforts for increasing the consumption of Steel
in various sectors of economy should be intensified at both the micro and macro level

Durgapur Steel Plant (DSP), an Integrated Steel Plant of Steel Authority of India Limited
(SAIL), with an initial capacity of 1 million. tonnes of ingots per annum was. set up a the
Consortium of British firms, namely Indian Steel Works Construction Company Ltd (ISCON).
The Contract was signed on October 31,1956 and the plant was commissioned in phases between
1959 and 1962. The plant launched its expansion programme during the Third Plan period for
increasing its ingot capacity to 1.6 MTPA. The various units under expansion were
commissioned by 1969. Salient areas of activities of DSP in terms of production are Base
blending of ores of RMPHP; Coke and sinter for Blast Furnaces; Hot Metal for steel making
shop; Crude steel for long and flat products and Railway items. With the completion of the.
modernization programme, DSP is in possession of state-of-the-art technology for quality steel
making Stabilization of the modernized units has brought about improved productivity,
substantial improvement in energy consumption and better quality products. With the successful
commissioning of the modernized units, DSP is all set to produce 2.088 million tonnes of hot
metal, 1.876-million tonnes of liquid steel and 1.586 million tonnes of saleable steel annually as
per the diversified products-mix .

6.0 TIME OVER-RUN & REASONS

6.1 The Sub-Committee was informed that the commissioning of various packages started
‘progressively as early as Nov’91. Wheel & Axle Plant Commissioned in September, 1992,
Continuous Casting Plant in August, 1994 and BOF in December, 1994 and 2™ (last) Blast
Furnace in April, 1996. The modernization process was completed in March, 1998 with an
overall delay of 60 months.

Reasons for Delay

(i) Disintegration of erstwhile USSR which resulted in delays in supply of imported
structurals, equipment, refractories etc. from TPE, Russia and affected BF, BOF, SP

& RMHC packages.

(ii) Delays in equipment and structurals supply by indigenous suppliers affected most of
the packages.

(iii) Increase in quantity of work in respect of civil & structurals job for BF, SP and
RMHC packages as compared to original estimates of the consortium resulted in
extra time for execution.

(iv) Inadequate mobilization of resources at site work by contracting agencies resulted in
slow pace of work as compared to targets.

(v). Funds constraint of contracting agencies and intra-consortiuin disputes resulted in
slow progress in major global packages.

6.1 The DSP management stated that prior to disintegration of the erstwhile USSR, all the
economic activities in CIS Nations were controlled from Moscow and the manufacturing units
and transporting authorities had to adhere to the delivery schedules and commitments.
Subsequent to the break-up of USSR into different Nations, these manufacturing units were being
controlled by different authorities and a number of new regulations were introduced. This
resulted in delay in manufacturing activities. Tyazhpromexport (TPE)’s job has suffered


seriously, resulting in delays in supply of imported.equipment, structures and refractories from
Russia for four global packages viz, Blast Furnace, Sinter Plant, Basic Oxygen Furnaces and Raw
Material Handling Complex.

6.3 As regards the Under-Estimation by Contracting Agencies, it was stated that the increase
in volume of work, due to under-estimation by package contractors, resulted in increase in time of
execution and also caused funds constraints with consortium members leading to serious intra-
consortium problems, which took time to resolve. There is an overall increase in quantities of
work ranging from. 24 per cent to 71 per cent for various activities. The maximum increase in

volume of work was in Blast Furnace. package wherein, original estimates were based on हे

realizing maces. During — negotiations, _Mannesmann. Demag. Huttentechnik - (MDH)/
Tyazhpromexport (TPE) offered reconstruction of the furnaces resulting in substantial increase in
volume of civil and structural work over those envisaged earlier. ip
6.4 It was further added that cash constraints with the contracting agencies like HSCL, Birla
Technical Services (BTS), Dodsal, Engineering Projects (India) Ltd. (EPI), etc. was one of the
major reasons which affected the execution of work, ‘The main reasons for higher requirement of
funds by consortium members had increased volume of work.and procurement of indigenous
equipment in some cases instead of imported ones as envisaged etc.

6.5 Delay due to Indian Contracting Agencies was caused as the indigenqus agencies like
HSCL, BTS, Dodsal, EPI, etc. were slow in mobilization of resources. There were delays in
erection of structurals and equipment by HSCL. Delays took place in equipment supplies and
erection by BTS in the Raw Materials Handling Complex (RMHC), Sinter Plant (SP), Blast
Furnaces (BF) and Basic Oxygen Furnaces (BOF) packages.

6.6 Delays in Completion of Design Engineering resulted in’ delayed supply of equipment,
structures and refractories, both imported and indigenous. The maximum impact of this was on

the RMHC.

6.7 Lack of intra- consortium co-ordination led to disputes regarding scope of work and
commercial matters, leading to delay and calling for frequent intervention by SAIL/DSP.

6.8 The Committee feels that there may be a variety of reasons for time over run in the
, implementation of modernisation projects. Some of the reasons might be beyond the control of
management, but the fact remains that lack of management by objective also contributed to time
over-run. The Committee feels that the then management failed to act promptly in right
direction. There was a definite lacunae in managerial supervision and direction, the Committee

feels

estimate of DSP modernization works out to Rs.5074.71 crore (FE: 1375.42 crore) on base date
of 2" quater 99. As per Government’s approval, the project was to be completed by March 93.

The modernization has been completed in March 98 with an overall delay of 60 months.
(Para 7.4)

The Committee notes that Reasons for cost over-run are mainly due to increase in volume
of work, inclusion of new items, price escalation, exchange rate variation, increase in duties &

taxes and increased in interest payments due to change in mode of financing.
(Para 7.5)

AN ENQUIRY COMMITTEE

The Committee feels that the- examination of Report ( of the enquiry Committee headed
by Shri 7.5. Baijal, former Secretary, Planning Commission ) on enquiry into the delay aspects
of implementation of DSP and RSP modernisation projects of SAIL is since long pending in
the Ministry of Steel, and it, itself, is suffering from time over run. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Steel should expedite the process of examining the said Report
and furnish, in the Action Taken Note of the present report, the detailed of the Enquiry
Committee and the penal action taken against the authority/officials upon whom the
responsibility has in fixed. é

(Para 8.2 )

PERFORMANCE OF PLANT

The Committee notes that the DSP , in post- modernisation phase , is performing at near
tated capacity levels. Moreover, production beyond capacity level has been achieved in Blast
Furnace No.4 (102 per cent), Continuous Casting Plant (108 per cent) and Merchant Mill (101.4
per cent) during 2000-01.

(Para 9.4)

From the above it is evident that the basic objectives of modernization are being
progressively achieved with respect to integrated operation. There has been improvement in
product quality with introduction of _ continuous casting, which is operating above capacity.
In addition, the plant has been able.to produce higher quality products like TMT bars, special

quality semis and loco wheels.
(Para 9.5)

28

(Para 6.8)

|



FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF DSP seit

The Committee is of the opinion that during the modernization of DSP new technologies
were introduced in the primary areas. Hot metal and crude steel productions have been stabilized
qualitatively and as well as quantitatively, which is giving financial benefits. The modernization

of DSP has yielded satisfactory results.
(Para 10.5)

FURTHER MODERNISATION AND = RESTRUCTURING FOR TECHNOLOGY
UPGRADATION

The Committee recommends that the DSP management would push ahead ,without delay
, the issue of . further technology upgradation in DSP’in regard to Bloom Caster with ladle
furnace, New Finishing Mill, Introduction of coal and dust injection and Introduction of SGP for
BF-2 for revenue géneration and improvement in environment. The Committee hopes that SAIL
and the Ministry of Steel would extend its helping hand to DSP.
, (Para 11.3)

CONVERSION OF CC BILLETS INTO FINISHED PRODUCTS .

The Committee understands that almost 55 per cent of DSP production comprises of
semis, which are low contributory items and fetches lower realization. This product mix of
DSP is unfavourable and is affecting the profitability of DSP. The Committee recommends that
DSP management should: chalk out necessary course of plan for. converting CC Billets into
finished products through conversion agents. The Committee hopes that SAIL would lend its
helping hand to DSP management in chalking out the plan and proposing the same to the
Ministry, of Steel , as the same would help DSP in improving its physical and financial

performance .
(Para 12.2)

REQUIREMENT OF FUNDS

The Committee is of the opinion that modification replacement in existing machineries
and addition of new equipment is essential to keep the production process going on
smoothly and effectively. The Committee feels that since DSP is , continuously , making loss
and. is not in a position to generate internal revenue , therefore, itis. but natural that budgetary
support . from the Government. is required to carry on the AMR schemes. The Committee
hopes that once DSP is put on the revival track and start making net profit, it would not require

budgetary support, any longer.
(Para 13.3.5)

The Committee further recommends that DSP management would take every effort to
complete AMR scheme without time and cost over-run.

(Para 13.3.6)
SWOT ANALYSIS (STRENGTH, WEAKNESS, OPPORTUNITIES AND THREATS)
The Committee desired that DSP management should make an allout efforts | to

capitalise its strength and should avail all the opportunities knocking at its door at the first
instance. The Committee is of the view that since modernisation process has injected sufficient

29


resilience in the working and operation system. of DSP, DSP management should chalk out
concrete steps to combat all weaknesses that come on way to the company's better physical and
financial performance . The Committee further hopes that the DSP management would analyse

threats to DSP and would take timely step to remove the threats.
के (Para 14.2)

* The Committee is of the opinion that since DSP has acquired the State - of the - Art
Technology, including the benefits of high degree of computerisation and automation, the DSP
would be able to improve its working and performace, thereby, marching ahead towards

achieving the goal of a profit making plant.
(Para 14.3)

The Committee, while appreciating the steps taken by DSP management for reducing
the cost of production, feels that DSP management may capitalise the introduction of CDI in
the modernised Blast Furnace for further reduction in input cost of coal. The Committee is
hopeful that DSP management, taking advantage of modernised steel. making route in DSP,
would go for product - mix arid diversification be it special quality of billets or conversion of

‘CC billets into finished products through conversion agents.
(Para 14.4)

The Committee recommends that DSP management in tandem with SAIL and the
Ministry of steel should chalk out ‘Areas for further modernisation ' for improving the
performance of the company , further DSP management in its estimation for examining the
need for further modernisation would take care of adequate finishing facility for favourable

products mix and replacement of energy consuming ingot route.
(Para 14.5)

The Committee hopes that with the recent sign in improvement in the steel market and
price hike, DSP would be ina better position to compete in the market.
(Para 14.6)

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS

The Committee understands the importance of R&D project in removing the. technical
problems in steel plants. The Committee is happy to note that R&D projects in DSP has helped
in improving productivity, developing product-mix and reduction in the cost of production and
energy consumption. The Committeesrecommends that DSP management should have

appropriate sufficient fund for R&D projects,
(Para 15.2)

SURPLUS MANPOWER

The Committee is of the view that ore of the key element of Human Resources
Planning is the determination of right,size of manpower. Surplus manpower only adds to the
cost of production, therefore, optimum manpower strength in a company is the first and. foremost
concern of anenterprise. The Committee is pleased to note that DSP management has chalked
out a proper Human Resource Programme, whereby, it has been decided to optimise its
manpower from existing strength of 20,431 10 14,456 by 31% March, 2003. The Committee
recommends that DSP management: should carry. out the programme of right sizing: of
manpewer within stipulated time and-approach the Government for financial assistance for

reducing the manpower .
(Para 16.4)

30



MARKETING STRATEGY OF DSP

The Committee is pleased to note that the present demand for DSP's product is

satisfactory.
(Para 17.2)

The Committee, while noting the elements of DSP's marketing strategy, recommends
that DSP management should undertake an all-out efforts for actual implementation of the
strategy: envisaged. Then and only then, DSP would be able to enhance its market share.

(Para 17.4)

While the Committee is pleased to note that DSP management has taken steps for
aggressive marketing of DSP's products; the Committee feels that the steps so taken must
have: a bearing on the financial performance of the plant, otherwise, measures so envisaged will
‘remain an-expression on paper.
(Para 17.7)
The Committee understands that CMO, with Head Quarters at Kolkata, has elaborate
structural ‘arrangement for marketing SAIL's product but CMO would lose its relevance
unless its role is recognised and felt in improving the marketing share of SAIL's plant, here at,
DSP. The Committee feels that, CMO's Head Quarter being in Kolkata , it can play pivotal

role in promoting DSP's products.
(Para 17.9)

WORK -ORDER FROM RAILWAYS

The Committee feels that there should be close coordination and mutual co-operation
between railways and DSP management since DSP was conceived to cater the needs of
Railways. The Committee is surprises to observe that when there was already a plant (DSP)
to cater the needs of Railway, Government went for another plant ( Wheel and Axles
Plant) in Bangalore to produce the products which DSP was already producing . Now, Railway
is finding it difficult to distribute placement of orders between DSP and WAP. The Committee
finds it an error of judgement in setting up of WAP, when there was already DSP _ to cater the
needs of Railways. This is glaring example of improper planning and lack of foresightedness
on’ decision on investment at apex level 1.6 Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA).
Not only this, huge amount of money was spent on modernisation, restructuring and expansion
programme of DSP. The question arises why a decision for investment on modernisation of DSP
was made when the Railways had to set up WAP? Can not the Government department have

an integrated and co-ordinated planning? . The Committee wonders.
(Para 18.10)

In a situation, when modernisation of DSP and setting up. of WAP has now become a
reality, the Committee feels that an equitable and balanced view of whole thing should be taken
into consideration while placing orders to DSP and WAP. In this regard, care should be taken ,
that ,the principle of equity and justice is applied for the survival and sustenance of both DSP
and WAP. Railways should ensure that DSP gets orders and runs the mill properly.

(Para 18.11)

wo
a


The Committee recommends that Railwayssheuld‘streamline its demand projects, and
place orders to DSP and WAP in equitable manner in a placed way. That is so, because , steel
plant cannot switch off and on, frequently, otherwise, it would collapse. It would be in the
fitness of things, if SAIL, on behalf of DSP, and Railways enter into "a long term agreement"
and sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for planned placement of order and supply".
The Committee hopes that Railways would give due consideration. to the question of survival of

DSP while distributing orders to 987 भाव WAP.
(Para 18.12)

COST REDUCTION- MEASURES

The Committee is happy to note that substantial improvement has taken place in aimost
all the operating parameters. These improvements are also reflected in reduction cost of
production by more than six percent in last five years in spite of substantial input cost escalation
in almost all the major inputs like indigenous coal, imported coal, exchange rate, power rate,
salary & wages etc. The Committee is pleased to know that DSP has made cash profit of Rs.58
crore during 2000-01 after a gap of six years, The trend continues during the current year also as
it has made a cash profit of Rs.17 crore during April-December, 01. There is continuous reduction
in the loss incurred by plant after completion of modernization schemes. In the current nine
months also there is reduction in net loss by about 35 per cent as compared to corresponding

period of last year.
(Para 19.6)

EEL PRODUCTS: (AS ON 30-06-2001)

INVENTORIES OF SALEABLE

The Committee, while taking note of accumulation of saleable steel. products 10 the
tune of Rs.13800 tonnes at stocks yard and ~ 27500 tonnes at plant as a 307 June, 2001,
recommends that’ DSP management would~ undertake adequate measures to dispose of-the

inventories so that DSP may add to the profit.
(Para 20.3)

DSP MANAGEMENT GUIDED BY MANAGEMENT BY OBJECTIVES

The Committee is pleased to note that DSP's production:and other related activities
such as R&D projects, capital repairs, raw-material procurement are being carried out as per
internal improvement targets and annual performance plan (APP) as -envisaged in
memorandum of understanding signed between DSP and SAIL on the one hand and SAIL and

Ministry of Steel as the other.
(Para 21.2)

The Committee hopes that DSP management, while striving to active the objectives as
set in MOU signed between DSP and SAIL and SAIL and Ministry of Steel, would ~ensure
that all the targets as set in MOU are being achieved in time. The Committee further expects
that SAIL and the Ministry of Steel would have a regular monitoring on the management of
DSP's activities for better performance of thé plant. MOU system must act as a catalyst to the

improved physical and financial performance of the company.
(Para 21.23 )

require more allocation for their modernisation bu_!..-.SAIL is concentrating more on the major 
plants whereas the subsidiaries _..are dying. The Committee, therefore, recommends that SAIL

While explaining the causes for decline in the production the Performance Budget states:­
"Delay in reconstruction of BF2 under the modernisation scheme by M/s. Tiazpromex­
port Jed consortium due to political disturbances in erstwhile USSR prolonged testing time 
due to subsequent indigenisation of supplies and mishap in BF1 have severely affected the 
production at Durgapur. Low coking coal stocks all through the year leading to frequent 
blend changes and high and widely fluctuating ash indigenous coking coal affected the 
productivity at the blast furnaces. Inconsistent and restricted power supply from the grid, 
particularly from DVC to Bokaro resulted in a severe Joss of production. The major 
disruption in power supply from DVC to Bokaro on 16th September caused considerable 
damage to equipment and its impact continued for nearly a month. Rourkela operations 
suffered a set back due to flooding resulting from unprecedented heavy rains on 14th 
August, 1993. 
However, the production of saleable steel will be as per target." 
The Committee is not convinced that delay in reconstruction of BF2 under the modernisation 
scheme at Durgapur due to political changes in erstwhile USSR was the cause for lower 
production at the plant. After all the political changes in erstwhile USSR had not occurred all of 
a sudden. There were indications that the erstwhile USSR may undergo political changes. The 
SAIL and Government should have prepared alternative plan to meet the eventuality but they 
opted to remain static to the happening in erstwhile USSR without bothering for its impact on 
the production of steel in the plant. 
The committee is surprised to find that low coking coal stocks throughout the year and ash 
contents of the indigenous coking coal also affected the productivity of blast furnaces. It is a 
matter of regret that SAIL which is largest producers of steel not only in the country but also in 
the World did not maintain enougl'l coking coal stocks at its major plants and also could not 
distinguish the ash contents of coal supplied to its plants indigenously. 
Similarly, a strange reason has been given for the less production in Rourkela. It is stated 
that Rourkela operations suffered a set back due to flooding resulting from unprecedented heavy 
rains on 14th August, 1993. The Committee is not convinced with this alibi of SAIL that such a 
prestigious plant which once had the state-of -the-art technology in the field of LD process could 
not withstand a downpour and submerged in the flood waters. 
The Committee, therefore, recommem,Is that SAIL should instil a sense of work culture in its 
plants so that production targets are achieved through concerted e~forts ratl)er than blaming 
natura) calamity and other causes for its decline in production. Of course, inconsistent and 
restricted power supply from the grid; particularly from DVC to Bokaro might have resulted in a 
severe loss of production but the performance budget is silent about the steps taken by SAIL to 
overcome this situation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that matter be taken up with the 
Ministry of Power on priority for the release of enough power for the steel plants in the country or 
as an alternative possibility of private participation for generating power exclusively for steel plants 
may also be explored by the Government.

5.07 Impact of Excise Duty:-Th e Committee finds that in the current Budg et excise duty on 
all iron and steel items has been increased both in non flat as well as flat produc ts. Tn re~pect of 
flat products excise duty has been increased from 11.5% to 12.5% ad valorem . This has furthe r 
aggravated the burden of excise duty component on flat products particularl y i.n the case of 
stainless steel items. Excise duty on semis and long products has been increased from Rs . 920 per 
tonne to Rs. 1000 per tonne. The duty on pig iron and sponge iron has been increased from

5.08 Steel Development Fund (SDF):- The SDF was set up in the year 1978 because it was 
felt that prope r atten tion had not been given to consistent modernisation of steel plants in the 
past leading to lower productivity and higher cost of production of steel. It was essencial to 
provide adequ ate resou rces for rehabilitation and replacement of machinery. As one of the 
methods for findi ng these resources and lessening the dependence on budgetary supp ort SDF was 
introduced. The administration of the fund is run by a Managing Committee or:-
