@ 10 paisa per hank in weaving. Further, the State Government has reserved a portion of Khadi materials for
the requirement of hospital to be procured from the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board. The Committee
appreciates and recognizes the efforts of the State Government in extending support to Khadi and Village Sector.
MARKETING
4.8       The Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board is running 163 numbers of sales outlets. A considerable quantity
of Khadi and Village Industries products produced by the Board and its aided units are being sold out through these
outlets. Nowadays, Board is giving particular attention in opening more sales outlets under the direct control of the
Board. The objective behind this is to dispose of the heavy accumulation of Khadi goods turned out in the production
centres.
4.9       Out of the above, 9 sales outlets are run by the Director (Marketing) directly. In addition to this, the Project
Officers are also running 20 of Khadi Grama Soubhagyas in all districts. There are 49 agency Bhavans and 84 numbers
of Grama Soubhagyas attached to the production units. The total sales achieved during 2001-2002 from all the Grama
Soubhagyas is Rs. 847.90 lakhs.
4.10     The Board has launched two types of readymade shirts with the brand name 'Summer cool' and 'Millenti'. It has
great demand in Kerala. The Board is also thinking of supplying the products to other State Boards. Similarly the Board

96th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/96threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:52]
has a brand new product of honey named 'Naruthen'. The Board is thinking of exporting their brand products to outside
the country, especially to the Middle East. A focal point will be set up in the Khadi and Village Industries Board shortly
to explore possibilities of exporting Khadi and Village Industries products.
4.11     The Committee observes that the major concern in the field of marketing of Khadi products is the rebate
policy of KVIC. The Committee hopes that the KVIC will announce its policy on time.
4.12     In the budget estimate for 2002-03 KVIC was requested to allot Rs. 40 lakhs for exhibition and Rs. 60 lakhs for
renovation of existing sales outlets. For the expansion and renovation of existing outlets funds are required.
4.13     The Committee recommends that the funds demanded in the budget proposal for the above items for
2002-03 may be considered sympathetically.
CENTRAL  SILVER  PLANT,  KUTTUR,  TRICHUR
4.14     The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) has set up a Central Silver Plant (Muslin Project) at
Kuttur, near Trichur for ensuring supply of silver/roving to the institutions of this State. The centre caters to the need of
silver/roving to the institutions of West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, U.P., Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat also. The
total supply of roving within the State comes to around 2 lakh kgs., and that of outside the State comes to 1.40 lakh kgs.
During 2001-02, the production of the unit was 3.69 lakh kgs. worth Rs. 441.00 lakhs. The actual sale was to the tune of
3.40 lakh kgs. for an amount of Rs. 419.00 lakhs. The accrued profit as on 31.3.2002 is to the extent of Rs. 176.15 lakhs.
The total investment of the plant and machinery of the unit is Rs. 166.18 lakhs. The silver/roving is being supplied to
the institutions on credit against the rebate payment so that the working capital is not blocked and ensured continued
production.
4.15     The Committee observes that Kerala being a consumer State more silver plants on the pattern of Central
Siler Plants, Kuttur, Trichur should be set up so that demands of the State of Khadi Products can be met.
BIO-TECHNOLOGY/NON-CONVENTIONAL  ENERGY  PROGRAMME
4.16     "Bio-technology and Non-conventional Energy" is one of the major industries functioning in Kerala. Various
programmes such as national project on biogas development, community/institutional and night-soil based higher
capacity biogas plants etc. are being implemented as per the guidelines and financial support of the Ministry of Non-
conventional Energy Sources. During 2001-02, 300 biogas plants, 3 Nos. of institutional and night soil based plants
were installed. This will directly influence in reducing cooking fuel needs. Besides, this provides direct employment to
30-60 rural unemployed artisans. The subsidy rates varies from Rs. 1800/- to Rs. 2300/- per biogas plant and
supervision charges to the Rural Energy Technicians to the tune of Rs. 700/- for each biogas plant.
4.17     KVIC is also engaged in development of "bio-manure". KVIC is extending technical expertise in disseminating
various bio-manure techniques, bio-digested slurry etc. besides financial assistance under the scheme. So far half a
dozen units have been installed and a good number of units are under different stages of installation.
4.18     The Committee appreciates the efforts of Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board in developing bio-
technology/non-conventional energy programme. The Committee hopes that action will be taken to install more
such units in the State.
RURAL  EMPLOYMENT  GENERATION  PROGRAMME  (REGP)
4.19     The REGP is being implemented in the State, with the active involvement of the State KVI Board and Public
Sector Scheduled Commercial Banks. So far, 5246 Village Industries Projects have been set up in the State under the
programme.
THE  PERFORMANCE  OF  STATE  KVI  BOARD
4.20     The State KVI Board aided agencies are actively involved in the implementation of REGP. KVIC has placed Rs.
14.19 crore Margin Money advance with the State KVI Board for speedy implementation of the programme. The Board
has already sanctioned and released Margin Money Assistance to the tune of Rs. 14.18 crore to 1403 Village Industries
Units generating employment opportunity to 11844 persons in rural sector. The Board is providing Margin Money
Assistance to all industries included under the schedule of industries approved by Khadi and Village Industries
Commission.
4.21     With a view to overcome the unemployment situation and to create additional employment opportunities in rural
area, the Board is introducing certain dynamic programmes under Margin Money Scheme, in addition to the ongoing
programmes. One of the prestigious programmes to be implemented by the Board is the introduction of "Cyber Cafe" in
all Panchayats in Kerala. The Project envisages to set up Cyber Cafes in all 991 Grama Panchayats in Kerala with a
specific objective of giving fillip to an IT based endeavour for rural development. The Board also proposes to impart a
short-term training to the prospective entrepreneurs in this regard.
4.22     The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should help the Kerala
Government to tap the inherent skills of the rural populace and transform them into economic assets for self-

96th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/96threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:52]
employment and higher earnings.
4.23     The Sub-Committee was informed that adequate attention is being paid to publicity of the following programmes
:-
            l         Booklets, pamphlets have been printed and made available to the public.
            l         Spreading message through various forms like State Level Bankers Committee, District Level Bankers
Committee and Block Level Bankers Committee.
            l         Periodical review meetings, conducting of seminars, workshops etc.
            l         Advertisement through newspapers, All India Radio and Doordarshan.
            For promotional activities an amount of Rs. 25 lakh was sanctioned and released to the Board and the entire
amount has been utilized.
4.24     The Committee is happy to note the painstaking efforts made by the Kerala KVIB and to popularize the
scheme. The Committee appreciates the progress made in the direction.
MONITORING  OF  THE  PROGRAMME
4.25     The success of the scheme lies in the effective monitoring. In order to ensure that the scheme achieves its
intended objective, monitoring Committees are constituted at two levels :-
            l         The State Government have constituted a State Level Task Force to oversee the implementation of Margin
Money Scheme, with Special Secretary to Government, Industries Department as Chairman, Secretary, Kerala Khadi
and Village Industries Board as Convenor and the representatives from the various implementing agencies as members.
The Committee reviews the progress of the scheme in the State.
            l         For the speedy implementation of the Margin Money Scheme, the Government have constituted a District
Level Task Force with the District Collector as Chairman and the Project Officer, Kerala Khadi and Village Industries
Board as the Convenor. The Committee reviews the progress of the scheme at District Level.
4.26     The Committee recommends that REGP beneficiaries may be given I.T. based assistance so as to enable
them to collect data relating to agro and rural based industries for formulating their own market strategy. The
Committee further suggests that free of cost I.T. training may be provided to REGP beneficiaries.
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
            The Committee observes that in order to identify the drawbacks in the functioning of the Khadi institutions and
to take timely remedial measures, KVIC should closely monitor Khadi institutions under various categories like A, B, C
and D especially those institutions whose functioning is not at the desired level. KVIC should ensure decentralization in
decision making and delegation of more powers to State KVIB alongwith development of a strong monitoring
system.     (Para 2.4)
            The Committee observes that Khadi sales pick up only when rebate is offered to the customers. Sans rebate,
khadi sales have shown downward trend during the year. The Committee recommends that KVIC should encourage
individual entrepreneurs to sell khadi products on commission basis. There should also be attempt to make the khadi
products cheaper, qualitatively better and market competitive.      (Para 2.6)
            The Committee during the interactive session with KVIC/AP KVIB, was informed about the malpractices and
mismanagement at various levels of the Khadi institutions. The Committee is of the view that this may be one of the
reasons of cost of khadi going up and products being unaffordable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that certain
in-house activities like concurrent evaluation, data collection etc. of these institutions should be verified by outside
professional agencies.                                              (Para 2.8)
            The Committee observes that there is vast scope for implementation of the programmes like pottery (Mineral
based industry), mango jelly (fruits and vegetables processing industry), palm gur, lime industry, beekeeping, carpentry
and blacksmith, rural transport, processing of cereals and pulses, medicinal plants, paper bags conversion units, service
sector industries, dhabas and fast food units under tourism, bio-manure. Under the UNDP training programme
extraction of banana fibre programme is going to be organized by batches at Kasturba Gandhi National Memorial Trust,
Seethanagaram, Rajahmundry, East Godavari District. There is need to explore their potential in the state as these areas
have not been tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made by KVIC/KVIB to develop
these programmes in the State on priority basis and realize their fullest potential. NGOs may also be invited and
encouraged to popularize these programmes.    (Para 2.11)
            The Committee observes that cluster approaches need to be encouraged in a big way in the rural sector as it not
only builds community spirit but also provides employment at a low cost. The Committee recommends that proposals

96th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/96threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:52]
sent by the State agencies for cluster forming like mango-jelly cluster, brass/copper cluster, palm fibre extraction cluster
should be expedited at the Central office level to give a boost to the community programme.          (Para 2.13)
            The Committee observes that REGP is meant for lower strata of society, people of labour class who earn their
bread on daily basis. The Committee recommends that every effort should be made to achieve the target for the year
2002-03 by the regional office, Visakhapatnam and more funds should be infused in the State for the scheme
considering the number of such people in the State.                       (Para 2.18)
            The Committee observes that EDP training to beneficiaries forms an important part of the village industries
programmes. It is a sorry state of affairs that sanction for EDP programmes for 2001-02 and 2002-03 have not been
received by the KVI office in Andhra Pradesh. The Committee views this seriously and recommends corrective
action.            (Para 2.20)
            The Committee is constrained to note the denial of loan and margin money by the beneficiaries. The Committee
observes that such loopholes need to be plugged to the KVIC/KVIB if village industries are to strengthened.      (Para
2.24)
            The Committee observes that there are no Departmental or non-Departmental Training Centres in the Andhra
Pradesh. There is no training centre either under KVI Board. The officials of Regional Office, Andhra Pradesh are
deputed to attend training outside the state. The Committee, therefore, recommends that training centres should be set
up in the state so that maximum number of persons can be trained and benefit from the programmes.    (Para 2.26)
            The Committee is of the opinion that Marketing needs to be given new orientation. Marketing is the area where
utmost attention has to be paid. In spite of providing some good quality products the marketing has been poor which has
affected Khadi sales adversely. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sales outlets in the KVI sector should be
modernized with proper computerized inventory management system. A joint advertisement campaign on cost sharing
basis with KVIB and KVIC institutions should be started. If proper attention is paid to it and goods/products are
branded and packaged, like private companies do, Khadi products can not only do good business in the domestic
markets but also can be sold in international markets because there is good demand for some Khadi products like silk,
cotton etc.      (Para 2.28)
            The Committee recommends that the proposal for quality control/testing lab on Khadi goods and yarn is in the
interest of the industry and it should be materialized at the earliest.          (Para 2.30)
            The Committee observed that proposals to set up verm compost/bio-manure need be 
processed speedily and all kind of assistance in this regard should be given including training to the
entrepreneurs.            (Para 2.32)
            The Committee observes that traditionally, the artisans of Andhra Pradesh from time immemorial belong to the
weaker sections of society. Most of them are below poverty line. Crafts in Andhra Pradesh are surviving because of
their skill. The Committee recommends that KVIC should help A.P. Khadi and V.I. Board to identify and help such
talented artisans/craftsmen as the Andhra Pradesh Khadi and Village Industries Board has to play a major role in
implementing the Village Industries programme. The Committee also recommends that KVIC should encourage
APKVIB to take up schemes such as vermiculture, iodised salt, gum paper tape, screen printing, imitation jewellery and
ancillary units of medium and small scale under automobile and engineering industry and implement them.     (Para
2.34)
            The Committee, however, observes that out of 64 institutions financed for production of Khadi cotton, Muslim
silk and wool only 19 institutions are reporting progress. This is a low turnout which requires immediate attention of
APKVIB. KVIC should try to remove the bottlenecks in this regard so that all such institutions become functional. 
(Para 2.36)
            The Committee observes that KVIC should see that institutions implementing interest subsidy scheme monitored
by APKVIC utilize the subsidy properly and achieve the desired goal. Their progress should be reviewed periodically
and appropriate action be taken for the purpose.      (Para 2.38)
            The Committee recommends that more silver plants should be set up in the state to help Khadi
programmes.            (Para 3.3)
            The Committee observes that Margin Money Scheme is at present being extended for establishing Industries,
Business and Service ventures mainly in rural areas. This has resulted in creation of large capacities in production side
without much support in marketing of products produced. Therefore, it is necessary to create forward linkages by
supporting and assisting in marketability of the products. The Committee recommends that exclusive KVI retail sales
outlets in urban and semi-urban areas should be opened by extending Margin Money assistance. If necessary, waiver of
rural criteria as in the case of leather units should be done in which exemption is available to those leather units as are
located in rural areas.            (Para 3.5)

            The interest subsidy scheme is being in force for almost two decades. This scheme is not extended to the units
established under CBC and Margin Money Scheme. There are quite a good number of units like Rice Mills, Dal Mills,
Rava Mills, Stone Cutting and Polishing etc., which require huge working capital for the viability. In all these cases, the
Committee observes the only one cycle requirement of working capital, has been provided with the presumption that
units should avail remaining working capital from the Banks. The Committee, therefore, recommends that interest
subsidy eligibility certificate should be extended to the units established under CBC and Margin Money Scheme.     
(Para 3.6)
            The Committee came to know that a proposal has been prepared for modernization of cotton khadi production
centres in Karnataka. This proposal envisages conversion of 1125 charakas from the present 6 spindles to 8 spindles
charakas. The estimated cost of the proposal is Rs. 101.25 lakhs towards capital expenditure i.e., replacement of 6
spindle charaka by 8 spindle charaka and Rs. 54.64 lakhs interest subsidy on working capital to be borrowed from the
financial institutions/Banks. The Committee observes that the modernization of cotton khadi production centres will
improve the productivity of khadi institutions and khadi artisans will be able to earn increased wages due to increased
production. The Committee, therefore, recommends that proposal submitted to KVIC should be examined and the
required amount under budgetary sources should be sanctioned without delay.              (Para 3.7)
            The Committee recommends that sufficient funds be provided to Karnataka KVIB for providing direct loan and
Margin Money assistance to the entrepreneurs willing to establish industries in rural areas at the earliest.  (Para 3.9)
            The Committee recommends that all avenues should be explored to build capacity of the existing traditional
artisans and to introduce new technology in pottery under cluster programme like non-conventional energy programmes
etc. Besides, product diversification, skill upgradation and establishing backward and forward linkages to these artisans
should be followed up in the project. Accordingly, appropriate training should be given to them.     (Para 3.14)
            The Committee hopes that target for employment generation under the programme would be achieved
satisfactorily by the Karnataka Khadi Village Industries Board and KVIC during the year 2002-03.  (Para 3.19)

approved by the Banks.   (Para 4.2)
            The Committee appreciates the efforts made by Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board for revival of sick
units in the state and pro-active role played by it to provide financial and technical assistance to them. The Committee
hopes that these efforts will help a lot in improving the condition of sick units in Kerala.       (Para 4.4)
            The Committee observes that Kerala is a leading State in the welfare measures for Khadi artisans. The State
Khadi Workers' Welfare Fund is a model to be examined by other State for implementation. The State Government
gives support to the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board by providing substantial funds under plan fund in
addition to non-plan funds for salary and rebate. A rebate of 10% on the sale of Khadi is available throughout the year.
The State Government has introduced an incentive scheme to the Khadi artisans @ 10 paisa per hank in weaving.
Further, the State Government has reserved a portion of Khadi materials for the requirement of hospital to be procured
from the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board. The Committee appreciates and recognizes the efforts of the State
Government in extending support to Khadi and Village Sector.                                             (Para 4.7)
            The Committee observes that the major concern in the field of marketing of Khadi products is the rebate policy
of KVIC. The Committee hopes that the KVIC will announce its policy on time.                            (Para 4.11)
            The Committee recommends that the funds demanded in the budget proposal for the above items for 2002-03
may be considered sympathetically.  (Para 4.13)
            The Committee observes that Kerala being a consumer state more silver plants on the pattern of Central Siler
Plants, Kuttur, Trichur should be set up so that demands of the State for Khadi Products can be met.    (Para 4.15)
            The Committee appreciates the efforts of Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board in developing Bio-
technology/non-conventional energy programme. The Committee hopes that action will be taken to install more such
units in the state.           (Para 4.18)
            The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should help the Kerala Government
to tap the inherent skills of the rural populace and transform them into economic assets for self-employment and higher
earnings.            (Para 4.22)
            The Committee is happy to note the painstaking efforts made by the Kerala KVIB and to popularize the scheme.

2.         At the outset the Chairman welcomed the Members and apprised them of agenda for the meeting 
of the day.
3.         The Committee thereafter, took up auto policy for discussion. The Chairman apprised the Members that the
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry had recommended in its 59th Report that the Government should
formulate an Auto Policy in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. Obligations. In response to
the Committee's recommendations the Department of Heavy Industries in its Action Taken Note has informed the
Committee that Government of India has brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002.
3.1       The Chairman stated that the Committee on Industry took up the auto policy for detailed discussion as the policy
laid down certain recommendations for the growth of the Industry. Since most of these recommendations required
actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far these recommendations had not been
translated into real Government Policy.
3.2.      The Chairman apprised the Members that the Committee had already taken up the matter for discussion and in
this regard the Committee had held two meetings on 24th June and 16th July, 2002. Based on the discussion held on
24th June, 2002 a questionnaire was prepared and replies thereon was obtained from Department of Heavy Industries. In
the meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotive Research Association of India
(ARAI); Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA);
and Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of Fuel saver). Apprising
the Members the details of discussion held in these two meetings, the Chairman spelt out the scope for discussion in
auto policy which inter-alia included import of second hand imported cars; lack of testing facilities; foreign direct
investment, research and development; construction of bus-body building, terminal life policy, lifting of quantitative
restriction; Using spurious items and related 'e' mark issue; excise duty on tyre and concession on import tyre; Ban on
used tyre; difficulties due to octroi on 5-6 States, switching over from Tube tyre to tubeless tyre; encouragement to
small car industries; infrastructure import tariff; environmental aspects etc.
3.3       The Committee, thereafter, discussed in details the aims of Auto Policy which aimed at to promote integrated,
phased, enduring and self-sustained growth of the Indian Automobile Industry. The Committee discussed also the
objective of Auto Policy which inter-alia include promotion of a globally competitive automotive industry; Exalting the
sector as a lever of industrial growth and an employment; Establishment of an international hub for manufacturing small
affordable passenger cars and key centre for manufacturing Tractors and Two wheelers in the world; Ensuing a balanced
transition to open trade at a minimal risk to the Indian Economy and local industry; Modernisation of the industry by
facilitating indigenous design, research and development; Steering up India's software industry into automotive

technology; Development of domestic safety and environmental standard at par with international standards; assisting
development of vehicles propelled by alternative energy sources.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised by the
Committee, hereby present this Ninety-seventh Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the
74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on Demands for Grants for (2002-03) pertaining to
the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.
2.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report at its meeting held
on the 11th December, 2002.
3.      The 74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid
on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
11 December, 2002
NEW DELHI;
Dr.  P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
        The Ninety-seventh Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in
the 74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on the Demands for Grants (2002-03)
pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the
14th May, 2002.

        The Ministry is alive to the significance of R&D to promote global competitiveness of the indigenous industries. Therefore,

and quality standards of goods produced in rural areas by the Village Industries.

Control/Assurance Mechanism of final products are some of the important areas where organizations like Khadi and Village Industries
Commission (KVIC), Mumbai under this Ministry, could play an important role either through its own infrastructure or using
infrastructure available elsewhere for the strengthening of Rural Industrialisation.

Para 3.12
        While appreciating this initiative, the Committee expresses its concern that JPRGY should not meet the fate of NPRI (National
Programme for Rural Industrialisation as announced in the Budget for the financial year 1999-2000. The allocation of Rs.40 lakhs was
kept for the NPRI scheme in the BE 2001-02 which was reduced to nominal amount of Rs.1.00 lakh in the RE of that year. The scheme is
yet to take off. However, in the BE  2002-03 a provision of Rs. 90 lakhs has been made. The Committee, therefore impresses upon the
Ministry to review the progress of NPRI so that the earlier mistakes are not repeated by the administration.
Comments
        The scheme on NPRI was announced in the year 1999-2000 with a mission to set up 100 rural clusters every year. Office of the DC
(SSI) was made the coordinating agency of the programme. KVIC, SIDBI and NABARD are the major implementing agencies. No fund
was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own programmes in this
area which could be coordinated and their synergies exploited for better impact.
        Efforts were made to firm up the scheme at the initial stage. A number of meetings were called in which all the agencies involved in
rural industrialization participated. A national level Steering Committee was constituted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (SSI &
ARI) to guide, implement and monitor the programme. Consequently, KVIC identified 50 clusters for development for each year, SIDBI
25 and NABARD 50 for a period of 5 years. So far, KVIC has launched the programme in 20 clusters, NABARD in 14 and SIDBI in 13.
The other clusters are also under consideration and preliminary/diagnostic studies are being conducted of these clusters. It was, however,
felt that some fund was required for certain gap filling exercises towards cluster intervention. Therefore, the Office of the DC (SSI)
launched a scheme on NPRI in the year 2001-02 to supplement the efforts of the various agencies. The amount provided in the scheme is
only Rs.5 lakhs per cluster. The purpose of financial assistance is to fill certain gaps in the development of clusters, and it does not
constitute the entire amount required for such development. As the scheme has been approved in the year 2001-02, it is expected to yield
results in the coming years.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee fails to understand as to why a scheme is announced by the Government without any budgetary provision. Ministry's
reply that no fund was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordinated and their synergy exploited for their impact does not appear to be sound because this
Committee has its own experience that coordination among Central Ministries and Departments is a difficult preposition to achieve. The
Committee now expects that with the provision of funds the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would implement the programme.

CHAPTER - I
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
Recommendations    (Para 7.1.7)
 
MODERNISATION OF THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee understands that in the wake of radical reforms in economic and mineral policies of the country, up-to-
date high quality database for optimum development of natural resources both on land and offshore, management of
natural hazards and protection of environment became essential. A quantum jump to the modernisation and technology
up gradation in all spheres of activity is prerequisite for the goal.
Action Taken
            The Department is giving full support to the modernization efforts and capacity building of GSI so that GSI is
geared to make available the high quality database for optimum development of natural resources both onland and off
shore.
 
Recommendations  (Para 7.1.8 )
EARTHQUAKE STUDIES BY THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA       
After the devastating effect of the Gujarat earthquake, the Committee feels more emphasis should be given on the
earthquake studies to save human lives and property in the urban as well rural areas. The Committee recommends the
adequates funds may be made available to the G.S.I. for the purpose. The G.S.I. should also take the aid and assistance
of the experts available across the World.
Action Taken
GSI has given thrust to active fault mapping and microzonation studies of urban clusters, as a part of earthquake
studies towards deleneation of potential risk zones and mitigation of impact of disasters.  It is also collaborating with
Indian Metrological Department and participating in a Department of Science & Technology sponsored Indo-Italian
Collaborative Research Project for seismic studies.  Provision has been made for the procurement of the state-of-art
field location cum data collection equipments as a part of modernization programmes of Geological Survey of India .
Recommendations  ( Para 7.2.7 )

FUNDS FOR MINERAL EXPLORATION CORPORATION LTD.
            The Committee notes that   in case the provision    of Rs.8 crore as earmarked in BE 2002-03 proves insufficient
for MECL for  its  promotional projects the shortfall amount should be  made available from `Mineral  Exploration
Fund'  which has a provisional fund of Rs.12.00 crore .
Action Taken
            There would be no problem of funds in view of availability of funds in Mineral Exploration Fund.
 
Recommendations (Para 13.2)
Non-Plan Loan to Mines PSUs
The Committee   is of the opinion that   non-plan loan is a necessary evil as it is   essential   for loss making PSUs to
maintain its  operation and   separation of surplus  work force and  sometimes even to meet the  cash loss, all depending 
upon the quantum of  loss being incurred by a  PSU.  Non-plan loan is an evil in the sense   that the amount of non-plan
loan gets added to the liability of the Company, which is always a burden on the Company.  The Committee notes that
during  2002-03  no non-plan loan has been allocated to mines PSUs, although rationalisation of manpower is being 
undertaken in almost  all mines PSUs.
Action Taken
            During the year 2002-03, no non-plan loan has been allocated to the PSUs under the Department of Mines.  The
position of non-plan loan given earlier to the PSUs is as follows:
(a)
                Hindustan Copper Ltd.
(i)                  A total non-plan loan of Rs.440 crores has been converted as grant.
(ii)                Additional grant of Rs. 130 crores for rationalization of manpower is being provided.
(b)               Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd.
(i)         The conversion of non-plan loan will be taken into account at the time of disinvestment.
 
Recommendations   (Para 13.4.5 & 13.4.6.)
FINANCIAL RESTRUCTURING OF HINDUSTAN COPPER LTD.    
The Committee is pleased to note that as a result of implementation of VRS in HCL during last three years the wage
cost as percentage of turnover has come down   from 35.81% in 1999 -2000 to 22.98% in 2000-01 and turnover per
employee has increased from Rs. 3.30 lakh to Rs.5.11 lakh during the same period.
The Committee understands that HCL is sailing through adverse financial situation and is a loss making PSU, therefore,
the Committee is in agreement with the Department of Mines regarding incapacity of repayment of non-plan loan by
HCL. The Committee   feels that since the financial restructuring     of HCL is on the card the Department of Mines
should not delay any longer the submission of the proposal for conversion of non-plan loan   of Rs.440 crore   into grant
and the Government should not hesitate in clearing the proposal, as cleaner the balance sheet   of the Company larger
the possibility of a potential purchasers coming forward.
Action Taken    (Para 13.4.5 and Para 13.4.6)
            The Government has already approved the financial restructuring of Hindustan Copper Limited which includes
conversion of non-plan loan of Rs.440 crores into grant. Besides following measures have also been taken:-
(i)
                  Conversion of outstanding plan loan as on March 31, 2002, amounting to Rs.71.50 crore into equity to
improve the net worth of the Company.
(ii)                Waiver of outstanding interest on plan loan amounting to Rs.25.72 crore as on March 31, 2002.
(iii)               Extension of period of the Government guarantees already provided for raising working capital term loan
by a further 2 years or disinvestments which is earlier, in order to facilitate meeting the obligations for the
Secured Bond repayment.

(v)                To provide for an additional amount of Rs.130 crore as grant to meet the expenses of closing underground

Since with the passage of time technology becomes   obsolete the Committee feels that modernisation of technology is a

respect of MECL and a provision of Rs.25 crore for replacement and renewal is but natural to meet the requirement of

BUDGETARY SUPPORT TO HINDUSTAN CORPORATION LTD.

PRESENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOMINEE DIRECTORS IN THE MEETING  OF BALCO
            The Committee understands that Government’s stake in BALCO is 49% even after disinvestment and 4
Directors     from Government side are  there  on the  Board of Directors.   The Committee has been given to understand
that as per the SHA the presence of at least one   representative or nominee each of the Government and the purchaser
shall be required   for taking decision  on all  such matters  that may have a material impact on the business of the
Company.  The Committee hopes that the nominee from Government side  would participate in all the   meetings  of the
Board of Directors and participate  actively  in   the  discussion ensuring the proper   utilisation of national resources in
best possible ways.  Higher performance of the Company and protection of national interest should be the prime
consideration of Directors from Government   on the BALCO’s Board of Directors.
Action Taken
            BALCO is regularly convening Board Meetings at suitable intervals, and there has been participation of more
than one Government nominee Directors in every meeting.  All major decisions and performance of the Company is
appraised to the Board in the meetings.
Recommendations   (Para 15.5.4)
DIVERSIFICATION PROGRAMMES OF MECL
The Committee opines that diversification programmes of MECL contain the element for survival and improved

            MECL has already carried out CBM drilling on contractual basis for ONGC and negotiations for further work

 Recommendations (Para 16.5)
DIVERSIFICATION PROGRAMMES OF JNARDDC, NIRM AND NIMH
The Committees recommends that NIRM, JNARDDC and NIMH should   make concerted efforts towards
diversification of services rendered by them through consultancy services.
Action Taken
(i)         JNARDDC
JNARDDC has been making conscious and concerted efforts to diversify the services.  To this end, an
impressive brochure called “profile” of the Centre has been printed and distributed widely to very large number
of industries both in the aluminium as well as non-aluminium sector. JNARDDC proposes also to diversify its
activities to cover industries dealing with other non-ferrous metals like copper, zinc, titanium etc. 
(ii)        NIRM
NIRM provides research and consultancy services to Hydroelectric and tunneling projects and to coal and non
coal mining companies.
(iii)       NIMH
NIMH carries out studies in the occupational health/hygiene problems in metal ferrous mining sector.
Recommendations ( Para 17.3)
Impact of withdrawal of the SSI exemption   on   granite in the budget 2002-03 on the granite industry.
            The Committee observes that the exemption of excise duty on small scale and cottage scale granite industry upto
limit of Rs.1.00 crore in the budget 2002-03 has rendered 5 thousand granite units in complete doldrums and
employment of 3 lakh workers is in jeopardy.  The Committee has been given to understand that SSI granite industry is
already reeling under high cost of production, adverse affect of recession and dumping of  cheaper   product  from China
and the  withdrawal of the SSI exemption  on granite SSI  sector would  further   hit the granite SSI  sector adversely. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends, that the Government should take due note of the provisions enshrined  in the 
budget 2002-03 and  do justice  to the granite SSI  industry.

            Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance vide notification No.26/2002-Central Excise dated 27

MINES PSUs CONTRIBUTION TO NATIONAL EXCHEQUER
 The Committee is pleased to note the contribution made by Mines PSUs to National Exchequer especially contribution
made by HZL and NALCO.  The committee understands that   due to dwindling physical and financial performance by
HCL its contribution to National Exchequer has been declining over the year.  However, the Committee hopes that once
the capital restructuring of HCL takes place physical and financial performance of HCL would start improving and
therefore its contribution  towards    national  exchequer would   automatically  improve.
Action Taken

            Department of Mines’ PSUs would continue to contribute to the national exchequer to the maximum extent
possible.
           
Recommendations Para (18.3):
Contribution Of Mining Sector To The Nation  
The Committee further observes  that the more and more private  sector players   are coming to the mining sector and
mines PSUs are either have already been disinvested  i.e. BALCO  and HZL     or  are on the verge of disinvestment  as
in the  case of HCL  and NALCO and   due  to  on-going  liberalisation  process , the contribution of   mining sector  to
national exchequer would improve in the years to come.  The Committee hopes that the on-going  liberalisation process
should enhance the capabilities  of making  contribution of mining sector to the nation   and society in general.  In this
regard the  Committee  hopes that the Government would give due consideration towards  the contribution  made by
units of private  sector and PSUs in mining sector.
Action Taken
            Under the National Mineral Policy, 1993, 13 minerals hitherto reserved for exploitation by Public Sector were
thrown open for exploitation by Private Sector also and thereby provided a level playing field to private companies in
the mineral sector.  Thus entire mining sector is open for private investment including Foreign Direct
Investments(FDI).  A number of leading global mining companies have evinced interest in Indian mining sector
resulting in expected FDI inflow of Rs.3963 crores.  The National Mineral Policy, 1993 has also recognized the need for
encouraging private investment including FDI and state of art technology in the mineral sector and has therefore
contributed towards national exchequer and society in general.  Besides this, a number of amendments have been carried
out in the MMDR Act, 1957, MCR, 1960 and MCDR, 1988,  since 1994 to make Indian mining sector investor friendly
and hassle free.

Action Taken:
 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993, recognised the need for encouraging private investment including foreign
direct investment and state-of-the-art technology in mineral sector. Further , National Mineral Policy 1993 has  stressed 
that the Central  Government in consultation with the State Governments, shall continue to formulate the legal measures
for the regulation of mines and the development of mineral resources to ensure basic  uniformity  in mineral 
administration and to ensure that the development of mineral resources keeps pace, and is in consonance with the
national policy goals.
 
It is therefore evident that review of the policy and consequent amendment(s) in the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and rules framed there under to cater to future demands is(are)  an ongoing
process, and can not be a one time exercise.
 
 For a structured  and institutionalized review of the policies and procedures affecting the mining and the mineral
sector and for all matters connected or incidental thereto, the Mineral Advisory Council has been constituted by the
Government. The Hon’ble Minister for Coal and Mines is the Chairman of the Council. The Council has balanced
representation from State Governments, Industry Associations , Experts in mining sector as well as Members of
Parliament. The Mineral Advisory Council inter alia reviews the status of implementation of the National Mineral
Policy, advises the Government on mineral policy and legislation and the status of the mining and the mineral sector,
including inter alia  all the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its Report.
 
After the National Mineral Policy was announced, Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
has been amended in 1994 and 1999. After amendment in the Principal Act in 1999, the Mineral Concession Rules,
1960 have been amended on January 17,.2000, September 25,.2000,January 22,2000, and on January 11.,2002 .
Similarly, after 1999, the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules 1988 have been amended on 17.1.2000,
25.9.2000 and 11.1.2002.
The  amendments in the legislation have been extensively discussed prior to their enactment and honed as per
recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council in its various meetings. As a recent example, minerals for which the
State Governments would be empowered to approve mining plans have been identified, time limits have been prescribed
for  conveying a decision on application(s) for mineral concessions and mining plans, and fees payable for various
applications under the rules have been revised as per recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council.
 
            Two meetings of the Mineral Advisory Council have been held since 1999. In addition the Department of Mines
organized a Conference of State Ministers of Mining and Geology, as well as a Tripartite Meeting of the Central
Government, State Governments and Investors in the Mining Sector in 2001. These meetings also discussed inter alia
the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. The review of the National Mineral Policy
and the other issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee will therefore appropriately be listed for
discussion in the next meeting of the Mineral Advisory Committee.         
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee expects  that the  Department of Mines  understands the concern  of Department related
Parliamentary  Standing Committee on Industry  and  therefore  appreciate its desire accordingly.  Interchanging and
intermingling  and  the functions of  Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee with  Mineral Advisory
Council  would not only be belittling and undermining the status of  this Committee   but also juxtaposing  the role   of
Mineral Advisory Council.    The Department of Mines placed  the issues identified  by the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry in the meetings of  Mineral Advisory Council  but deprived the Committee of the outcome of the
meetings and  discussion held.  The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should  furnish the details of 
Action Taken in its Note and  apprise the Committee comprehensively.   The Committee recommends that  the
Department of Mines should forward the  minutes of the meeting of Mineral Advisory  Council  to this Committee
whenever  the Mineral Advisory Council discusses the issues identified by the Committee.

FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN MINING SECTOR
 The Committee appreciates  the  efforts made by the Department of Mines towards making the  mining sector more  
investor friendly  but  at the same time hopes that  pace of foreign  investment  in the mining sector may be  
accelerated.
Action Taken:
            The liberalisation of policy has provided a conducive atmosphere for the international mining companies to
invest in the country and bring with this investment and world class mining technology.  The policy of the Government
of India has been to actively encourage foreign investors to participate in the exploration and production of minerals and
mineral based industries.  Sustained inflow of private including foreign investment is desirable to bring in state-of-the-
art technology, coupled with foreign capital for the exploration and exploitation of mineral resources and in-country
value addition.
            As a part of the policy to actively encourage such investments, in order to give a further push for the FIPB
approved projects to get off the ground quickly, a monitoring system has been put in place.  This involves a periodic
review by the Foreign Investment Implementation Authority (FIIA), which looks at the progress made in implementing
the major projects.  Also, within each Ministry, there is a Fast Tract Committee (FTC) which closely monitors the
projects in that particular sector.
            The Department of Mines has been effectively utilizing various international fora, to highlight the policy and
legislative initiatives undertaken to project India as an attractive investment destination and the opportunities available. 
In this context the response has been good.
            Meetings with foreign investors have also been organized to identify the problems in implementation of various
Projects.  A time frame for disposal of applications for mineral concessions have also been fixed in the Mineral
Concession Rules.  These initiatives will accelerate the inflow of foreign investment in the mining sector.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee observes that the Department of Mines have  furnished in its Action Taken Note only the
institutional  arrangement for accelerating  the pace  of foreign investment in the Mining Sector   but that is not
sufficient, the Committee feels.  The  Department of Mines should have furnished the details of  course of action
undertaken to promote foreign investment in the mining sector, region and  mineral-wise  and the outcome of efforts  so
made in the  form of quantum of  foreign investment.  The Committee recommends that FIIA and FTC should play  pro-
active role   for promotion of foreign investment.

Performance of  HCL 
The Committee observes that HCL is in deep trouble as the  performance of  HCL  has been affected adversely
by   steep  fall in the prices of copper in   Landon Metal Exchange (LME) .   The Company has been incurring losses
(Rs.147.46 crore in 1999-2000; Rs.105.80 crore in 2000-01 and Rs.49.84 crore till December 2001-02)  and
accumulated loss  stands out to be Rs.556.75 crore as on March 31,2001.  The Committee further observes that
reduction in customs   duty of copper from 25% to  35%  would  further  add  to the losses of  HCL.
HCL lacks even the working   capital and it is dependent wholly     on budgetary support for keeping the mill
running.  The increase in the budgetary support from Rs.25 crore in BE to Rs.110 crore in RE 2001-02 was made to
provide fund for working capital.  And the budgetary support of Rs.25 crore for the year 2002-03 is meant for
replacement and renewals.

I, the Chairman, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
First Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants for 1993-94 of the Ministry of 
Industry.

pertaining to Department Related Standing Committees, Hon-'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha 
and Hon 'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha nominated 42 members of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha to 
the Committee on Industry for the functions assigned to it under the Rules. Further 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha and Speaker, Lok Sabha decided that all the provisions of Rule 270 
of the Rules relating to the functions of the Committee shall become operative with effer1 
from 30th March, 1993.

Demands for Grants for the year 1993-94.

sought for in this current year Budget Estimates is to be spent for meeting expenses on two 
items, i.e., transport subsidy and establishment of Growth Centres. From the funds asked 
for under the Scheme, the Committee notes that adequate planning has not been done. The 
implementation is tardy. The backward areas in the country are in difficult terrain and Jack 
of basic infra!'.tructure. Concrete steps have, therefore. to be taken to motivate people to 

avail of the facilities and concessions under the Scheme. State Governments sometimes do 
not keep any provision for the purpose. The infrastructural deVelopment in the area for the 
establishment of Growth Centres is done by the Central Government only when the 
concerned State Government is ready to provide with the required funds. The entrepreneurs 
are caught in the cobweb of Central Government grant, State Government grant, loans from 
financial institutions and market borrowings. The entrepreneur finds extremely difficult and 
feels demotivated when he faces diffculties right from the acquisition of land, power supply, 
availability of water, etc. Many entrepreneurs have left midway their projects due to these 
factors and non-cooperation from different sections of Governmental machinery . The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that for the development of Growth Centres in the 
backward areas 'single window scheme' may be adopted as one of the motivating factors to 
willing entrepreneurs to establish industrial units in backward areas. The Committee would 
further recommend perfect coordination among the Central Government, concerned State 
Government and the financial institution· to make the Scheme successful. The Committee 
would, therefore, like that Government should give re-orientation to the programme and 
ensure its proper implementation. 
9.4. Administrative Expenditure: The Administrative expenditure under the Head '3451' 
indicates an amount of Rs. 5.37 crores for the Budget Estimates. Out of this 11 lakhs is a 
plan expenditure for computerisation and 5.26 crores is for non-plan expenditure on the 
salaries and other expenditure on the maintenance of the Department. The estimates do not 
indicate any perception of the Department for the re-deployment of its surplus personnel on 
account of the reduction of the work load of the Department due to delicencing and other 
steps taken under the new Industrial Policy. The performance Budget of the Department is 
also silent on the extent of the austerity measures taken to curtail non-plan expenditure. The 
staff in any Department should reflect the work load". and surplus staff, if found should be re­
deployed for better use. The Committee, therefore, recommends that an assessment of the 
surplus staff may be made for their re-deployment in other spheres of Governmental 
activity.

9.6 (ii) The Committee, therefore, finds that foreign investment and technical collabora­
tion has been approved in Industrial Sector relating to even Food Processing Industries to 
the tune of 8472.2 millions of rupees without any consideration for the growth of indigenous 
industries in this Sector. Food Processing Industry have to a large extent depend on the local 
ancillary small scale and village and cottage industries and thereby there is no safeguard for 
the survival and development of such industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that :-
fa) disinvestment by PSUs and the funds accrued on account of the disinvestment 
should be utilised for reviving, and restructuring of the sick PSUs. The demand for 
grants and performance budget are totally silent on this aspect; 
(b) foreign investments should be approved in areas where we are yet to develop the 
technical know-how and depend upon foreign technology, The Government should 
ensure that foreign investment is earmarked for industries in the export sector to 
boost up the export of our industrial production. It should not disturb and dislocate 
the existing industrial growth of the country in the long run. The foreign 
collaboration should be identified for industries where we are lagging behind in 
international market. The Committee regrets to note that the demand for grants for 
the Department of Heavy Largest Industry does not perceive this situation and no 
funds have been allocated to organise and regulate foreign investment in our 
industrial sector particularly in the PSUs which we have developed and grown over 
a period of several decades but for which the present infrastructure for further 
development could not have been there; 
(c) every effort should be made to ensure that all the eight· benches of Board for 
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) are made functional and the cases of 
sick PSUs pending before them are disposed off expeditiously to minimise the drain 
on the public funds. The Demands for Grants of the Department and the 
Performance Budget do not reflect any concern on the depleted strength of the 
BIFR benches and the expenditure and efforts to be made by the Department to 
make them functional; 
(d) the details of disinvestments made by the Public Sector Undertakings, undertaking­
wise, should be compiled by the Department and the data relating to the sale prices 
of shares, undertaking-wise and the amount of money so collected and spent, 

undertaking-wise may be collected may be furnished to the Committee for further detailed 
examination in order to allay the misgivings in the minds of general publia that the shares 
were sold at throw away prices by some Public Sector Undertakings; and 
(e) concrete steps should be taken by the Department to ensure that foreign investors 
are not allowed to dump their unsold products in India to the detrement of 
indigenous industries. 
9.6 (iii) MUL Incidentally , the Committee finds that the CISF was providing security at 
Maruti Udyog Limited at Gurgaon since 1983. In June 1992, MUL became a non­
government company and it was felt by MUL that the continuance of CISF would probably 
not be possible. MUL looked for alternative arrangements. It was found that Group 4 
Securities India (P) Ltd. was the best. Group 4 Securities is an international security 
company with operations in 40 countries. It started operations in India in February 1990 and 
has six branches in India. After a period of familiarisation and training the Group 4 
contingent has taken over security responsibility for MUL plant w.e.f April 1, 1993. 
The Committee notes with regret that even in the matter of switching over the Security 
network, Maruti Udyog Limited had to opt for an international security company thereby 
opening the door to a multinational company for a job for which trained and adequate 
manpower and resources were available within the country, if it was a necessity to dispense 
with the security cover provided by CISF, local talent and manpower could have been 
engaged by Maruti Udyog.

The performance Budget of the Department is silent on the steps taken by it to check the 
downward graph. The Budget estimates for the year 1993-94 for this item is reduced to 40 
crores compared to 45 crores in the preceding year inspite of escalation in prices. 
This is a scheme to benefit educated unemployed youth with low income families and 30% 
of the beneficiaries are from SCJST categories. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the scheme should be implemented with all the available resources so as to ensure that the 
benefits envisaged under the scheme for self-employment provided to large number of 
persons and more funds are allocated. 
9. 7 (ii) Small Scale Industries: A sum of Rs .• 190.40 crores has been provided in the 
Budget Estimates for 1993-94. The revised estimates of 1992-93 were to the tune of Rs. 
147.41 crores. The Development of Small Scale Industries is organised through Development 
Commissioner of Small Scale Industries of the Department. The Committee finds that on 
administration and maintenance of the office of the Development Commissioner an amount 
of Rs. 3.68 crores is provided in the Budget Estimates with a component of 3.10 crores as 
non-plan expenditure. Rs. 58 lakhs are only for plan expenditure on two items i.e. publicity 
for 40 lakhs and for modernisation of library for 18 lakhs in the Budget Estimates. 
Comparing the budget figures for an important item like training which is 3.41 crores with 
that of the expenditure on the maintenance of the office of Development Commissioner, it 
may be seen that expenditure priorities are not on sound lines. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that every step should be taken to regulate the expenditure on this item and 
the money thus saved may be earmarked for other developmental item(s) of the Small Scale 
Industries. 
9. 7 (iii) Khadi and Village Industries: Khadi and Village Industries have been earmarked a 
sum of Rs. 525.64 crores in the current year Budget Estimates compared to 352 crores in the 
last years revised estimates. The Khadi and Village Industries cover a vast majority of our 
population in different areas of the country and primarily cater to the needs of our 
economically weaker sections. The Khadi and Village Industries generate vast potential for 
local employment and if given correct direction and infrastructural support, Kha.di and 
Village Industries can be more helpful in our rural economy. The Committee, however, 
finds that inspite of budgetary support, Khadi and Village Industries have not been able to 
compete in the open market and stand on their legs. The reasons , therefore, have to be 
studied and perceptive planning is to be made to make a beginning so that Khadi and 
Village Industries become self-sufficient in their functioning in all respects. The Commit tee 
finds that no thought is given in the Demands for Grants and there is no expenditure on this 
account. The Committee therefore , recommends that the priorities of expenditure may be 

re-fixed and monetary allocation be made. The Committee further recommends that every 
effort should be made to ensure that Khadi and Village Industri es do not suffer from 
shortage of financial resources, lack of infrastructural support and bureaucratic red-tapi sm. It 
is essent ial that the problem of marketing of the finished goods is taken on top priority. The 
Government should issue instructions at least to their Departments that Khadi/Village/Small 
Scale Industries Products are purchased for their requirements on the pattern of encourage­
ment given for Handloom cloth. The other point the Committee emphasises that it should be 
made obligatory on the part of the establishments of such industrie s to pay minimum living 
wages to the employees. The Committee further recommends that concrete steps are to be 
taken to ensure for the general health and welfare of the workers. Co-operatives in the field 
are to be activised and finished goods are marketed for adequate return. The Committee is 
aware of the fact that rural masses are not gainfully employed throughout the year. Some 
programmes for motivating the rural masses to utilise their spare time in engaging 
themselves in such industries are to be devised. The Committee finds that though a sum of 
Rs. 525.54 crores has been earmarked in the Budget Estimates for this item yet no money 
has been allotted for motivating people and for awareness programm es on the role and the 
utility of Khadi and Village Industries to rural masses. The programme for training 
undertaken by the Department also lacks perception. The Committee opines that prog­
ramme for training should be so designed and chalked out so as to give on the spot training 
and guidance by mobile training personnel in the first instance to familiarise the rural masses 
about various projects/schemes under Khadi and Village Industrie s. The initial phase may 
inrer-alia include ground level information about project, equipment, finance and marketing 
facilities for finished products. Once this phase of training is completed and the masses are 
motivated and assured of additional revenue to the person or to the family then additional 
training programmes as envisaged by the Department in the Budget Estimates would yield 
positive results. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the thrust of the training 
programme should be reoriented and grouped into two phases as mentioned above. 
The Committee trusts that its observations and recommendations will receive serious 
considerat ion for implementation.

TENTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I the Chairman. Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry having been authorised 
by the Committee to present the report on its behalf present this TENTH REPORT of the Committee on the 
Demands for Grants for 1994-95 of the Ministry of Mines. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on the 23rd March, 1994 considered relevant documents and papers 
received from the Ministry of Mines on the Demands for Grants for the year 1994-95 and held a general discussion 
thereon. 
3. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry of Mines alon~~th the heads 
of the various PSUs falling under the jurisdiction of the Ministry on the Perforn1ance Budget in the Context of 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Mines. 
4. The Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in two sittings and considered and 
adopted the Report at its sitting held on the 12th April, 1994. 
5. The Demand s for Grants of the Ministry for the year 1994-95 as presented arc as under:-

6. Taken into account the documents and other material made available to it and oral evidence tendered before 
it the Committee concludes as under :-
6.01 The Performance Budget of the Ministry of Mines for the year 1994-95 states that the Ministry is 
primarily responsible for the regulation and development of the mineral sector including the mining and 
metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum 
coal and Atomic minerals. Mmeral resources are national assets. Conservation and planned exploitation of 
minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth 
of this sector. It is the onus of the. Ministry of the Mines to develop this sector with utmost care and caution 
to enable this sector to compete with the contemporary globalisation in the internatio nal area. But the 
Committee finds that the entire mines and minerals sector is in doldrums. Large number of mines have either 
closed or at the brink of closure. The situation is very alarming particularl y in the States of Bihar , Andhra 
Pradesh , Rajasthan, Goa, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh etc. where a good number of Mines have closed dov·m. 
There is no provision in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the revival of closed Mines in the 
country. The Committee has not been told of any kind of package prepared by the Ministry for the reopening 
of closed mines in the country and make them viable. Rather the Committee has been told that the minerals 
belong to the State Governments. The onus of re-opening of closed mines is therefore the responsibility of 
the States and Ministry has washed its hands off by pointing out the responsibihty on the States ignoring 
the loss being caused to the nation due to the closure of mines throughout the country. The States faced with 
acute resource constraints and are unable to divert their attention towards the closed· mines. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government must also pay attention towards the closed/ 
closing mines throughout the country and prepare a comprehensive package for their revival in 
consultation with the State Governments concerned. There must be a perfect co-ordi nation between 

2 
the Governme nt and the Gove rnm ent of the States in thi s •·egard . The Governm ent should constitut e 
a tea m of experts to find out the causes of closure of mines and suggest the ways for their revival within 
a t ime frame. 
6.02 The Committee finds that there is lack of coordination between the Government and the Government 
of the States as far as regulating of mining is concerned. Responding to a query about the foreign investment 
in the mineral sector after the enactment of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) 
Amendment Act, 1994 the Secretary of Ministry of Mines states that the minerals belong to the State 
Governmen ts. All applicat ions have to be submitted by entrepreneurs to the concerned State Governments 
and it is they who have to give the prospecting licence or the mining lease as the case may be. The 
Government did not have precise information whether any State Government had received any formal 
proposa l and whether any foreign party has applied for any prospecting licence. The Committee finds it not 
convincing. After opening the mineral sector of the country for foreign investment and participation in order 
to accelerating i nflow of domestic and foreign capita l into the mineral sector the Governme nt has left the 
matter entirely to the State Governments. On such a vital issue there should have been a perfect 
understanding and coordination between the Central and State Governments. The Committ ee, ther efor e, 
recommends· that Governm ent must keep a watch on every foreign investment propo sal in the miner al 
sector and advi se the c once rn ed State Government to make best u se of such a propo sal with out 
compr omising nationa l interest and prioritie s and maintain the closest coordin ation with the State 
Govern ment in thi s regar d. If there are stron g sentiment s expr essed by the State Gove rnmen t, as far 
as possib le such sentiments should be respecte d. It is import ant th at compensation money reac hes the 
peo ple allocated to Geological Survey of India (GSI) in Major Head 2853. GS I plays a dominant role for 
the gro\\th of the Mineral sector of the country. According to the Perforn1ance Budget (1994- 95) of the 
Ministry GSI is responsible for collection. collation and dissemination of geological data and providing 
basic geologic~ I information essential for the successful implementation of practically are the developmen­
tal programmes of the count!). The investigation carried out by GSI contribute directly to the discovery and 
evaluation of mineral resources ensuring thereby the continued and steady supply of vital ra\\ materials to 
the core industrial sector . The results of investigation aid in the better understanding of the cmstal 
framework and the geological process with bearing on development in other as vital sectors such as 
agriculture, land use management, irrigation and power development. utilisation of water resources. 
development of transport and communication, educat ion and scientific management of environment. Thus 
survey and mapping and mineral exploration are the most important functions ofGSI for Mineral sector 
and geological process having bearing on other important sectors oft he country but the committee finds that 
out of the total allocation ofRs. 125.74% crores in BE 1994-95 only a sum ofRs. 11.20 crorcs has been 
earmarked for survey and mapping and Rs. 12.90 for mineral exploration. Thus a total sum ofRs. 25.10 
crores will be spent on the vital functions of Survey and mapping and Mineral exploration whereas more 
than Rs. I 00 crores will be spent on other purposes mainly administration etc. The committee, therefore, 
recommends that additional funds be allocated for such primary functio ns as survey and mapping and 
Mineral exploration of the GSI. Such Su rveys and exp lorat ion should conform to a precise ly ind icated 
time frame so that a check would be possib le on tangible res ults achieved. The Committee appreciates 
the gesture of the Government in increasing the resource Budgetary allocation to GSI as per its 
recommendations made in its Thjrd Report on the Demands for Grants of the Ministl) ' of Mines ( 1993-94 ). 
However, the Committee recommends that instead of allocating a substa ntial amou nt for other 
purposes to GSI more thr ust should be given for its basic work. T hough the GSI is achieving its 
ta r gets, additiona l resources will certain ly bring an improveme nt in basic work and the nat ion will 
be benefitted. 
6.05 During the course ofhis oral evidence before the Committee the Secreta!) · of the Ministry reposed his 
confidence in the PS Us functioning under the jurisdiction on his M inistl) "hich inspite of a lot of pressure 
are doing quite \\ell. Citing an e-.:ample he stated that BALCO has recorded a profit of almost two and a 

3 
half crores of rupees last year and it seems to have touched a profit of more than Rs. II crores by the end 
of February, 1994. The company is likel~ to maintain its profit earnings. The Committee appreciates the 
example shown by the Management and Trade Unions of the BALCO which came together and removed 
the bottlenecks in the smooth progress of the company. The Committe~ hopes that similar gesture will 
prevail in other PSUs falling under the jurisdiction of the Ministry and a new era of hope and trust will 
emerge in employer-employee relations of such PSUs. However in case of Aluminium which holds good 
promise for exports and industrial development of the country the production during the last fi\'e years 
remained belo'' targets as has been shO\\n in the Perfom1ance Budget (199~-95) ofth~ Ministry :

6.08 The Committee finds that Mineral Exploration Corporation Limited (MECL) falling within the

National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) , a Government of India Enterprise and  a “Mini

8.1       Iron ore Mining: NMDC Management is always in search of latest Mining technology and equipment.
Accordingly, higher capacity drills, shovels and dumpers have been deployed in various existing Mines. In new Mines
120 ton capacity Dumpers against 50 T Dumpers and 8 meter cube Shovels against 4.6 meter cube Shovels and single
pass Drills against multi pass Drills are being planned. Latest information technology is being adopted in OCSL Plant
like; PLC, CCTV etc. The modern technology will enhance the productivity of Mines and also will result in reduction in
cost.
 
8.2       Diamond Mining: Mechanised Diamond Mine at Majghawan had a capacity of 24,480 carats per year by
adopting jigging technology. By adopting latest heavy media separation and X-ray sorting machinery, capacity of the
Mine has been enhanced to 84000 carats per year.  During the year 2001-02 the Mine could achieve 81,100 carats of
production. This has resulted in reduction in cost of production.
 
8.3       NMDC has identified the ROMELT technology of Russia which can  make use of low grade iron ore slimes to
convert  into pig iron. The technology has not so far been commercially used and NMDC would be the first Company in
the world to use ROMELT technology on a commercial basis in Bailadila Sector at an estimated cost of Rs.300 crores
including Rs.20 crores as loan from Technical Development Board, Govt. of India.  The ROMELT SAIL India Ltd

10.1     The main components of the cost of production are  Fixed Cost and  Variable Cost.
The fixed cost consists of salaries and wages, depreciation and office/ selling expenses. The fixed cost is being reduced
by introduction of multi-skilling concepts and by adoption of CCTV at OCSL Plants. The variable cost consists of
explosives, drill bits, tyre & tubes, spares and consumables. It also consists cost incurred towards royalty and
electricity.

additional Railway freight and Port handling charges  before product reaches the consumer. The port charges and
Railway freight charges are not under the control of NMDC. It may be worth mentioning that the cost incurred in
Railway freight and port charges amounts to 60% of the cost and balance 40% cost is in the control of NMDC. This
situation creates difficulty for NMDC to compete in the  international market for iron ore. Unless efforts are made to
reduce the railway freight and port charges, it will be difficult for NMDC to sustain the progress of the Corporation.

12.0     MOU RATING OF NMDC 
 
12.1     NMDC is one of the Public Sector Enterprises which has been signing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
with the Government of India since 1991. At the beginning of each financial year, an agreement is reached to achieve
certain parameters such as production, sales, gross margin, ratio of net profit to capital employed, energy conservation,
R & D efforts, human resource development, project implementation etc. based on the past performance into account,
the growth need and the potential to achieve such levels of performance.  These achievements at the year end are
evaluated for the said parameters and the company gets ranked based on the evaluation score. NMDC has been
consistently achieving the rating of “ EXCELLENT” from the very first year of signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was
placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92, from which it moved to third rank in the
year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s performance of excellence and the
achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU performance evaluation, NMDC has
been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This has been a unique achievement as the Joint Top Rank  
has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98, 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and
2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “EXCELLENT”, barring 1998-99 during which period there was general recession. 
NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production, despatches of iron ore, production and
sales of diamonds, profits, increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has been consistently scaling new
heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including foreign exchange earnings to
the country.   For the year 2001-2002, the company has surpassed the MOU target of dispatches of 180 lakh tonnes of
iron ore by achieving 182.04 lakh tonnes. The company has achieved an ever highest profit before tax of Rs.320.15
crores during 2001-2002.
