industry. Though the Price and Purchase Preference Policy has been in existence for a long time, there is need to take
several other measures.
16.2   Finance is a major area, which small-scale units report as a major impediment for marketing. The credit extended
by the units to their customers, to the trade and to the Government departments, and public sector enterprises, blocks a
major part of their funds.
16.3   Market Development Assistance (MDA) Programme has been launched for SSI Associations for participating in
international fairs, exhibitions, collection of information on marketing/exports, conducting surveys for filing anti-
dumping cases etc.
16.4   Marketing is an integral part of any commercial ventures. The Committee recommends that banks and other
financial institutions provide marketing oriented financial assistance to small-scale sector, particularly for advertising,
product promotion and setting up of regional marketing offices. Factoring services by the banks may also be given
greater priority. The Committee further recommends that Sector specific export thrust/policy measures and more Export
Promotion Zones should be established.
XVII. TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION
17.1   The technological upgradation of the SSI units in India has been quite slow. There are a number of factors that are
responsible for this. The Indian market has so far been basically a sellers' market. Therefore, entrepreneurs have not
made any efforts for modernisation. Moreover, there is non-availability of proper information regarding latest
technologies and their suppliers. There is inadequate availability of credit for investment in technological upgradation
and testing facilities are also not readily available. Even the technological institutions set up for assisting the small-scale
industries themselves lacks sophistication and coordination amongst each other.
17.2   The Ministry apprised the Committee that the number of units benefited under Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme for
Technology Upgradation upto 31st March 2002, was 6, and the amount of Subsidy disbursed was Rs. 25.95 lakhs.
However, during 2002-03 (upto February, 2003), 37 more units have availed subsidy totalling to Rs. 84.88 lakhs.
Though the progress of this Scheme has been slow initially, it has picked up momentum subsequently. However, there is
a need to further accelerate the pace of subsidy off-take under the Scheme. The following measures have been taken in
this regard :
          (i)     The progress of implementation of the Scheme is constantly monitored by a Governing and Technology
Approval Board (GTAB).
          (ii)    A Technical Sub-Committee has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Addl. Secretary and
Development Commissioner (SSI) for suggesting the inclusion of new sub-sectors/products and well
established and improved technologies under the Scheme.
          (iii)   Revised guidelines have been prepared by the Technical Sub-Committee. The salient features thereof are as
underlined:
                  a.     Number of eligible products/sub-sectors increased from 14 to 21.
                  b.     Number of eligible Primary Lending Institutions (PLIs) increased by addition of 34 Cooperative Banks
and 21 Regional Rural Banks for which NABARD will be the new Nodal Agency.
                  c.     In-house testing and on-line qualitative control equipments now eligible for assistance.
                  d.     Units availing subsidy under Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation of the
Small Scale Industries (CLCSS) shall not avail any other subsidy for Technology upgradation from the
Central/State/UT Governments.
                  e.     Release of subsidy will be to the extent of 50% with the first instalment of the loan and the balance 50%
with the last instalment.
                  f.      The term "Proven Technology" replaced by "Well-established and Improved Technology".
                  g.     List of Proven (now termed as "Well-established and Improved") Technologies expanded by adding six
new technologies.
          (iv)   Seminars and awareness programmes are organized to popularize the scheme.
17.3   For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.
17.4   Technology Bureau for International Industrial Partnerships and Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises, Delhi
has been providing useful services for technology upgradation in the small-scale units. These organisations need to be

117th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/117threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:27:03]
strengthened further and their activities need to be marketed/advertised in an effective manner. The small-scale
industries in India have added strength to the industrial infrastructure and have been the engine of growth for
industrialisation. However, they are known for producing poor quality products. This makes the Indian goods less
competitive in the international markets.
17.5   The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of technological
upgradation and quality improvement in the SSI units. However, the impacts of these facilities are not adequately felt.
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective and beneficial to the
small industries.
17.6   The Committee further recommends that training to significantly improve quality by creating awareness among
personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and enforcing technical
discipline should be institutionalized. There is a need to conduct a comprehensive research study of SSI units to
determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop methodology for quality improvement and cost
reduction programmes. Further ISO 9000 certification, may be made more attractive to introduce quality-consciousness
among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be upgraded from time to time in tune with the developments in
quality worldwide.
XVIII.        LABOUR REFORMS IN SSIs
18.1   The Committee has been getting requests from various Industry Associations on the need to implement labour
reforms so as to make the SSI sector competitive. The Association representing the SSI sector have also time and again
stressed upon the need to free the SSI sector of archaic labour laws and also to free the SSI sector from the Inspector
Raj.
18.2   In this context the Committee observes that the present structure of labour laws does not encourage efficient
performance by the SSIs Managements find it difficult to manage their human resources optimally because of the
constrained labour laws. As of now, the same set of labour laws is applicable to all industrial undertakings, irrespective
of their size.
18.3   The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with simple
provision understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons should be
kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to govern the
relationship between the Employer and the Employee has to be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments Act
may also be suitably modified so as to adapt itself to the needs of the present day SSI sector.
18.4   The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund
& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance Act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small-scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated on a priority basis for providing for one insurance cover to each
workman. The Committee strongly feels that the small-scale units should be able to devote more time to quality
management rather than inspector management.
XIX.  MULTIPLICITY OF AGENCIES
19.1   The Committee observes that at present, there are several Government agencies to deal with small-scale industries
in India. These include Ministry of SSI & ARI, Office of Development Commissioner (SSI), Small Industries
Development Organisation, Small Industries Service Institutes, National Small Industries Corporation, Small Industries
Development Bank of India, Product-cum-process Development Centres, Regional Testing Centres, District Industries
Centres, State Financial Corporations, State Industrial Development Corporations, State Small Industries Development
Corporations, etc.
19.2   The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined. It
needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities of
these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small-scale sector.
XX.    DE-RESERVATION OF SSI ITEMS
20.1   The Union Minister for Commerce announced the removal of restrictions while announcing the EXIM policy for
2002-07. While the impact of the removal of QRs is being felt directly by industries, which were earlier protected, there
is likely to be greater impact on the SSIs, especially with regard to their competitive ability and integration with the
global markets against the opportunities of an expanding global market.
20.2   The policy of reservation, was not brought as a measure of protection alone, but was brought for some other

117th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/117threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:27:03]
factors as well as provisions of employment opportunities, development of industrial activities in the backward and rural
areas, utilization of local raw-materials, restraining migration of labour etc. Large industries and MNCs are not barred
from manufacturing the reserved items. They have only to adhere to the stipulation that 50% of their production of the
reserved items should be exported, which they could easily do with their latest technologies and their professional
management.
20.3   De-reservation of over 50 items which were marked for exclusive production in the SSI sector has hit hard such
affected and related units. The Committee fails to see any supportive and promotional measure in the latest Budget for
such affected units. It is to be noted that the Government had accepted the Abid Hussain Committee Report in full in
1997. The Abid Hussain Committee recommended that the abolition of reservation should accompany a support
package for the small industries, which include equity support, interest rate concessions, technology assistance etc. The
Abid Hussain Committee, therefore, recommended allocation of Rs. 500 crore per year i.e. Rs. 2,500 crore over the next
five years for the purpose.
20.4   The Ministry apprised the Committee that SSI reservation is in respect of manufacturing only. Export
opportunities on the other hand are a function of marketing for which there is no reservation. Even a reserved item can
be manufactured by a non-SSI unit when it undertakes to export more than 50% of its production. In any case, out of the
total of about 8,000 items being manufactured in the SSI sector, only 749 items are currently reserved and a further de-
reservation of 75 items has been announced in the Union Budget 2003-04.
20.5   Phased de-reservation of 881 items relating to laboratory chemicals and re-agents, leather and leather products,
plastic products, chemicals and chemical products and paper products is in tandem with the recommendations made by
various expert committees. It is desirable that the ceiling of investment in plant and machinery for manufacture of such
products is also increased to a limit of Rs. 5 crore to enable those units for taking up capacity expansion,
technology/upgradation/modernization and export promotion.
20.6   As such, no adverse impact on export can be attributed to the policy of reservation. Government constantly
reviews the situation through a conscious policy of fostering dialogue with stakeholders and putting in place support
measures as required.
20.7   The Committee feels that the Government should have given a support package to the affected units before doing
away with the reservation for such SSI units. The Committee recommends that this may include timely and low cost
credit; export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time frame may be
simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival. In the absence of such package, the
Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive. Moreover, effecting de-reservation without any package
will bring deleterious socio-economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic growth.
XXI.  INTEGRATED INFRASTRUCTURAL DEVELOPMENT SCHEME  (IIDS)
21.1   Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO), Ministry of Small Scale Industries, Government of India has
been operating a number of promotional schemes for the growth of the small-scale industries in the country. The
Integrated Infrastructural Development Scheme is one such Scheme to facilitate the location of industries in rural
backward areas and to generate employment opportunities by establishing close linkages between agriculture and
industry.
21.2   IID Scheme is a Central Sector Scheme in which the Central Government and SIDO contribute to each IID Centre
Rs. 5.00 crore in the ratio of 2: 3 and the cost in excess thereof is met by State/UT Governments. Suitable land for this
purpose has to be provided by the State Government and this cost is not included in estimated cost of Rs. 5 crores.
21.3   The Committee recommends that unless State Governments play a proactive role in creating infrastructure for
industries, integration and harmonization of villages with industrial development cannot be achieved. Active
participation of State Governments, NGOs and SSI Associations should be ensured by providing appropriate
encouragement to them. This is in keeping with the Industrial Policy announced in 1991, to give special thrust to the
promotion and strengthening of small, tiny and village industries.
XXII. DELAYED PAYMENT TO SSIs
22.1   The Committee observes that the Delayed Payment to SSIs by large company continues to be a major problem for
SSIs sector. SSI Association informed the Committee that there is a 'Delayed Payment Act' to sort out the problems but
that has failed to give the desired results. SSI associations have also been suggesting that some punitive action be taken
against those large companies, which make undue delay in making payment to the small scale sector. Whenever they
file their income tax returns, certain amount should be charged from them. If there is some outstanding bill and they
have not paid them on account of delay payment, that amount should be adjusted at the time of filing the returns.
22.2   The Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, during oral evidence of

117th Report of Committee on Industry

Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries, stressed upon problems of delayed payment and stated that many
complaints have been made by SSI Association in this regard.
22.3   The Representatives of Federation of Indian Small and Medium Enterprises (FISME), during their oral evidence
before the Committee, stated that Parliament passed a Bill called Delayed Payments Bill, but unfortunately the
jurisdiction of that Bill does not cover the Government organizations. It pertains to private sector only. The Government
Departments are not adhering to the payment schedule and the problem of delayed payment remain as it is.
22.4   The Committee, therefore, recommends that Comptroller and Auditor General should be advised to devise some
system so that the payments due to SSI are automatically paid within a specified time.
22.5   The Committee is of the opinion that the timely payment to SSIs could be ensured by issuing an appropriate
circular of the Ministry of Finance for the Ministries/Departments at least of the Central Government. The Central
Government should also impress upon the State Governments to take similar measures to expedite payments to SSIs.
22.6   The Committee reiterates its recommendation that stringent action should be taken against the erring large
companies which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time. Necessary amendment for taking punitive action
may also be contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.
XXIII.        PURCHASE PREFERENCE FOR SSI SECTOR
24.1   In USA, there are special laws for small-scale sector. But in our country, there is no such provision for small-scale
sector. Moreover, 50 items have been de-reserved which were exclusively reserved for the small-scale sector. Marketing
facilities for the small-scale sector are also not adequate. Majority of the consumption of items manufactured by small-
scale sector is for domestic consumption. Only 8-10% of the items made by SSIs are exported.
24.2   The Committee reiterates its recommendation, made in its 75th Report, that in order to protect small scale sector
from multinational companies and others, a certain per cent of items, say 33% should be purchased from SSI sector by
Central and State Government Departments/Agencies specially when the items reserved for SSI sector have been
withdrawn and majority of the items have been put on OGL list. The policy of purchase preference system as followed
by USA Government for protection of indigenous industries may be emulated. Necessary action in this regard should be
initiated by the Ministry of SSI immediately.
XXIV.        LIMITED PARTNERSHIP ACT
25.1   Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) in its written memorandum stated that Issues that presently
the partners in a partnership 551 unit have unlimited liabilities resulting from the activities and liabilities of the 551
units. Hence Limited Partnership Act should be inacted which, in turn, will limit the liability of the partners to their
equity contribution as well as facilitate bringing in external equity participation.
25.2   A mention has been made about the Partnership Act in the Union Budget 2003-04 and the Ministry of SSI is
addressing the matter. The Committee desired that the legislation should be enacted without much delay.
XXV. IMPACT OF GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALISATION ON SMALL SCALE SECTOR
26.1   The SSI sector continues to be a major generator of employment, next only to the agriculture sector. The sector
has been consistently meeting the targets fixed for employment generation. Given the vast employment opportunities in
the SSI sector, the Government has envisaged creation of 4.4 million additional jobs in this sector during the Tenth Five
Year Plan period (2002-07).
26.2   The Government is constantly monitoring the impact of globalisation and WTO arrangements on the economy
including SSIs and has put in several measures to safeguard the interests of domestic industry. These include special
focus on areas such as technology upgradation, infrastructure assistance through cluster approach, enhanced fiscal
support, timely availability of credit, adoption of modern management facilities, use of electronic infrastructure and
other IT applications to face the emerging challenges of trade liberalization. Protection of these industries is available in
the form of raising customs duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-dumping duties and countervailing duties,
taking safeguard measures in case of surge in import etc.
26.3   While the globalization and liberalization have exposed the SSI sector to greater competition both domestically
and globally on the one hand, they have on the other provided the SSI sector greater access to markets, cheaper
imported raw materials and technologies. Keeping in view the available trends in employment, exports, production,
number of units etc., which indicate high rates of growth, no major visible adverse impact has been noticed on the SSI
sector.
26.4   With a view to provide a level playing field and help the SSI sector to compete in the international market, the
following measures have been taken by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries:

products and also to impart training to the Small Scale Entrepreneurs for upgrading their knowledge and
sharpening their skills.
26.5     From the oral evidence rendered before the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
by various SSI Associations, it appears that the impact of the above activities have not been as it should have been. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that activities like seminars/workshops should be intensified to bring adequate
awareness among the SSI entrepreneurs.
XXVI.  SINGLE "COMPREHENSIVE LAW"
27.1     Because of the complexities involved in the altering legal statues and the country's Constitutional separation of
Centre-State powers, the Central Government has appointed the Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI) to
propose, inter-alia, a draft of a Comprehensive law for Small Industries. The draft of the Small Enterprises
Development Bill, 2002 was tabled as an Agenda.
27.2     Deputy Director General, CII, during his oral evidence before the Committee stated that there should be "Single
Comprehensive Law" because small scale industry today is really bogged down with all kinds of pressures, the
Inspector-raj, various laws, various records that they are required to maintain. A comprehensive draft law has been
tabled at the last SSI Board meeting, which was then forwarded to various states, because most of these controls are
under the power of various States in India.
27.3     The Committee recommends that the Comprehensive law should be enacted. It should be an encompassing one
and should enable the SSI Sector to come out of the clutches of inspector raj. The Committee is of the opinion that
inspector raj has persisted despite attempt at the higher level to change it and time has come to enact suitable legislative
action to bring the inspector raj to an end.
XXVII.        SURVIVAL OF MINI CEMENT PLANTS
28.1     The Committee in its 81st Report discussed the problems relating to Mini Cement Plants. On receipt of a
representation of U.P. Mini Cement Owner's Association, Kanpur, the matter was again taken up with the Ministry of
Small Scale Industries. The reply received is as under:
            "The issues raised in the above referred representation were taken up with the Uttar Pradesh Financial
Corporation, Kanpur and the Commissioner & Director of Industries, Government of Uttar Pradesh. The
comments/status as reported by the U.P. Financial Corporation is briefly given as under:
            (i)     The problem of Cement Sector as represented by the Association was placed before the UPFC's Board
meeting held on 19.5.2000 after receiving the study report from M/s ICRA Ltd. The concessions sought by

that with further relaxation some more cases came forward for OTS. However, the Association's continued

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
          The Committee observes that in the era of globalisation and liberalisation of the economy, the Small Scale
Industries should be strengthened to compete in the international markets. Policy measures should be formulated and
relevant data should be obtained through surveys, investigations and studies. The Committee recommends that the role
of Development Commissioner for SSI should be oriented in accordance with the ever-changing scenario so as to make
the SSI sector internationally competitive.                                                                                                 (Para 3.5)
          The Committee further observes that it has become extremely essential to create awareness about India's
obligations under the WTO regime and their impact on various sectors. Having heard the representatives of Powerloom,
Readymade garment, Pan Masala Associations, the Committee draws an inference that there is some communication
gap between the SIDO and SSI Associations. Therefore the Committee recommends that there should be regular
interaction between the Government and Small Scale Industries. A Committee at local level should also be formed
between Bankers and local chapters of SSI Associations to sort out their problems relating to credit related issues at
local level in all the States. The local committee should give quarterly report to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries,
Ministry of Finance (Banking Division) and Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry.                            (Para 3.6)
          The Committee expresses its concerns on the role of NSIC in the small scale industry sector. The Committee feels
that the Corporation is still very much relevant in the present scenario and recommends that the Ministry should
wholeheartedly support its restructuring business plans and ensure that Corporation does not lose its focus i.e. providing
marketing and technology upgradation support to the small sector.                                      (Para 4.6)

          The Committee hopes and recommends that NSIC would be able to restart its discounting of bill to help SSI units
whose dues have been stuck up with their clients.                                                               (Para 4.7)
          The Committee recommends that more emphasis should be laid on research studies to know the lacunae hindering
the growth of NSIC so as to stop its declining influence.                                                          (Para 4.8)
          The Committee feels that technical assistance along with other basic necessary inputs for production such as
power, fuel, raw materials and credit at reasonable prices should be provided to make SSIs more competitive. The
Committee further recommends that Cluster-wise tool rooms and CAD-CAM rooms should be set up. (Para 5.4)
          The Committee feels that the process of liberalization has exposed the Small Scale Industries (SSI) sector to
intensified competition both globally and domestically. In order to help building up the capabilities of the units in the
SSI sector to face the emerging challenges, there has to be a further increase in the flow of financial assistance to
facilitate additional capacity generation, expansion of the existing units and improving their capacity utilization,
diversification and to enhance the competitiveness of the sector with a thrust on technology upgradation and
modernization.    (Para 6.8)
          The Committee is of the opinion that there should be effective implementation of these schemes. Further, once a
loan has been sanctioned, a time frame for the release of various installments should be committed in accordance with
the needs of the entrepreneurs. The Committee also feels that it must also be ensured that with the provision of the
concept of single window, the time involved in making the disbursements is considerably reduced. As far as the
National Equity Fund (NEF) scheme is concerned, it may be noted that the disbursements under the scheme are very
small. The scheme needs to be made more effective and efficient.                                                                                   
(Para 6.13)
          The Committee recommends that cost of credit should be directly linked with the benchmarks achieved by a small
unit in terms of Financial, Marketing, Technical, Quality, and Environmental standards.            (Para 6.14)
          The Committee further observes that the implementation and enhancement in the limit for guaranteeing loans
under the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme should include the following :
          (a)    Time bound and effective implementation;
          (b)    Increase of corpus to Rs. 1250 crores over the next one year;
(c)    Enhancement in the maximum availing credit limit to Rs. 50 lakhs.  (Para 6.15)
          The Committee desired that the working of credit guarantee scheme and the availability of credit should be looked
upon as a major issue. The Committee observes that the amount of Rs. 397.56 crore for Credit Guarantee Scheme is
worth Rs. 172.80 crores is very thin inspite of the fact that this is main item on the budget of the Small Scale Industry
Ministry. The Committee strongly recommends for enhancement of allocation and impresses upon the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries to take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance and Planning
Commission.                                                                    (Para 7.8)
          The Committee further observes that credit facility is one of the basic inputs that have to be provided to SSIs if
they have to enhance their competitiveness in the era of globalisation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
banks should come forward in extending a helping hand to the small and tiny sector in sanctioning collateral free loan to
SSIs. The Committee also reiterates that income tax exemption may be provided to the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust of
the Small Industries to make it self-sustainable.                                                                                 (Para 7.9)
          The Committee recommends that more Venture funds should be set up for information technology, biotechnology
and food processing. The Committee feels that Venture Capital could be a successful concept in bringing out the latent
entrepreneurship spirit of the youth of the country. In this context the Committee recommends that a suitable policy
framework may be designed expeditiously to promote setting up of such funds in the public as well as the private sector.
Banks should be encouraged to entertain Venture Capital funding to SSI units.                                                              
          (Para 8.3)
          The Committee observes that removal of quantitative restrictions has brought Indian industry face-to-face with
foreign products, which are technologically for superior. Moreover, technical barriers to trade are emerging as major
non-tariff barriers to access the markets of the developed countries. Therefore, Indian Industry, particularly the SSI
sector, needs support to upgrade to the high technical standards set by the developed countries.              (Para 9.8)
          The Committee recommends that in order to initiate the activities of the proposed fund and run the same on
sustainable basis, initially a fund support of Rs. 20 crore may be provided by the Government of India to SIDBI. The

          The Ministry has informed that it was pointed out by the industry that the imports from Nepal are basically re-
exports without any significant value addition to take advantage of the facility of 0% customs duty. The Committee is
also concerned that goods like Vanaspati are being imported which is adversely affecting the domestic producers. In the
absence of proper rules of origin, Nepal has become a re-export point for many of the products from China and other
South Asian countries. The provision of certificate of origin was dispensed with in the Indo-Nepal Treaty, which gave
rise to a spurt in flow of Chinese goods in the guise of Nepali goods. The Committee recommends that adequate
safeguards be taken to stop misuse of Indo-Nepal Treaty for import of goods from China and other
countries.                                             (Para 12.2)
          The Committee observes that the major option for limiting imports that remains for use by policy-makers in a
QR-free regime is that of higher tariffs. The Committee recommends that QRs may be converted into tariff and non-
tariff equivalents to give an adequate protection to the domestic SSIs. While this measure would be a discouraging
factor for foreign producers to export their cheap goods to India, it would also mean increasing revenue for the
Government of India.          (Para 12.8)
          The Committee recommends that on account of almost all products coming under Open General License (OGL)
list, the Government may further strengthen the anti-dumping mechanism so that remedial measures may be initiated
expeditiously. Countervailing duties and safeguard duties may be imposed in order to protect domestic producers from
cheap imports.                                                                                                                (Para 12.9)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends tariff and non-tariff barriers may be imposed in the form of higher safety
standards, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures as are permissible within the WTO framework.                             
          (Para 12.10)
          The Committee further recommends that compulsory printing of manufacturing date, maximum retail price (in
Indian rupees) and composition of the products, by foreign exporters should be introduced. This would, of course, be
compatible with the national obligation under WTO, as domestic manufacturers are already required to comply with
these requirements.          (Para 12.11)
          In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends that :
          I.      A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSIs and the commercial banks may earmark a
portion of loans to ailing SSIs.
          II.     The State Level Institutional Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalized and DICs may be used as a forum
to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation.
          III.   Local committees should be formed between the State Government and SSI Association and Banks to sort
out the credit related issues at local level.
          IV.   The Committee reiterates its observations given in its 75th Report that an Arbitration Clause may also be
included in all borrower-lender arrangements in terms of Indian Arbitration Act to avoid protracted litigation
and costs. Although Entrepreneurship Development through small enterprises is basically owner-managed, a
significant number of them do employ persons for performing managerial functions. The SSI units on the
growth path should encourage their key personnel to think and work more as entrepreneurs than as mere
employees.                                                                                                                     (Para 13.4)

The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective and beneficial to the
small industries.   (Para 17.5)
          The Committee further recommends that training to significantly improve quality by creating awareness among
personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and enforcing technical
discipline should be institutionalized. There  is a need to conduct a comprehensive research study of SSI units to
determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop methodology for quality improvement and cost
reduction programmes. Further ISO 9000 certification, may be made more attractive to introduce quality-consciousness
among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be upgraded from time to time in tune with the developments in
quality worldwide.          (Para 17.6)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with simple
provisions understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons should
be kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to govern
the relationship between the Employer and the Employee has to be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments Act
may also be suitably modified so as to adapt itself to the needs of the present day SSI sector.                                             
(Para 18.3)
          The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund
& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance Act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated on a priority basis for providing for one insurance cover to each
workman. The Committee strongly feels that the small scale units should be able to devote more time to quality
management rather than inspector management.          (Para 18.4)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined. It
needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities of
these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small scale sector.          
          (Para 19.2)
          The Committee feels that the Government should have given a support package to the affected units before doing
away with the reservation for such SSI units. The Committee recommends that this may include timely and low cost
credit; export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time frame may be
simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival. In the absence of such package, the
Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive. Moreover, effecting de-reservation without any package
will bring deleterious socio-economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic
growth.                                              (Para 20.7)

`Sickness in SSI Sector in the city of Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh' which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 11th December, 2002.
 
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report. They have been categorised as follows :-
 
(i)
                  Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government :- Paras 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, 1.10 and 1.11 (Chapter - I)
 
(ii)        Recommendations/Observations, which   the Committee does not desire to pursue in  view  of  the Government's replies :- Paras 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7  (Chapter-II).
 
(iii)       Recommendations/Observation in respect of  which   the Committee has not accepted replies of the Government :- Paras 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8, 3.9,  3.7,  3.8,  3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14,
3.15, 3.16, 3.17 and 3.18 (Chapter-III).
 
(v)
               Recommendations/Observations of the Committee have been placed separately. (Chapter-IV).
 
3.         The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries has accepted its recommendations as mentioned in Chapter - I of the Report.
 
4.         In respect of the recommendations made in Para 2.11, 2.18, 2.22, 4.0, 4.5, 4.6 and 4.9 in Chapter-II, the Committee is convinced with the explanation given by the Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue
further.
 
5.         The Committee expresses its concern over non-implementation of recommendations contained in Chapter-III and therefore the Committee desires that the ministry  should furnish logical explanation in respect of
these recommendations.
 
6.            Observations and Recommendations at a glance may be seen in Chapter IV.
 
ACTION TAKEN REPORT ON OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE 90 TH REPORT OF THE DEPARTMENT RELATED PARLIAMENTARY STANDING COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRY ON
SICKNESS IN SSI SECTOR IN THE CITY OF KANPUR, UTTAR PRADESH
 
 
 
 
CHAPTER – I
 
LABOUR REFORMS IN SSI SECTOR
 
Recommendation
 
1.1       The Associations brought it to the notice of the Committee that the Union Finance Minister had assured that units employing less than one thousand persons would not be brought under the ambit of labour laws, but in
reality, when these units are required to resize their manpower, they are not able to do it as the employees go in for arbitration where dates of hearing are fixed six months after filing the application.  When labour is given
some rights, they start misbehaving with the management.  Management of SSI units spend a lot of time in solving the problems posed by the labourers.  In Kanpur 90 per cent of SSI units have become sick due to leadership
of labour.  There is no power in the hands of the management to discipline the labour.
 
Wherever the statutory dues were paid in the industry, sickness started to surface and whenever workers were made permanent, they stopped doing work and started misbehaviour with the management.  Labour
reforms should, therefore, be done in a way so that the constraints coming in the way of running units could be removed.  Hire and Fire system may be one of the options  which can be considered by the Government. 
(Para  2.3)
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Amendment proposals in the Industrial Disputes Act,1947 are under consideration of the Government as informed by Ministry of Labour which deals with the issue.
 
 
PROVISIION FOR TESTING FACILITY
 
1.2            Recommendation
 
There is no provision for a testing facility in Kanpur for the paint industry. Consequently, they have to go to Kolkata for getting their products tested. To an enquiry the Association informed that IIT and CIGS do not
have any provision for testing facilities for SSI units. These institutions cater to the needs of the defence sector only. Even if SSI sector get any tests done at these institutions, the test results are not accepted by other
organizations like Railways, etc. The Associations, therefore, requested for providing a testing facility for the paint industry.
(Para  2.5)
 
Action taken by the Government
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/118threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:28:04]
            The Regional Testing Centre (NR), New Delhi is having complete testing facilities for testing paints, enamels, dry distemper, varnish, solvents, thinners, pigments and extenders as per relevant Indian Standards. This
Centre provides services to all small scale industrial units located in the northern region of the country, which include the State of UP. Small scale industrial units located in Kanpur can avail the testing facilities for getting
their products tested at RTC, New Delhi. It is further stated that concessional testing charges are levied for test samples received from registered small scale industrial units. The laboratories of Regional Testing Centre(NR),
New Delhi are having  recognition from the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), New Delhi and accreditation with the NABL, Department of Science & Technology, Govt. of India, New Delhi.  SISI, Kanpur has been advised
to disseminate the information on test facilities available at the Centre regarding paints, varnishes, etc. and motivate the SSI units to take advantage of these testing facilities.
 
BANKING OMBUDSMAN SCHEME
 
1.3            Recommendation
 
Even if an industry falls sick, it does not mean that it will not survive.  If the proper aid is given to the industry at the initial stage of sickness, it can survive.  The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has given a guideline for
assessing the sickness of SSI but it is on paper only.  The banks and Financial Institutions (FIs) are not adhering to it.  It should be mandatory for the banks/ Financial Institutions to adhere to the RBI guidelines regarding
assessment of sickness of industries.  There should be an ombudsman with whom complaints against banks/ Financial Institutions can be registered.
Para  2.12
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The detailed guidelines have been issued by RBI to all scheduled commercial banks for implementation, wherein banks have been advised to take a sympathetic attitude and strive for rehabilitation in respect of viable
SSI units, particularly wherever the sickness is on account of circumstances beyond the control of entrepreneurs.  The guidelines also provide for a mechanism for early detection of sickness in SSI units and the package for
rehabilitation of such units for implementation by the financing banks.
 
The RBI has advised the banks to implement the guidelines fully and to submit a report to their Boards on the progress made in assisting the SSI units under the new guidelines.
 
            The Banking Ombudsman Scheme exits which covers aspects relating to non-observance of RBI directives on interest rates, delays in sanction, disbursement or non-observance of prescribed time schedule for
disposal of loan applications, etc. The RBI has given directives that banks should comply with the Banking Ombudsman Scheme.
 
 
TELECOM NETWORK
 
1.4            Recommendation
 
Poor telecom network in semi-urban areas sometimes prove to be a hindrance for SSI units.  A little communication gap between the supplier and the client due to absence of proper telecommunication system may
result in business loss.
Para  2.14
 
Action taken by the Government
 
With infrastructure growth in the communications sector, telecom services, Internet services, etc. have expanded vastly reaching even to semi-urban and rural areas.  The telecommunication system has improved
considerably and SSI entrepreneurs should not find any major difficulties in accessing the services.
 
MINIMUM WAGES
 
1.5            Recommendation
 
Industrial unrest and wages are inter-linked.  If the industry is using skilled labour, it cannot be engaged on minimum wages.  Wages are determined by demand and supply.  Skilled workers will go to an industry
where  they get higher wages.  If the industry sticks to the stipulated minimum wages, it will give rise to industrial unrest, which will hamper working of the industry.  Government should make a fresh survey to define
minimum wages.
Para  2.16
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Ministry of Labour has informed that the Minimum Wages Act,1948 provides for fixation, revision and enforcement of minimum wages of the workers engaged in the scheduled employments both in the Central and
State sphere mostly in the unorganized sector. The Act safeguards the interests of these workers, as they are susceptible to exploitation due to illiteracy and lack of bargaining power. The Act binds the employers to pay the
minimum wages fixed under the Act. The minimum wages are fixed and revised separately for highly skilled, skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers. The rates of wages of the workers are fixed at higher level with the
rise in merits of the skills.
 
PURCHASE PREFERENCE POLICY FOR SSI
 
1.6            Recommendation
 
Government institutions are not giving priority to SSIs in the matter of purchase of various items, Government bodies are purchasing items from outside the state although the same items are available in the state at
competitive rates.
 
Action taken by the Government

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

There already exists a Government Purchase & Price Preference Policy wherein certain facilities/ benefits are being provided to the SSI units as a marketing support measure. The Draft “Small Enterprises
Development Bill” under  consideration of the Ministry of SSI  also covers the aspect of measures for trade protection.
 
 
WORKSHOP IN KANPUR
 
1.7            Recommendation
 
The Committee desired that the Ministry should reach the grass-root level and for this purpose, it should hold regular orientation courses, seminar, workshop etc. in Kanpur.  The Committee hopes that this kind of
action would enable the SSIs to reap benefit of the schemes formulated for them by the Government of India.
Para  4.1
 
Action taken by the Government
 
SISI, Kanpur has been organizing Skill Development Programmes, Industrial motivational campaigns, Entrepreneurship Development Programmes, Management Development Programmes, Vendor Development
Prgrammes, Buyer Seller Meets, etc. on a regular basis at Kanpur. Besides, Awareness Programmes/ Workshops, Training Programme on Packaging for Exports/ISO 9000, Sensitization Programme on WTO, etc. are also
organized. These programmes are organized in collaboration with the concerned Central/ State Departments and information on the various schemes being implemented for the promotion and development of SSIs is
provided for the benefit of SSI entrepreneurs/participants.
 
 
MONITORING OF CREDIT FLOW TO SSIT SECTOR
 
1.8            Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that there was some mismatch between the RBI figures and the associations contention about the non-availability of credit.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries should strictly monitor the credit flow to SSIs so that the true picture in this regard emerges.
Para  4.2
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            The Reserve Banks of India (RBI) regulates the scheduled commercial banks and is therefore, is the only authentic source of information on credit flow to the SSI sector from the commercial banks.  The data on
advances to the sector by the various banks is compiled and monitored at the RBI level. 
 
            In order to have a constant and focused vigil on flow of credit to SSI and address the problems faced by the sector in securing adequate credit, etc. the RBI has constituted the Standing Advisory Committee to review
flow of Institutional Credit to SSI sector under the Chairmanship of the Deputy Governor, RBI.  The representatives of SSI Associations are also members in this Committee. The Committee inter-alia reviews the flow of
credit to the SSI sector and problems faced by the sector in securing an adequate flow of credit. Therefore, it may be seen that there is a transparency in the mechanism of monitoring of credit flow to the SSI sector wherein
the SSI Associations are given the opportunity to give their views or suggestions.    
 
DISPOSAL OF LOAN APPLICATIONS IN BANKS
 
1.9            Recommendation
 
The Committee recommends that the banks should give receipt to the applicant  after taking the application and inform the applicant within two months the reasons for rejecting the application.  Banks should be
persuaded to be SSI friendly.  As regards non-supply of required financial data by the applicants, the banks should give the applicant proper counselling at the initial stage of the scrutiny of the application.
Para  4.3
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The RBI has advised the banks that a clear cut monitoring system may be laid down which captured the process of sanctioning loan from the receipt of application to sanction or rejection and the reasons for rejection.
The banks  have also been advised to prepare the necessary ‘Check List’ and circulate it among the controlling offices and branches to make available the same to the potential borrower while giving the loan application
forms.
Further, the RBI has recently instructed the banks to dispose off loans up to Rs.25,000 within 2 weeks and in other cases for loans up to Rs. 5 lakhs within a period of 4 weeks on receipt of loan applications complete
in all respects and duly accompanied by a check list. All such loan applications which are complete in all respects and accompanied by a check list should also be acknowledged by the bank branches on the same day i.e. on
the day the application is received by the branch.
 
ROLE OF LEAD BANKS
 
1.10            Recommendation
 
The Committee further recommends that all the lead banks should have interaction with the State Industries’ Association on regular basis regarding credit and its recovery etc.  and the decisions taken in the meeting
may be conveyed to the Ministry of SSI and RBI for further necessary action.
Para  4.4
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/118threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:28:04]

            Lead banks in their quarterly meetings of DCC/ DLRC critically reviews the position of flow of credit as well as recovery position of all member banks.  The RBI is of the view that in order to avoid the list of

Hosiery industry in Kanpur is linked with cotton and textile but there is no centre for Uttar Pradesh to develop cotton and textile. Hosiery industry has to go all the way to Tirupur for development purpose. A process
and product development centre should be established at Kanpur to help the SSIs in the matter of technology. This will give hope to the closed cotton and textile mills.
Para  2.15
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Ministry of  Textiles has stated  that the Government of India supported Powerloom Service Centre (PSC) at Kanpur, is providing very valuable support to small scale industry located there. The Centre provides
technical advice and testing facilities to the industry. The PSC is proposed to be provided with modern looms and strengthened in 10 th plan. At the moment Textiles Ministry has no new scheme to establish process and
product development centre. However, the Powerloom Service Centre can provide all necessary assistance to the SSIs located at Kanpur in the matter of technology. 
 
A Textile & Hosiery Park is proposed to be developed at Kanpur by UPSIDC Ltd. at an estimated cost of Rs. 21 crores with an objective to impart focused thrust for setting up of apparel manufacturing units of
international standards.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee happy note that Powerloom Service Centre (PSC) at Kanpur can provide all assistant to the SSIs located in Kanpur in the matter of technology. The Committee also notes that a Textile and Hosiery
Park  is proposed to be developed at Kanpur. The Committee recommends that SSI association be informed about this information in a suitable way.
DELAYED PAYMENTS TO SSIs BY PSUs AND LARGE INDUSTRIES
 
3.9            Recommendation
 
Public Sector Undertakings and other large industries buy from SSIs on credit basis and the credit period varies from three to six months.  But SSIs are  not able to realize the payment from such buyers and thus their
money remains blocked for a long period.  The Delayed Payments Act, which is supposed to resolve the issue, proved to be ineffective.  Government should suitably amend the Act to make it more effective.
Para  2.17

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/118threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:28:04]
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            To ensure prompt payment by large industries to small scale industrial units, the Government has enacted Interest on Delayed Payments to Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings Act in 1993. The Act as
amended provides for payment of penal interest by the buyers to supplier, if payment are made after due date, at one and half time of Prime Lending Rate charged by State Bank of India. The Act also provides that
notwithstanding anything contained in the Income Tax Act, 1961, the amount of interest payable or paid by any buyer under or in accordance with the provisions of this Act, shall not for the purpose of computation of
Income under Tax Act, be allowed as deduction. However, the problem of delay in payment of bills for supplies made by Small Scale Industrial (SSI) units to large industries continued despite enactment of the Act.
 
To make the Act effective, the Act was amended in 1998. The most important change that has been brought about by amended Act is that the SSI supplier can now approach the Industry Facilitation councils (IFCs)
set up by States for settlement of their disputes with the buyers in regard to delay in payment etc. of the supplies made by them. Facilitation Council has been set up in Uttar Pradesh which is working for about last 2 years. 
    
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The SSI association has informed that if they approach the Industry facilitation council for settlement of disputes with the buyers in regard to delay in payment, they would not get orders from such buyers in future.
To that extend the amended act has failed to achieve its objective. In fact IFCs should impact the books of PSUs and other large industries to ascertain the extent of delay by them in making payment to SSIs.  
 
SOAP INDUSTRY
 
3.10            
Recommendation
 
With the arrival of MNCs and concession given to Khadi industries, sickness in the soap industry commenced. The methodology and size of manpower required for hand made soap industry is the same in both the
SSI and Khadi industries. But Khadi industries get concession while SSIs do not get any such relief. Kanpur had 150 soap factories in SSI sector. Today, it has not more than 20, which are struggling to alive. Soap is made
out of imported non-edible oil on which 55 per cent import tax is paid by the industry. For the last one and a half year the rate of import duty has been raised to the extent of 45 per cent. In Nepal, there is no import duty.
They import duty- free non-edible oil, manufacture finished product and re-export to the third country. While the manufacturing cost of Nepal soap is Rs. 16,  the same is manufactured in Kanpur at a cost of Rs. 24.  To save
the soap industry in Kanpur, the rate of import duty on non-edible oil has to be reduced.
Para  2.19
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Laundry soap is reserved for exclusive development in the small scale sector and thus no MNC / organized sector unit is permitted to manufacture laundry soap (except in certain specific conditions of meeting export
obligation or having COB licence). However, it may be stated that due to the introduction of Detergent Powder / Cakes, the consumers are slowly and slowly switching over to Detergent Powders/cakes for laundry purpose.
Accordingly, a large number of small scale laundry soap units have also diversified their production to the manufacture of Detergent Cakes/Powders in the country.
 
              There is no concession given to the KVIC/KVIB or any other organization approved by KVIC/KVIB manufacturing laundry soap. Both KVIC/KVIB units and small scale units manufacturing laundry soap without
the aid of power are chargeable NIL rate of duty.
 
             There is no specific exemption from import duty levied on imported non-edible oil used as raw-material in the manufacture of laundry soap in Khadi Industries and SSI units. At present, the non-edible oils such as
Palm Fatty Acid Distillate (PFAD) or Palm Acid Oil which are most commonly used by KI or SSI units with more than 20% free fatty acid content are levied import duty at 30%.It may also be stated that to eliminate
misdeclaration of crude oil e.g. Crude Palm Oil as non-edible oil, a condition of minimum 20% FFA has been added for availing concessional rate of duty.
 
              As regards imports of laundry soap from Nepal, where 0% import duty is leviable on raw-materials for products which are subsequently exported, it is to be stated that this is applicable to all products.
 
            The renewed Indo-Nepal Treaty has been appreciated and it been observed that the Agreement takes care of most of the problems. Due to incorporation of value addition norms in the Renewed Treaty, goods of Non-
Nepalese origin would not be accepted(in the guise of Nepalese goods) in India as per the Renewed Agreement.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee notes that SSIs engaged in laundry soap has lost its market as consumers are snitching over to detergent cake/powder and how many SSI units have diversified their production to manufacture
detergent cake/power.  The Committee recommends that SSI associations be also persuaded to diversify their production to suit the consumers choice. The Committee further notes that import duty on non edible oils which is
raw material for soap industry are levied import duty at 30%. The Committee is still of the opinion that duties on import of non edible oils for use in SSI sector should be suitably reduced to assist the SSI soap units which are
at present struggling to remain in the market.
 
INTEGRATED INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT SCHEME
 
3.11            
Recommendation
 
Industries are given sites at places where basic infrastructure like roads, communication, drainage etc. are not provided. Industrial sites are allotted far away from the urban area where basic amenities like drinking
water are not available. No redressal measures have been taken by the Government despite the fact that this was brought to their notice.
Para  2.20
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The State Governments provide necessary infrastructure facilities to develop the small scale industries in their respective States.
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

            The Integrated Infrastructure Development (IID) Scheme launched by the Government of India extends to all areas in the country with 50% reservation for the rural areas. The scheme aims at creation of basic
infrastructure on cluster basis for the small scale sector. The thrust of the scheme is on creation/ upgradation of infrastructural facilities like power, water, tele-communication, drainage, pollution control facilities, effluent
treatment & disposal system, roads, banks, raw material depots, storage, and marketing outlets, etc. in the new /existing Centres/ Industrial Areas.
 
            The Central Government and SIDBI contribute to each IID Centre up to Rs. 5 crores in the ratio of 2:3 (4:1 in case of NE Region) and the cost in excess of Rs. 5 crores per centre are to be met by the State/ UT
Governments.   Under the Scheme, the State/UT Governments have to provide suitable land for the Centres the cost of which may be recovered from the implementing agencies. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee desires to know the details of infrastructure created/upgraded in and around Kanpur under the Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme. Similar information may be given in respect of other
states.
 
ANTI SOCIAL ELEMENTS IN INDUSTRIAL AREAS
 
3.12            Recommendation
 
Due to power cut, anti-social elements are thriving in industrial areas. State police authority expresses their helplessness,as they do not have enough force to tackle the law and order situation there. The SSI branches
of banks are located outside the urban area of Kanpur. It is quite difficult to go to the SSI branch to deposit or collect money. Banks should be located in safe areas.
Para  2.21
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Maintenance of law and order primarily comes under the purview of the State Governments. After the nationalization of Banks, it was one of the basic objectives to expand the network of branches all over the country
and take banking to the remotest corner so that access to credit facilities becomes easier for various categories of borrowers including SSI borrowers.  Banks have been advised by the RBI to make concerted efforts to
operationalise at least one specialized SSI branch in every district and centres having clusters of SSI unit. As at the end of March, 2002, 395 specialised SSI branches of the public sector banks are functioning.  Further, banks
have been permitted to categorise their general banking branches having 60% or more of their advances to SSI sector as specialized SSI branches in order to encourage them to open more specialized SSI branches for
providing better service to this sector as a whole. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Government has not appreciated the apprehansion expressed by the SSI units about the anti social elements thrives in industrial areas. The Committee recommends that the concern of the Committee may be
conveyed to the State Govt. for  appropriate action. 
 
COMMENEFFLUENT TREATMENT PLANT           
 
3.13            Recommendation
 
Pollution control for the industries is necessary, but generally, problems keep on cropping up due to various reasons. Therefore, in industrial areas where SSIs are situated as a cluster, facilities should be provided by
the administration for setting up of a common effluent treatment plant.
Para  2.23
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The Scheme on Common Effluent Treatment Plant(CETP) which is for the prevention and control of pollution from the small scale industrial sector has been initiated by the Ministry of Environment & Forests. New
and the existing CETPs need technological up-gradation in order to meet the new standards, waste management policies prescribed by the Ministry from time to time.  The pattern of the funding is Central & State subsidy
25% each, entrepreneur contribution 20% and loans from financial institutions 30%. The entrepreneurs are required to have financial and technical appraisal of the project and then the project has to be routed through the
State Pollution Control Board for Central subsidy.
 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee desires to know the details of the scheme on common ------ Treatment Plant  initiated for Small Scale Industrial sector in and around Kanpur.
 
REPRESENTATION OF SSI IN STATE LEGISLATURE AND MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS
 
3.14            Recommendation
 
In the absence of any representation of SSIs in the State Legislature and Municipal Corporations, the problems of SSIs are not highlighted and even if these are highlighted Government does not take them seriously. A

Para  2.25
 
Action taken by the Government

3.16            Recommendation
 
SSIs receive their payments in smaller denomination notes (like one, two or five) and coins. The banks do not accept these currencies. SSIs have to suffer the loss of approximately five per cent (brokerage) in

The Committee is happy to note that RBI  has issued a guideline in the matter. The Committee desires that SSI associations may be informed of the RBI instructions given to the banks.

The Committee has been informed that as per RBI’s recent instructions, NPAs are affected within three months of sanction of loan.  In addition, interest is charged every month, which in turn affects the credit

SSIs.

Action taken by the Government
 
The RBI advised the banks to adopt 90 days’ norm for recognition of loan impairment from the year ending March 31,2004 and that they should move over to charging of interest on advances at monthly rests with
effect from April 1,2002. Ministry of SSI had taken up with the RBI the issues that 90 days’ over due norm for identification of NPAs would be disadvantageous for the SSIs and charging interest on monthly rests would
make credit costlier. The RBI has clarified that the above norm for recognition of loan impairment and the consequent charging of interest at monthly rests has been introduced after due consideration and in keeping with
international best practices. Since our financial system is also under scrutiny from various international agencies, it is not feasible to depart from these norms without affecting the confidence of the international and financial
capital markets. Besides, 90 days’ norm will come into effect only after a considerable lapse of time viz., March 31,2004 and hence both banks and the industry will have sufficient time to adjust to the new requirement.   
 
            The RBI has subsequently advised the banks in May,2002 that they should ensure that the effective rate does not go up merely on account of switchover to the system of charging of interest on monthly rests. The
banks have been advised not to compound interest at monthly rests till March31,2003.

REPORT
 
        The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel
management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains information on several areas in respect of
PSEs. In fulfilling its roles, it associated itself with other Ministries and Organizations.
1.1   The important role and tasks of the Department of Public Enterprises are :
          (i)    General policy relating to Public Sector Enterprises;
          (ii)   Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to Public Sector Enterprises;
          (iii)  Formulation of Policy Guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) in areas like performance
improvement and evaluation, financial management, personnel management, board structures, wage
settlement, training, industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.;
          (iv)  Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central PSEs under VRS;
          (v)   Matters relating to reservation of posts in PSEs to certain classes of citizens;
          (vi)  All matters relating to Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Public Sector Enterprises and the
Administrative Ministries/Departments;
          (vii)Matters relating to the delegation of powers to the Board of Directors;
          (viii)To undertake in-depth studies in respect of significant areas of functioning of Central PSEs;
          (ix)  Matters relating to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE);
          (x)   Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE);
          (xi)  To monitor and evaluate the performance of PSEs and to act as a repository of data and to bring out an
Annual Survey for the Parliament;
          (xii)Permanent Machinery of Arbitrators for settlement of disputes among Public Sector Enterprises and
Government Departments except disputes relating to tax matters;

COUNSELLING RETRAINING AND REDPLOYMENT SCHEME
3.     The Scheme for Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment was introduced by Department of Public Enterprises
from the year 2001-02, and has been carried out continuously for the year 2002-03. The Scheme inter alia aims at
providing an opportunity of short duration orientation programme to the rationalised employees of Central PSEs. As per
the recent trends, on an average around 45,000 employees are being released under VRS/VSS every year. Further the
nodal training agencies selected for carrying out the CRR programme have also projected higher targets for the
coverage. However, considering the availability of the fund and in order to maximize the utilization of the resources,
targets are distributed among the agencies considering their capacity, potential to train and support the redeployment
drive. For carrying out the CRR programme, 17 nodal agencies were selected out of which 16 agencies were functional
during 2001-02. The number of nodal agencies have been increased from 17 to 25 during 2002-03. During 2001-02
selected nodal agencies were allowed to operate through 40 Employee Assistance Centres (EACs). The number of
EACs has increased to 80 during 2002-03.
3.1   The Department of Public Enterprises has apprised that considering the need to have flexibility and also economy
of the scale, the training has been distributed in 20 days/30 days/40 days module depending upon trade/skill being opted
by the rationalized employees. The projection under the CRR programme is made on year-to-year basis. For the year
2001-02, against a projection of 8000 employees to be trained, 8423 persons were trained. For the year 2002-03, there is
a projection to train 10,000 persons and it is likely to meet the target as per available trends being received from the
agencies. For the year 2003-04, it is projected to meet a target of Rs. 11,000 person. The Expenditure Norms per person
are separate for 20 days/30 days/40 days modules of training. Similarly, a separate element of sensitization programme
for providing 3 days counselling camp in the vicinity of the PSU has been made available under the CRR programme so
as to provide the basic inputs, counsel the employees prior to their release from the organizations and to assess the
training needs so as to enable  them to rejoin the productive process once they part with the CPSU.
3.2   With regard to monitoring mechanism, agencies have been asked to submit the batchwise information for the
training undertaken, the progress on redeployment of the persons so trained etc. Besides, the officials of CRR Cell, DPE
also inspects the site of the training, inter-act with the participants. In order to support the mechanism, endeavour has
also been made to set up the Coordination Committees consisting of Members of Central PSEs in the vicinity, lead bank
managers and the nodal agencies carrying out the programme so that some of the basic issues could be discussed locally
and the CRR programme could be monitored at the local level by the said Committee.
3.3   Out of the total plan allocation of Rs. 10.00 crores in BE 2003-04, the major part of it i.e. 9.00 crores is for
Retraining and Redeployment of rationalized workers of CPUs. The Ministry has apprised that the Plan allocation of Rs.
8.50 crore was made in 2002-03 (RE) and in B.E. 2003-04, Rs. 9 crores has been allocated for the implementation of the
Scheme for Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment of rationalised employees of CPSUs.
3.4   The Committee finds that there has been constant increase in the plan allocation of CRR Scheme over the
earlier years. As against Rs. 6.75 crores allocated in RE 2001-02, an allocation of Rs. 8.50 crores was made in BE
2002-03 for CRR which was taken up by DPE since 1st April, 2001. Earlier it was dealt by the Department of
Industrial Policy and Promotion. In BE 2003-04, the amount has been increased to Rs. 9.00 crores. This is the
third year since the scheme commenced. The Committee recommends that in view of the increasing trends in the
plan allocation for CRR scheme and time factor, a suitable mechanism for appraisal of the scheme should be
evolved by DPE so as to evaluate the results in this regard and assess the desired impact of the scheme.
3.5   During the year 2003-04, the Plan allocation is of Rs. 10 crore of which 10% has been earmarked for North East
(NE) Region and the balance i.e. Rs. 9 crore is for the CRR programme for other regions inclusive of project monitoring
element. The allocations for the year 2001-02 was Rs. 8 crore. Of this, 10% i.e. Rs. 0.80 crore was earmarked for NE
Region and the balance of Rs. 7.20 crore for CRR programme for other regions including project monitoring. For

3.6   The Committee observes that North Eastern Area and Sikkim comprising of seven states i.e. Arunachal

The Committee, therefore, recommends that the plan allocation for North Eastern area and Sikkim should be

wider coverage of 
the scheme.
3.7   The Ministry has further apprised that the CRR programme is voluntary in nature. Ex-employees who have availed
of VRS and who are willing and eligible being within 58 years of age are selected by the Nodal Agencies after a
thorough counselling and within the target set for these agencies based on the availability of the fund. The trainees
themselves decide the area of training. Nodal agencies help them in identifying the areas having potential to set up new
ventures. The ex-employees of those PSEs, which are located in and around the location of the training centres, are
invited for the programme. Department of Public Enterprises is in the process of preparation of the list of the trainees,
PSE-wise.
3.8   The Committee in its 73rd report on Demands for Grants (2002-03) also dealt with the CRR scheme and observed
as under :
        "The Committee, however, observes that there may be cases where V.R.S. optees are in the age group of 50-57 and
by human nature they stop learning any new trade and imparting training to them would only result in waste of
time and Government money. The Committee, therefore, recommends that provision may be made for giving
training to the sons/daughters of such persons and that too before they are retired."
        The Ministry in their action taken note stated as under :
        "The recommendations of the Committee in regard to providing the facilities under the CRR programme to the
sons/daughters of the VRS optees who are in the age group of 50-57 have been noted. Considering the human
angle, as recommended by the Hon'ble Members, the matter would be taken up for consideration appropriately."
        The issue was again raised by the Chairman in the course of deliberation with the Secretary, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises. The Secretary stated the following :
        "As far as wards part is concerned, we have this suggestion with us. It is under examination. We will certainly
come back to you sooner than later whether we can include the wards in the training part, where the separated
employee is not able to undertake the training. This is under active consideration of the Ministry."
3.9   The Committee observes that the issue has been under consideration of the Ministry for the last one year
and a decision is yet to be taken. By that time, about 20,000 employees would have completed training. This
lukewarm approach needs to be put into the right perspective. The Committee, therefore, recommends that an
early decision may be expedited in the matter for the benefit of VRS optees.
3.10The counselling and training programmes is planned in order to equip VRS optees with skills and orientation to
engage themselves in self-employment activities and rejoin the productive process even after their separation from the
CPSUs. The aim is to provide alternative employment opportunities to the VRS/VSS opted employees of the PSEs.
However, the skill they possess is of the different nature i.e. they have the experience of working under the PSU of a
Heavy Industry where the employment opportunity has ceased to exist. However, on retirement they would need the
skill of different name for setting up their own venture a small scale business. In order to overcome this gap, DPE
should co-ordinate with the Ministry of SSI to offer them training. The Committee also feels the need of adequate funds
for such employees to start there own vocation. Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises in course
of his deliberation before the Committee on 20th March, 2003 stated that under this scheme, which started last year, an
allocation of Rs. 8.5 crores was made. This year an allocation of Rs. 10 crores has been made. This allocation falls short
of the demand as far as this scheme is concerned. One of the problems faced by the workers who have been separated is
