36.6     Tax Reforms :- The Ministry of Steel suggested the Ministry of Finance to address the adverse impact of tax
proposals on the steel industry by amending the tax proposals.
36.7     Customs Duty
36.7.1  Duty on Coin Blanks :- The import of Coin Blank is duty free. This puts the domestic Coin Blanks manufacturers
at a disadvantage since they have to pay sales tax and other transaction charges. In order to provide an even playing field
to the domestic industry it was proposed by Ministry of Steel that a customs duty of 30%, which is the same as the duty
on Cold Rolled Stainless Steel, (CRSS is the input for the manufacture of Coin Blanks) should be imposed on imported
Coin Blanks alongwith 4% SAD and 16% CVED. Alternately, deemed export benefits should be extended to the supply
of Ferritic Stainless Steel Coil Blanks to the Government of India Mints. In this case, in order to ensure a level playing
field with foreign suppliers, it is necessary that domestic suppliers also be provided drawback facility to offset 4% CST
payable.
36.7.2  Withdrawal of SAD from non-available inputs :- In addition to basic customs duty, all imported items (except old
ships) attract 4% SAD, which has been levied to neutralize 4% sales tax on domestic sales. From 1999, traders have also
been brought under SAD. However, to enable import of essential raw materials, SAD should be waived on items, which
are not available indigenously. A list of such items along with their custom tariff numbers is given in the table below :

36.7.4 Hot Rolled Stainless Steel Coils (HRSS) for Coin-Blanks :- HRSS imported for manufacture of Coin Blanks for
government mints are from customs duty, CVED and SAD. However the usage rate of HRSS Coils for manufacturing 1
metric ton of Coin Blanks as approved by the government is 1.8654 metric on whereas the exemption is available only
for 1 ton of HRSS. This anomaly is required to be removed and custom duty exemption on 1.8654 metric ton of HRSS
should be given against manufacture of every ton of Coin Blank.
36.7.5 Countervailing duty on Ship Breaking :- Restoration of status quo ante i.e. 5% import duty, 4% SAD and CVED
of 16% on import of old ships for breaking so that (a) tax evasion is reduced and revenue collection is increased and (b)
the industry gets the requisite boost in production.
36.8    Excise Duty
36.8.1 Reduction of excise duty on GP/GC sheets for rural/mass consumption :-
           One of the constraints in growth of domestic demand for steel is the high excise duty of 16%. Whereas
intermediate consumers such as machinery manufacturers can adjust the excise duty paid on steel inputs by way of
paying only CENVAT at the time of sales of their products, final consumers such as house builders, construction

122nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/122ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:35:49]
industry etc. have to bear the burden of excise duty. The situation is more alarming in the rural sector that consumes
large quantities of GP/GC sheets. In order to boost market demand of steel it is necessary to reduce the cost of
production as well as the market price of iron and steel products. In view of this the excise duty on GP/GC sheets should
be reduced from 16% to 8%. Apparently this may cause loss of revenue, but with production going up such loss will be
compensated.
36.8.2  Notification 345 dated. 23.10.97 regarding clearance of recoveries on ship breaking:-
           A section of the steel industry as well as ship-breakers have drawn our attention to provisions laid down in
Notification No. 345/61/97-CX dated 23.10.97. This notification clarifies that no central excise duty is payable on goods
and materials (recovered during the course of ship-breaking) which are outside the ambit of Section XV of the Schedule
to the CE tariff Act, 1985 and no reversal of MODVAT credit taken on input of entire ship is warranted in respect of
such recovered goods which are considered as not arising out of an activity of manufacture or processing. However, this
provision is being misused by excessive billing of non-excisable goods like generators, motors etc. and temptation for
ship-breakers for selling the same to scrap traders without payment of excise duty, thereby violating the norm of value
addition through breaking of a ship. This notification is giving an undue advantage to unscrupulous ship-breakers. It
would have been logical to charge ED on their sales also after recovery as scrap items from the ships. Therefore the
above CE Notification should be withdrawn. At the same time, non-excisable items such as generators, refrigerators etc.
which are a part of the imported ship, should also be charged customs duty under their respective heading as is being
done in case of bunk oil.
36.8.3 Excise Duty on pre fabricated items of steel used in construction:
           Both steel and cement are used for construction. Items fabricated both out of iron & steel (CH.7308.50) and
cement (CH.38) at the project site continue to be exempt from duty. However, while the prefabricated cement items
(ready mix concrete: CH 3824.20) are exempt from payment of excise duty, prefabricated steel items attract an Excise
Duty of 16%. Since steel and cement both are extensively used in construction prefabricated steel structure (73.08) and
prefabricated buildings (94.06) should be exempted from Excise Duty.
36.9  After having a detailed discussion with the representatives of Indian Steel Alliance, TISCO, Jindal Vijay Nagar the
Committee feels that the existing tax structure needs to be modified to become a source of support for the steel sector.
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Finance should examine the issue of rationalizing the tax structure on
the following lines :-
         (i)     Customs duty on charge nickel and Metcoke be fixed at 5% for all uses keeping in view the dominant user
industry. The Committee agrees with the proposal of the Ministry of Mines that a differential of in the import
duty between Coking Coal – the raw material for production of Metcoke, and Metcoke should be maintained
by reducing the duty on Coking Coal to 0% and retaining the duty of 5% on Metcoke.
         (ii)     Prior to the budget 2003-2004 integrated steel manufacturers were paying Excise duty on the factory gate,
even when goods were sold from the stockyard. It is now proposed that Excise duty has to be paid on
transaction value at depot. Withdrawal of the existing facility would imply an increase in price of construction
steel in particular for supply from stockyard, affecting SAIL and TISCO specifically. Reinstatement of the
existing notification is required.
         (iii)     While there is an exemption of customs duty on Stainless Steel coin blanks, domestic manufacturers such as
SAIL and other have to pay excise duty and local taxes on similar products made in India. This product is
bought by the Ministry of Finance only. Indian companies are loosing tenders to overseas companies. The
Department of Economic affairs must allow exemption of excise duty and sales tax for local producers
supplying to them.
         (iv)    Restoration of status quo ante i.e. 5% import duty, 4% SAD and CVED of 16% on import of old ships for
breaking so that (a) tax evasion is reduced and revenue collection is increased and (b) the industry gets the
requisite boost in production.
         (v)    Reduction of excise duty on GP/GC sheets from 16% to 8% for promoting rural mass consumption.
         (vi)    Withdrawal of Notification 345 dated 23.10.97 regarding clearance of recoveries on ship-breaking and
charging of custom duty on non-excisable items like generators, refrigerators, under their respective heading
as is being done in case of bunk oil.
         (vii)   Exemption of excise duty on prefabricated item of steel used in construction in line with exemption of excise
duty on prefabricated cement items.

39.0  Progress Made in Regard To Legislation Of The “Buy Indian Steel Act”
40.1  The draft ‘Buy Indian Act’, was circulated in December 2000 for comments of Ministry of Commerce & Industry,
Department of Finance and DGFT. While DGFT had proposed a few modifications, Ministry of Finance had stated that
they do not support the proposed legislation. Ministry of Commerce suggested pending the proposal for the time being.
In the meantime, various aspects of legislation like its administration, penal provisions as well as its real benefit to the
domestic steel industry are being re-examined. Since it is based on the lines of “Buy America Act” efforts are also being
made to collect information on its operational aspects. After re-drafting, the proposed legislation would be discussed
with the steel consumers and industry.
40.2  The Committee strongly feels that the government should take step towards legislation of the “Buy Indian Steel
Act” on the lines of “Buy America Act” in order to protect and promote the domestic steel industry. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Steel in tandem with the Ministry of Commerce should convince the Ministry of
Finance regarding the benefits of the proposed Act. The Ministry of Steel should not procrastinate in re-examining and
re-drafting the proposed legislation.
41.0  COMPARATIVE COST AND COMPETITIVENESS OF STEEL INDUSTRY ALONGWITH
CONSUMPTION PROFILE OF INDIAN STEEL PRODUCTS
41.1  The production process of steel can be divided into two stages – the preliminary stage is that of producing crude
steel and which is then subjected to downstream processing to produce the finished steel. Indian steel industry is amongst
the low cost procedures of crude steel in the world today. However, while the same is processed to produce finished
steel, it loses its competitive edge due to factors such as high price of input materials (like electricity), high cost of
finance and use of sub-optimal level of technology.
41.2  Within the country, Tata Steel (Tisco) has been adjudged by renowned global market research organizations like
Worls Steel Dynamics and CRU as one of the lowest cost producer of crude steel.

41.3  Some of the reasons why Indian industry loses its competitive advantage in downstream processing of steel are:
         (i)     Energy Charges: On an average power cost is Rs.3.50/- unit while users in most of the advanced countries pay
around Rs.1.50/- unit.
         (ii)     Cost of Finance : The international rate of lending is less than 5% while our industry pays at an average of
14-18%.
         (iii)     Unfavourable market condition: The Indian Steel Industry has suffered for quite sometime on account of
depressed market conditions. This has prevented them to finance their technology related projects that could
have led to improved competitiveness.
41.4  Indian steel industry is still globally competitive. As of now, it is producing steel of almost all grades and varieties
and conforming to international standards. It is to be noted that India is the 8 th largest producer of crude steel in the
world. The competitive position of the Indian Steel Industry can be enhanced by :
         (i)     Movement of domestic power tariff towards global rates at a faster pace.
         (ii)     Improving infrastructure for logistics including roads, railways and ports.
         (iii)    Reducing import duty rates in raw materials, like coal/coke, melting scrap, limestone etc.

42.0  REGARDING THE EXPORT INCENTIVE (WTO COMPTABILE)
42.1  Regarding the Export incentive (WTO compatible) that clearly establish a nexus between import of raw materials
and export of finished products are introduced as has been done in USA and EU, Ministry of Steel stated that it favors
introduction of appropriate WTO compatible export incentive schemes for the benefit of the steel industry in the country.
However, the matter concerns Department of Commerce and any such proposal will have to be considered by them.
42.2  Regarding the import of defective steel, the Secretary Steel stated as under:-
         “Coming to defectives, 32 per cent of imports are seconds and defectives. As of now, there are two prescriptions in
places, which are designed to keep this in control. One, of course, is that the duty on seconds is 40 per cent as
against 30 per cent earlier, and 25 early peak rate duty. The duty on seconds will remain 40 per cent. There is
another measure, which has been introduced by DGFT, that is called notification no. 44, whereby there is a twin
barrier to imports. One is, there is a minimum support price, and minimum import price should be 302 dollars.
Today, that is not very relevant. Importers still appear bringing in very cheap products primarily seconds and
defectives. The second is that the exporter, that is, the foreign exporter is required to register himself. So, it is not as
if seconds come freely. There is a policy to check indiscriminate and excess import. But, nevertheless, there is fairly
substantial quantum of seconds coming in. The other thing in this regard is that there are conflicting interests. In
fact, sir, the ministry has received – a large number of representations saying that Notification no. 44 must be
withdrawn. This is coming from the people who source HR coil as their raw material. So, they say, the prices of HR
coil have gone up internationally but availability may be a question. We should be allowed to import freely. So
Notification no. 44 prevents the free import and, therefore, it should be withdrawn”.
42.3  The Committee is of the view that the government should undertake adequate steps for prevention of imports of
seconds and defective steel.
43.0  GLOBAL STEEL INDUSTRY
43.1  For the major part of 2001 was a victim of slowdown in demand, sliding price levels, low realizations, losses
and/or falling profits. However, from the beginning of 2002, the industry entered a recovery phase, with the gradual
firming up of international prices and demand.
43.2    In 2001 (as in 2000), China emerged as the world’s largest steel producer (149 million tonnes of crude steel)
followed by Japan (103 million tonnes) and USA (90 million tonnes). India currently occupies the 8 th position (30.611
million tonnes). China’s position as the leading global producer and consumer of steel – as far as provisional data for
2002 shows – remain intact.
43.2.1 Production : The quarterly production trend of crude steel, both global and domestic, starting from 
1st quarter of 2001 to the 4 th quarter of 2002 indicates that domestic production is following an almost similar trend as
the global production.
43.2.2 Price : Global steel prices declined considerably for the most of 2001-02 but saw a revival from around the
beginning of 2002. HR coil prices, for exports from European mills, moved down from about $200 per tonne in April
2001 to about $180 per tonne in August and September 2001. The recovery, which began in early 2002, has persisted
and the price rise has been reflected more in the case of flat products than long products. As of now, internationally
(W.European fob levels), galvanized coil prices, are in the range of $445-485/tonne; cold rolled coils, $390-430/tonne
and hot rolled coils at around $300-325/tonne. (Source : Metal Bulletin)

as against 2.8% during the corresponding month last year and for the April’02-January’03 period, it reported a 5.5%
growth against a mere 2.6% growth in same period last year. For this period, Manufacturing (5.8), Electricity (3.8%) and
Mining (5.4%) – all recorded impressive growths, as compared to the same period last year, for which respective sectoral
growth rates are 2.8%, 2.9% and 1% (Source : CSO)
44.4  Impressive performance of the core sector continued in January 2003 with finished steel and cement continuing to
boost growth in the six infrastructure industries whose index rose to 5.2% in April-January’03 as compared to a low
3.1% in same period last year (Source : CSO)
45.0  BUDGET AND THE INDIAN STEEL INDUSTRY
45.1  Following the measures proposed in both the Railway Budget 2003-04 and the Union budget 2003-04, the outlook
in the steel industry is positive. The policy measures proposed in the Railway Budget 2003-04 promise to benefit
industry in general and the iron and steel industry in particular. The proposed rationalization of freight structure,
reduction in the number of classifications, the market orientation introduced through peak and off-peak rates, the
incentives to big shippers in the form of lower rates, if they move more materials, the reduction in freight rates for short

122nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/122ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:35:49]
distance ranging up to 100 km as well as the general reductions in the freight rates for finished steel and pig iron---all
carry the potential to boost bottomlines by lowering the overall costs and lead to increased competitiveness. Finally, the
stress on laying of new tracks, broadening of existing ones, addition of new trains and a series of development projects
are all expected to boost demand for steel.
45.2  Union Budget 2003-04 has proposed measures that are meant more for impacting the environment in which the
iron and steel industry operates rather than for the industry itself. Most prominent is the significant thrust provided to
infrastructure development in the country – roads, ports, airports and housing – and this is turn is expected to lead to a
substantial increase in the domestic steel demand. Reduction of excise on passengers cars and appliances like air
conditioner by boosting sales is also expected to indirectly impact steel industry favourably.
45.3  There may be no direct correlation between the International steel production growth rate and the domestic growth
rate. Although a global rise in demand may have similar impact on the industry in India as well as globally, a domestic
rise in demand may, in fact, lead to strong growth in production in the country leaving the global production rate
practically unaffected. Therefore, it may be difficult to estimate whether domestic growth rate will catch up with the
global trends. In fact, while the global annual production growth rate in the last ten years or so has been at less than 2 per
cent, the figure for India has been at about 6 per cent. There are greater chances that the steel industry growth rate in
India will be higher than the global rate in the medium and the long term.
45.4  Major Indian steel companies have already hiked prices of steel items – though, mostly flat products than long
products – from the beginning of the fiscal 2002-03. This is seen in line with international trends where prices have been
rising since beginning of 2002 and is an inevitable fallout of the globalization process. Domestic price rises have
persisted in 2003 in the face of a steel demand that has shown signs of stabilizing.
45.5  Price Volatility :- 2003 opened with rounds of price hikes – of both long and flat – that has given the current
market trends further buoyancy. In January 2003, SAIL, Tata Steel and other flat steel producers increased prices of flat
products by an average Rs. 600-1000 per tonne while SAIL and RINL have hiked long steel prices by Rs. 200-300 per
tonne. This has pushed up hot rolled coil prices in the domestic market, with basic grade price of the commodity being
around Rs. 17,500-18,000 per tonne (average). Similarly, the growth in the construction segment in particular and the
infrastructure segment in general has prompted fresh hikes in long steel prices. Internationally too, trends (W. European
fob levels) remain strong : galvanized coil prices are in the range of $445-485/ tonne; cold rolled coils, $390-430/tonne
and hot rolled coils at around $300-325/tonne. (Source. Metal Bulletin).
45.6  Financial performance
45.6.1  The turnaround in the market trends is reflected most prominently in the performance of the public sector steel
giant, Steel Authority of India Ltd. The unaudited financial results of SAIL for April-December (Q3) 2002 reveals a
sharp improvement of Rs. 507 crore over the corresponding period of the previous year. SAIL’s loss for April-December
’02 was brought to a level of Rs.558 crore, showing a recovery of 57 per cent over the results of the same period in 2001.
This helped the company to post a cash profit of Rs. 215 crore in Q3 ’02 as against a loss of Rs. 297 crore in Q3 ’01 and
a cash profit of Rs. 305 crore in the first nine months of the current financial year. SAIL had suffered a cash loss of Rs.
434 crore during the corresponding period in the last fiscal.
45.6.2  For the other PSU, namely RINL (VSP) for the period, Q2 (July-September) ’02 net profit has gone up by 119%
and turnover 16% as compared to quarter ending June'02 (Q1). The Indian steel companies are free to raise prices at any
time, depending on their commercial judgement. The conditions for price increases are local in the first place. Some such
conditions may be created by external developments in the context of the free external trade regime. Fluctuations in
international prices can always have corresponding impact on the pricing decisions of the Indian companies. The world
prices of almost all steel products have risen significantly since January 2002. The extent of price rise has been
significant for flat products like HR coils, CR sheets and galvanised sheets. In view of this, the Indian steel companies
have also raised prices to the extent that may be supported by domestic market conditions.
45.7  The Committee observes that simultaneous with price rise for flat products like HR coils, CR sheets and galvanised
sheets there have been increases in the costs of raw materials, labour etc. too. However, the Committee hopes that the
price rise would certainly help the steel producers across the board, including the major PSUs like SAIL and RINL.
45.8  The Committee recommends that Indian Steel PSUs, while keeping an eye to the world price index of steel
products, should keep on revising the price of Indian steel products under a definite marketing strategy.

continued rising price of steel products, the Ministry of Steel argued that there were several avenues open before the
secondary producers in view of the continued rise in prices which inter-alia included :-
         (i)     The secondary producers may endeavor to pass on the price rise to their customers of finished products,
thereby offsetting the higher prices of input steel.

47.0  FORMULATION OF NATIONAL STEEL POLICY
47.1  In pursuance of the recommendations contained in the 30 th and 34 th Report of the Department Related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, Ministry of Steel is formulating a National Steel Policy. A Drafting
Committee, consisting of members from the Steel Industry, DCI&S as the Chairman and the Chief Economist of
Economic Research Unit (ERU), JPC, as the convenor was constituted. Basic objective of the National Steel Policy is to
prepare a road map for the Indian steel Industry in the context of ongoing reforms, restructuring and globalization.
47.2  The Committee submitted the first draft in April 01. Thereafter a meeting was convened under the Chairmanship of
Secretary (Steel) on 25 th May, 2001 to discuss the draft with all major steel producers, their associations, consultancy
firms in the field of metallurgy and representatives of FICCI, Ministries of Commerce and Finance. The participants
suggested certain changes to be incorporated in the policy document and accordingly it was decided that the draft would
be modified in the light of the suggestions given and the revised document would again be circulated to all concerned
before giving it final shape.
47.3  While further consultations with industry were in progress, it was observed that the industry in general showed
signs of revival. In addition, concerned activity was observed on the trade front. Several developed and developing
countries have started adopting various tariff and non-tariff barriers to protect their domestic steel industry. In addition to
the increasing number of anti-dumping and countervailing duty cases, the strict surveillance mechanism put in place at
the EU and the cumbersome packing and quality standards imposed by Australia and Thailand have affected markets that
are of interest to India. It was felt that the imperatives of the changing scenario should be incorporated in the Steel
Policy. Accordingly, after a round of fresh informal consultations, a revised draft has been prepared.
47.4  The revised draft would be first circulated among major steel producers and their associations and then discussed.
Thereafter, changes would have to be incorporated in the draft on the basis of these discussions and the final draft sent to
Ministries of Commerce, Finance etc. for their comments. Depending upon the comments of other Ministries, the
preparation of National Steel Policy and its presentation to the Cabinet may take a minimum of six months.
47.5  The Committee is of the view that the preparation of National Steel Policy and its presentation to the Cabinet
should not take more than a period of six months as estimated by Ministry of Steel. The Committee is pleased to note
that basic objective of the National Steel Policy is to prepare a road map for the Indian steel Industry in the context of
ongoing reforms, restructuring and globalization.
48.0  DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE
48.1  Development of infrastructure can very well ensure an increase in steel demand, as steel is a major component of
construction activities. Promotion of steel in the construction sector has already led to the initiation of steel intensive
technology, which offers a better edge over its counterparts in factors like longer lifecycle and time economy. Moreover,
greater thrust given by the Central Government in channelizing resources for infrastructural developments in the country
like: better roads, highways, bridges, ports, power with a special thrust on rural infrastructure and also providing various
incentives for the housing sector (including rural housing), may all ensure a rise in construction activities in the economy
– accompanied by a corresponding rise in the consumption of steel.
48.2  Revival of infrastucture would automatically lead to the growth of the core sector, which has been witnessing
impressive performance over the last few months. Recent data published by the CSO shows that the index for the core
sector – comprising of the six infrastructure industries, rose to 5.2% in April-January ’03 as compared to a low 3.1% in
same period last year. This was achieved largely by a growth in finished steel (8% in April-January ’03 as compared to a
low 3.5% in same period last year) (Source: CSO)
48.3  Investments in infrastructure have a more direct linkage with the iron and steel industry insofar as the construction
of such projects (especially in the power, road and communications sectors) constitutes the single largest source of
demand for steel. Hence government’s infrastructure development programme – both, proposed (as in Union Budget

activities – all carry good potential for reaping benefits for the domestic steel industry in general and the steel PSUs in
particular.
48.4        The Committee is of the view that the domestic steel industry in general and steel PSUs in particular would be able
to reap benefit from the Government’s Infrastructure Development Programme as announced by the finance Minister in
his budget speech (2003-04) that Government would provide a major thrust to infrastructure like road, railways, airport
and seaport through innovative funding mechanism. The Ministry of Steel should chalk out the strategy for increasing
the steel consumption in government’s infrastructure development programme.

IMPACT OF RATIONALIZATION OF TAX STRUCTURE MADE IN BUDGET 2002-2003 ON THE INDIAN
STEEL
         After having a detailed discussion with the representatives of Indian Steel Alliance, TISCO, Jindal Vijay Nagar the
Committee feels that the existing tax structure needs to be modified to become a source of support for the steel sector.
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Finance should examine the issue of rationalizing the tax structure on
the following lines :-
          (i)    Customs duty on charge nickel and Metcoke be fixed at 5% for all uses keeping in view the dominant user
industry. The Committee agrees with the proposal of the Ministry of Mines that a differential of in the import
duty between Coking Coal – the raw material for production of Metcoke, and Metcoke should be maintained
by reducing the duty on Coking Coal to 0% and retaining the duty of 5% on Metcoke.
          (ii)    Prior to the budget 2003-2004 integrated steel manufacturers were paying Excise duty on the factory gate,
even when goods were sold from the stockyard. It is now proposed that Excise duty has to be paid on
transaction value at depot. Withdrawal of the existing facility would imply an increase in price of construction
steel in particular for supply from stockyard, affecting SAIL and TISCO specifically. Reinstatement of the
existing notification is required.
          (iii)    While there is an exemption of customs duty on Stainless Steel coin blanks, domestic manufacturers such as
SAIL and other have to pay excise duty and local taxes on similar products made in India. This product is
bought by the Ministry of finance only. Indian companies are looking tenders to overseas companies. The
Department of Economic Affairs must allow exemption of excise duty and sales tax for local products
supplying to them.
          (iv)   Restoration of status quo ante i.e. 5% import duty, 4% SAD and CVED of 16% on import of old ships for
breaking so that (a) tax evasion is reduced and revenue collection is increased and (b) the industry gets the
requisite boost in production.
          (v)   Reduction of excise duty on GP/GC sheets from 16% to 8% for promoting rural mass consumption.
          (vi)   Withdrawal of Notification 345 dated 23.10.97 regarding clearance of recoveries on ship-breaking and
charging of custom duty on non-excisable items like generators, refrigerators, under their respective heading
as is being done in case of bunk oil.
          (vii)  Exemption of excise duty on prefabricated item of steel used in construction in line with exemption of excise
duty on prefabricated cement items.                                                                                            (Para : 36.9)
         The Committee has appreciated from time to time the efforts made by the Ministry of Steel for taking up the matter
of rationalization of tax structure with the Ministry of finance and consideration of the Ministry of Finance would be
beneficial to the Steel Industry in general. However, as per the suggestions of the representative of the Steel Alliance and
also that of the Ministry of Steel, the Committee feels that steel industry still requires the due attention of the Ministry of
Finance for rationalization of the tax structure conducive to steel industry keeping in view also the continued
contribution of steel sector to the national exchequer. In this regard the Committee recommends that the Ministry of

         The Committee is of the opinion that the government should induct the use of steel in syllabus / curriculum of
construction/engineering studies in various technical institutes and universities for promotion of steel use in the
construction sector. The untapped areas for promotion of steel in rural areas may be reckoned forth.                     (Para :
41.6.4)
REGARDING THE EXPORT INCENTIVE (WTO COMPTABILE)
         The Committee is of the view that the government should undertake adequate steps for prevention of imports of
seconds and defective steel.                                                                                                                 (Para : 42.3)
GLOBAL STEEL INDUSTRY
         The Committee is pleased to note that global steel secnario is improving and thus coming out of recession. In a
globalized regime Indian Steel Industry would be definitely benefited.                                                    (Para : 43.5)
Indian Steel Industry : Outlook and major trends
BUDGET AND THE INDIAN STEEL INDUSTRY
         The Committee observes that simultaneous with price rise for flat products like HR coils, CR sheets and galvanised
sheets there have been increases in the costs of raw materials, labour etc. too. However, the Committee hopes that the
price rise would certainly help the steel producers across the board, including the major PSUs like SAIL and RINL.        
                                                                                                                                                           (Para : 45.7)
         The Committee recommends that Indian Steel PSUs, while keeping an eye to the world price index of steel
products, should keep on revising the price of Indian steel products under a definite marketing strategy.                (Para :
45.8)
PROTECTION OF THE INTEREST OF SECONDARY STEEL PRODUCERS
         The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should chalk out proper strategy for promotion of
secondary steel vis-a-vis improving market scenario of steel. Steps may be taken for ensuring the survival of mini steel
plants in secondary sector vis-a-vis improvement in the general status of integrated steel plants.                          (Para :
46.2)
FORMULATION OF NATIONAL STEEL POLICY
         The Committee is of the view that the preparation of National Steel Policy and its presentation to the Cabinet
should not take more than a period of six months as estimated by Ministry of Steel. The Committee is pleased to note
that basic objective of the National Steel Policy is to prepare a road map for the Indian steel Industry in the context of
ongoing reforms, restructuring and globalization.                                                                                                (Para :
47.5)
DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE

               REPORT
1.         Minerals have  been an important   basis of classification of human  civilization.   A civilization undertakes development in consonance with a
pattern of physical   endowment of valuable minerals like Copper, Iron Ore,  Aluminium,  Zinc, Lead, Gold,   Cobalt, Manganese, Graphite, Lime
Stone, Platinum etc.    Since mineral resources are wealth hidden   beneath the earth-curst, therefore, their conservation and planned   exploitation is
of paramount importance to  national economic development and growth .  As a matter of fact,  mineral resources not only provide the basic inputs to
domestic industry,  but also account for sizeable export and foreign exchange earnings.   The development and regulation of the mineral sector is
concomitant to the optimal utilisation of resources, which ensures all round development, and growth of national economy.
 
1.1.      The Ministry of   Mines is responsible for development and regulation of the mineral sector including  mining and metallurgy     of all non-
ferrous metals both in private and public sectors, but excluding   Natural Gas, Petroleum, Coal and Atomic   Minerals.  As per the Annual Report

(2002-03)   the Ministry of Mines has been   allotted subjects as under: -
i                       Legislation for regulation  of mines and development  of    minerals within the territory of  India, including   mines    and minerals 
underlying the ocean within the territorial waters  or the continental shelf, or the Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones of 
India as may be specified from time to  time by or under any law made by Parliament.
ii                     Regulation  of mines and development of minerals   other than coal,  lignite and sand  for  stowing and any minerals declared as prescribed
substances for the  purposes  of the  Atomic Energy Act, 1962 (33 of 1962)  under the control of the Union as declared by law,   including  
questions concerning  regulation and development of minerals in various States and the matter connected therewith with or incidental thereto.
iii                    All other metals and minerals not  specifically allotted to any  other Ministry/ Department  such as aluminium, zinc , copper, gold, diamond
and nickel.
iv                   Planning, development and control of and assistance to all industries dealt with by the Ministry.
1.2.            At the Secretariat level the  Ministry of Mines is  mainly engaged in direction, supervision and coordination of five divisions which inter-alia
include Survey and Exploration,  Mines, Metal, General Administration and Finance and Accounts Division.   Survey and Exploration has two
principal agencies i.e. Geological Survey of India (GSI) and Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. (MECL) for the implementation of the
programmes of this division while Mines Division has one subordinate office to implement the programmes of the division, viz. Indian Bureau of
Mines (IBM). Metal division of the Ministry of Mines deals with the planning, exploration, development, monitoring of programmes and research in
respect of non-ferrous metals both in the public and private sectors General Administration Division is mainly concerned with the establishment and
administrative matter of the Department and Finance and Accounts Division is concerned with the budget, financial scrutiny of projects and other
proposals, rendering financial advice and maintenance and compilation of accounts.
1.3.
            Ministry of Mines has two  subordinate offices, namely :-
(a)                Geological  Survey of India ( HQ Kolkata)
(b)               Indian Bureau of Mines (HQ Nagpur)
1.4.            Public Sectors Undertakings (PSUs) - Ministry of Mines has four   PSUs
 
(a)                National Aluminium Company Ltd.  (NALCO), Bhubaneshwar
(b)               Hindustan Copper Ltd. (HCL), Kolkata
(c)                Minerals Exploration Corporation Ltd. (MECL), Nagpur
(d)               Bharat Gold Mines Ltd.  (BGML), Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka (closed since  1st March, 2001)
1.5.      Joint Venture Undertakings ;  There are  three companies in which the Ministry of Mines held equity shareholding during  2001-02
(a)                Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd. (BALCO), New  Delhi. ( a company jointly owned by Sterlite Industries Ltd. and Government of
India)
(b)               Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (HZL).  ( a company jointly owned by Sterlite Industries Ltd. and Government of India)
(c)                Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC) ( a company jointly owned by the State  Government of Sikkim and the Government of India). 
The  allocation of business relating to Sikkim Mining Corporation  (SMC) has been transferred  to the Department of Development of
North  Eastern Region on 21.12.2001.
 
1.6       Research Institutions; There are three Research Institutions under the Ministry of  Mines, namely:
(a)                Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development and Design Centre, Nagpur;
(b)               National Institute of Rock Mechanics, Kolar Gold Fields. Karnataka; and
(c)                National Institute  of Miners' Health, Kolar  Gold Fields, Karnataka.
1.7       Regarding the exact role of Ministry of Mines in the overall structure of management and working of divested PSUs and whether  the
Ministry would  play the role of a mere co-ordinator or facilitator or can do something more in the functional structure of divested PSUs, the Ministry
of Mines stated that in view of disinvestment of PSUs the Ministry is to act as per Share Holders Agreement /Share Purchase Agreement. The
Government has nominee Directors in the Board who oversee that the new Management is adhering to provisions of the agreement. The Company
like any other legal entity incorporated under company law is accountable as per the provisions of law.
1.8       The Committee notes the structural and functional pattern of the Ministry of   Mines, the Secretariat for the Ministry of Mines and  is of the 
view  that structural aspect must  match the functional requirement and working   of  the  organisation with adequate degree  of co-ordination and
collaboration   among  various units  thus contributing on  their  part    in the overall functioning of the organisation in the interest of national 
economy .
1.9       The Committee, in the light of the fact that Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC)  has been transferred to Department  of North East Region,
Bharat Gold Mines Ltd.,  BGML has been  closed since 1
st March, 2001, Bharat Aluminium Company  Ltd. already  disinvested in March, 2001 and
transferring the management of  Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL)in new management after disinvestment and   remaining PSUs National Aluminium  
Company Ltd. (NALCO) , Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) are  on the verge of disinvestments and with the completion of process of
disinvestments of mining  PSUs,  Ministry of Mines would have nothing to direct, supervise and co-ordinate ,therefore, it is the right time for the
Government for pruning its departments.

and development of any other Ministry or Department (i.e. development of aluminium, zinc, lead, copper and diamond, etc.)   The Ministry has been
allocated the work of Geological Survey of India which is the premier agency in earth sciences in the country.  Ministry enforces the regulatory
measures on all mines pertaining to subjects under its charge including iron ore, through Indian Bureau of Mines.
1.11     The Ministry of Mines reacted that it was  enjoined to look after planning development and control of and assistance to all industries dealt
with by the Ministry including the Public Sector Undertakings.  It is obvious, therefore, the role of Ministry of Mines is not restricted to direct,
supervise and coordinate the PSUs, which is only a part of its overall role and functions in the Government.  Therefore disinvestments of PSUs,
closure of BGML and transfer of SMC to Department of Development of North East Region would  allow the Ministry of Mines to focus on its areas
of core competence, i.e. survey and exploration of all minerals other than natural gas, petroleum and atomic minerals, administer the mining statutes
as well as enter into new areas and develop competence in  the Off Shore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) law . 
1.12     Expenditure Reforms Commission was of the opinion that Ministry of Mines be merged with Ministry of Steel into a composite Ministry of
Mines and Metals with three separate wings (not departments) one dealing with public sector companies, another with the PSUs of Ministry of Mines
and the third dealing with policy issues and regulatory aspects including GSI, IBM etc. 
1.13       The Committee understands the core function of Ministry of Mines, however, the real  question arises   whether  a separate Department is
required for discharging the  core function only .  The Committee is of the firm view that the existence of structure of any department   presently the  
Ministry of Mines, must justify itself through discharging   its corresponding duties and functions since this involves substantial  financial
implications. 
1.14     When the Committee asked the Ministry of Mines to comment on the proposal of transferring National Mineral Development  Corporation
Ltd.  (NMDC) , Kudremukh Iron  Ore Company Ltd., Manganese Ore  (India) Ltd. and Metallurgical  &  Engineering Consultants India Ltd.
(MECON)  from Ministry of Steel to Ministry of Mines  in order to rationalise the allocation of business of Government, the Ministry of Mines stated
that since the subject matter relating to legislation, regulation and concessions of manganese and iron ore is allocated to this Ministry,  it is
anomalous that public sector corporations in this area namely; NMDC, MOIL, Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd. are dealt with by the Ministry of
Steel.  A proposal therefore has been submitted to the Cabinet Secretariat for transfer of these public sector undertakings to the Ministry   of Mines.
1.15     Reacting to the proposal of integration / merger of Geological Survey of India, Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. and India  Bureau of
Mines  (IBM)  and the same is transferred either to  Ministry of Steel and  Coal or Petroleum with suitable  change in the name of the Ministry, it was
explained that Geological Survey of India, Mineral Exploration Corporation and Indian Bureau of Mines were  mandated to take up different specific
responsibilities, which could not  be merged.  Geological Survey of India’s areas of activity include scientific survey and research for locating
mineral resources and geological studies while IBM is primarily responsible for promotion and conservation of scientific development of mineral
resources of the country and enforce Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act and Rules there under.  The basic aim of MECL is to
bridge the gap between preliminary exploration of mineral prospect and its commercial exploitation.  From this it is clear that these are responsible
for development and regulation of mineral sector including the mining and metallurgy and non-ferrous metals both in private and public sector
excluding natural gas, petroleum and atomic minerals and this cannot be transferred to the Ministry of Steel, Coal and Petroleum as these Ministries
have been allotted specific charters.
 
1.16     The Committee  understands  that GSI, IBM and MECL have their specific charter  of functions but it is also true that MECL  is   an  offshoot
of GSI and later on created a separate body to supplement GSI .Moreover, the submission of the Secretary Ministry of Mines that  GSI, and  MECL 
work  not only for the    Ministry of Mines  but also for  Department of Coal and  Ministry of Petroleum  and even for private sector, the argument of
the Ministry of Mines that GSI, IBM and MECL must remain within the jurisdiction of Ministry of Mines,  remains bereft of substantial and
conclusive logic as these organizations may remain with any of the department for which these organization work.
1.17     The Committee reiterates  its viewpoint as expressed in its 71
st Report that  that possibility of integration of  GSI, IBM and MECL may be
explored and the  efforts may be made for  rationalising  of  non-plan expenditure.  The Committee is of the further view that GSI  MECL and IBM
may  co-exist  under one organic unit and may remain either in the Ministry of  Coal or Petroleum  or Mines discharging  their  roles as mentioned  in
their respective  charter   of function   intact and in original  form.  The Committee opines   that GSI, MECL  and IBM  may be integrated with  their  
differential roles under one  umbrella  and which would not only rationalise   the  non-plan  expenditure  but also  inject synergy  and enhancement
of  brand  endowment.
1.18    The Committee also reiterates its recommendations  as contained in its 71st report on Demands for Grants (2002-03)  that  Government should
immediately constitute  a  Task Force having representatives from Department of Coal, Mines, Petroleum   and Steel   to examine the following
issues:-
(i)
                  Determination of continuation of Ministry of Mines with a view  to discharge its  core function;
(ii)                Feasibility and desirability of integration/merger of GSI, IBM and MECL  and  transferring of  same to either  Department of Coal,
Petroleum or Ministry of  Steel.
(iii)               Transfer of  NMDC, KIOCL, MOIL and MECON from the Ministry of Steel  to Ministry of Mines.
(iv)              Merger of Ministry of Mines, Coal and Steel in view of   the recommendation of Expenditure Reforms Commission . 
1.19     The very fact that the proposal has been submitted  by the Ministry of Mines to the Cabinet Secretariat for transfer of NMDC, MOIL,
Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd to the Ministry  of Mines, Ministry of Coal & Mines, reveals that even  as per view of Ministry of Mines there
are public undertakings which could be under the Ministry of Mines but at present these undertakings are under the Ministry of Steel.  Therefore, 
prima-facie it seems that the Ministry of Steel and Mines may be merged and their roles could be so integrated as to facilitate the discharge of both of
the departments.
1.20     The Committee further reiterates its recommendations contained in 99
th Action Taken Report on Demands for Grants (2002-03) that the
recommendations of the Expenditure Reforms Commission for abolition of just 87 posts is a conclusion arrived at in the pre-disinvestment  era and

things have changed a lot in post disinvestments phase when the spheres of functions of the Ministry of Mines have reduced considerably.  The
Committee understands that the decision of the Ministry of Mines to reduce the 35 posts consequent upon implementation of disinvestments in Mines
PSUs is a decision of the Ministry of Mines.  While the Committee desires that Government should consider whether it is the absolute necessity  for a

1.21     The reply of the Ministry of Mines that the Allocation of Business Rules allocate the business of the Government among its different
departments which are assigned to the charge of the Ministry by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.  Hence, Ministry of Mines does
not have the authority to determine whether there is a need for a separate Department/Ministry of Mines, reflects the  non-performing attitude of the
Ministry of Mines in regard to right sizing of manpower in the department and units under its administrative jurisdiction and thus the rationalization
of non-plan expenditure.  The Committee holds the argument of the Ministry of Mines as totally untenable and  unacceptable, as the Ministry of
Mines being an organ of the Government could have approached the appropriate authority for modification in the Allocation of Business Rules in the
best interest of the nation.   Therefore, the Committee is of the opinion that either the Ministries of Steel,  Mines,  Coal and Petroleum  may be
integrated and merged in the post liberalization phase or all these Ministries should come under the Ministry of Industry discharging the core role and
responsibility just from a desk headed by an Officer to the rank of Joint Secretary, assisted by reasonable number of staff (5 to 10).

2.5       Philosophy behind the budget proposals
2.5.1    The economic philosophy behind the budget proposals of the Ministry of Mines is broadly based on the principle that extensive survey and
investigation should be carried out in the field of minerals in which the country is deficient or which are of strategic importance.  The need for
advanced exploration and prospecting techniques in the field of geophysical and geochemical methods has been envisaged which requires 
participation of domestic and foreign private explorators  and prospectors. Stress has been laid on recycling of metal scraps and enhancement of
smelting capacities of metals like aluminium, lead,zinc , steel and ferro alloys.  Stress has also been laid on development of dimension and decorative
stones, mining and processing industry, minerals required for advanced ceramic and glasses etc.             States have been encouraged to ensure proper
linkage of raw materials to the industry along with development of necessary basic infrastructure.
 
2.5.2    The Committee is pleased to note that  the economic philosophy behind the budget proposals of the Ministry of Mines is broadly based on the
principle that extensive survey and investigation should be carried out in the field of minerals in which the country is deficient or which are of
strategic importance for the country. The Committee strongly feels that the budget proposals for the year 2003-04 pertaining to the Ministry of Mines
are expected to prove as an instrument to march forward towards the national goal of overall development in the era of liberalized and globalised
economy.   The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Mines, discharging its core activities as well as its responsibility and role as a facilitator
in the liberalized and globalised economy must guide the organizations and its PSUs to determine the national goals for growth and development of
Mining Industry (i.e. identification of goals, mineral specific industry wise), Chalking out set of programmes, course of Action required and overall
monitoring  for execution of the plans without time and cost over run.  Any effort for shrugging of its responsibility would raise a question mark on 
the raison-de-itre  for the Ministry of Mines.

3.1.14  Though the mineral resources are regionally distributed, the GSI has played the leading role of identifying them to provide a strong base to
the industrial development of the nation.Regional distribution of mineral resources has been  utilized by value addition.  Value addition is possible
broadly in three stages namely mining, mineral based processing industry and export oriented industry which contribute significantly to Gross
National Product.  Minerals are important source of foreign exchange earning.  The policy of export shall keep in view the mineral inventory position
and the long-term need of the country.
3.1.15  Presently GSI is the principal provider of basic earth science information to the government, industry and the general public, as well as
responsive participant in international fora.  After Independence, there has been added emphasis on locating and harnessing the natural resources for
meeting the growing demands of mineral/metal industries, power (thermal, hydro and nuclear), agricultural, irrigation sectors etc.  The thrust areas of
GSI’s activities have evolved with the changing national priorities through out the last nine Five Year Plans and is presently oriented in the light of
the current goals set up for X Plan.
 
3.1.16  Since independence GSI remained in the vanguard of nation building movement particularly in the fields of industrial revolution, power,
irrigation and water resources management.  Major organizations like Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), Oil and Natural Gas Commission (ONGC),
Atomic Mineral Division (AMD), Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) nucleated from GSI.  Important mining and mineral-based industries like
Hindustan Copper Ltd. (HCL), Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (HZL), National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC), Raw material Divisions of Steel
Industry, Coal and Lignite Corporations, Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd. (BALCO), National Aluminium Company Ltd. (NALCO) are the spin-
offs.             Vibrant Steel, Coal, Cement, Aluminium, Copper-lead-Zinc, Fertilizer and Chemical industries which expanded phenomenally in post-
independence era, bear eloquent .testimony to GSI’s sustained efforts towards augmentation of mineral resource base
 
3.1.17  The Committee was apprised that an expert  Committee was setup by the Ministry of Mines under the Chairmanship of  Shri Arvind Varma,
former Secretary(Mines), Government of India  on 23.5.2002 to study the role and relevance of Geological Survey of India in the light of
developments in the field earth sciences and recommend changes in the charter of GSI.  The Expert Committee has submitted its report on 2.1.2003. 
It recommended changes in the charter and function of Geological Survey of India.  It suggested that GSI should systematically explore the  shallow
sub-surface domain of the country and develop and maintain national drill core library and documentation center in addition to its other functions. 
World Mining Ministries forum in its meeting held in March 2002 at Toronto discussed the future role of geological surveys and there was a
consensus that building up of fundamental geoscientific data base could not be left to ever-changing market forces.   It was further exphasized that
Geological Surveys should continue to generate geoscientific data for long-term geological understanding.

8.1       Minerals are broadly categorized as fuel minerals, atomic minerals, metallic minerals and non-metallic minerals. Among metallic minerals,
iron and associated minerals are called ferrous minerals (iron, manganese, chrome). All non-fuel, non-atomic and other than ferrous minerals are thus
included in the scope and ambit of non-ferrous minerals (eg.bauxite, copper, gold, zinc etc. metallic minerals as well as limestone, diamond etc.
nonmetallic minerals), for which the Ministry of Mines is primarily responsible. Prior to the formulation of the Statement of Industrial Policy, 1991,
mining of iron ore, manganese ore, chrome ore, gypsum, sulphur, gold and diamond, copper, lead, zinc, tin, molybdenum and wolfram were reserved
for the public sector. Since 1991, the non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries are mostly in the private sector, for which no direct budgetary
support is needed. The Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under the administrative control of the Ministry of Mines in the non-ferrous mining and
metallurgical sectors are provided budgetary support to the extent necessary. Of the PSUs, only the loss making PSUs, viz. Hindustan Copper
Limited (HCL) and Bharat Gold Mines Limited (BGML) would require budgetary support during 2003-04 primarily for separating the manpower,
for which budgetary grants have been proposed. Apart from this, for extending support to the mining sector, the Ministry of Mines has proposed

budgetary support to the Geological Survey of India (GSI), and Promotional Exploration funds for  Mineral Exploration Corporation of India
(MECL), who undertake survey and exploration for minerals and to the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), who takes measures for regulation and
conservation of minerals. The budgetary support to GSI, MECL and IBM are expected to contribute to identification of new minerals reserves, help
in scientific mining and contribute towards overall development of the non-ferrous mining sector. 
8.2       The Committee understands that with the liberalization process in the economy the non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries are in
private sector where no budgetary support is required and only the loss making mines PSUs i.e. HCL and BGML require budgetary support in the
forum of grants –in –aid for sepration of manpower.  Right sizing of manpower has become the order of the corporate governance in order to cut the
labour cost.  The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry of Mines for the budgetary support to the Geological Survey of India and Promotional
Exploration Funds for Mineral Exploration Co-operation Limited (MECL), which undertake survey and actions, and exploration for minerals and to
the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) which takes measures for regulation and conservation of minerals. However, the Committee strongly believes that 
the budgetary support  provided to GSI, MECL and IBM would contribute to identification of new minerals reserves, help in scientific mining and
contribute towards overall development of the non-ferrous mining sector. 
 
8.3       The Ministry of Mines apprised the Committee that  the Central Government has laid down the broad policy governing the mining sector,
while  the State Governments as owners of minerals grant the mineral concessions for all minerals, including the non-ferrous minerals, within the
framework laid down by the Central Government. The Ministry of Mines has constituted Mineral Advisory Council under the Chairmanship of the
Minister in Charge, in which the State Governments, the Mining and Metallurgical Industry and all other stakeholders are invited. This Council is the
Apex think tank and advises the Government towards desired policy changes for problem solving, and it is the endeavour of the Ministry to hold
meetings of the Council every year. The 27 th meeting of the Mineral Advisory Council was held on 21 st Sept., 2002. From time to time, meetings
with the investors are also held.      As a result of the interaction meetings, changes in the mining statutes have been brought about, inter-departmental
discussions for solving overlapping areas of concern have been held, and State Governments have been sensitized about local level problems of the
investors in the mining sector for corrective action.
 
8.4       The Committee is of the view that the Mineral Advisory Council should meet  at least four times in a year to sort out the problems being
faced by Mining Industry and suggest possible solutions and if required modification in the existing legal framework.  The Committee feels that
interaction of the representatives of Central Government, State Governments and investors in Mining Sector would solve the mutual problems and
thus the consensus-ad-idem and common efforts so evolved would lead to rapid growth and development of Mining Industry in general.
 
8.5       During the course of interaction with the representatives of Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) the Committee  was apprised that
while the Government of India has liberalised the policies i.e. planned around the objective of making de-regulation and liberalization of mineral
production and processing industry a ground reality, however, the process of liberalization and dismantling regulatory regimes are yet to percolate to
the State level and to other implementing agencies. 
 
8.6       The Committee feels it imperative that policies that emanate from the Central Government should percolate to the State Government as well
as the implementing agencies in the spirit in which these policies are pronounced.  It is expected that the Mineral Advisory Council in its meeting
should persuade the representative of the State Government as well as the implementing agencies to bring out the necessary amendments in the
existing laws, rules and regulations to harmonize  the policy and practice.
 
8.7       In reply to the Committee’s query as to what extent the private enterprises has entered into non-ferrous Mining and Metallurgical Industries
and the steps  being taken to promote foreign investment, the Ministry of Mines replied that according to the information maintained by the Indian
Bureau of Mines (IBM), about 90% of the total mining leases in the country are held in the private sector, comprising about 65% of the total area
granted under mining lease. The National  Mineral Policy, 1993 promoted induction of private investment including foreign investment in the mining
sector, including in the non-ferrous mining sector. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) was amended in
1994 and 1999. The Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 (MCR) and the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 1988 (MCDR), framed under
the MMDR Act, 1957 have also been  modified.
 
8.8       In so far as the policy regarding foreign direct investment (FDI) is concerned, in 1994, the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation)
Act, 1957 was amended to remove bottlenecks to induction of foreign equity for mining proposals. While FDI was normally limited to 50% this
limitation did not apply to captive mines of any minerals processing industry, and enhanced equity holdings could also be considered on case to case
basis. In 1997, this policy was further fine-tuned to allow induction of FDI up to 50% on an automatic basis. Since February 2000, all proposals for
foreign direct investment in the mining sector are eligible for automatic approval, subject to ceilings on foreign equity on the mineral concerned for
such approval. Except for precious stones and diamonds, automatic approval of foreign direct investment up to 100% is permissible for gold, silver
and all other non fuel and non atomic minerals. For precious stones and diamonds, automatic approval for foreign direct investment is permissible up
to 74%. Till 31st January 2002, the total number of foreign direct investment proposals approved through the Foreign Investment Promotion Board
(FIPB) with most of the leading global mining companies evincing interest in India was 72, indicating an expected FDI inflow of Rs.4018 crore.   In
October 1996, the Ministry of Mines had issued guidelines to facilitate large area aerial prospecting, in response to which, the entrepreneurs have
taken 65 large area prospecting licenses, covering an area of over 90 thousand square kilometers. After the amendment in the MMDR Act, 1957 in
1999, 119 reconnaissance permits covering an area of over 1,55,000 (approx.) thousand square kilometers have been granted.
 
8.9       The Committee understands that    since the  adoption of the policy of liberalization and  privatization    Government is  withdrawing from
commercial ventures, and  therefore, the proportionate   increase in the participation of private sector in the transaction of business /commercial
venture is but natural .  The Committee   is in agreement with the view of Ministry of Mines that the promulgation of  new National Mineral Policy in
1993  has opened   the gate for  private player into non-ferrous mining and metallurgical   industries.  However, the Committee is of the view that   it
is the time to review the extent of participation of private sector  into the mining sector.  The Committee recommends that   a review panel should be
constituted  to examine the following issues  and the findings of the   panel  be furnished to this Committee for  forming   its final  opinion:-
(i.) to examine the comprehensiveness of National Mineral Policy, 1993 and suggest amendments if required.

restructuring proposals of MECL while on the other hand  merely Rs. 10.00 crore is provided for VRS instead of the actual requirement of Rs. 30.00
crore. The Committee feels that the insistence of the Ministry of Mines to keep the financial restructuring pending for some time till 500 more
employees are separated from the Company does not reflect the positive attitude of the Ministry of Mines regarding the possible revival and
resurrection of MECL.  The Committee is of the strong view that  the Ministry of Mines should not adopt dilly-dallying  approach and attitude in
forwarding and pursuing  the Comprehensive Financial Restructuring proposal to the Ministry of Finance.  And it is expected that the Ministry of
Finance should give due consideration for sanctioning the restructuring proposal.

16.0                 Fiscal Issues Pertaining to Mining Industry
16.1     Reacting to the budget proposals 2003-04 the representatives of FIMI highlighted the following issues:-
“The marginal rationalization of freight in Railway Budget 2003-04 has provided some relief to the industry.  However, there has not been any
significant rationalization in the tax and duty structure to benefit the mining industry.
16.2     Some of the changes are as follows:-
(i)
                  Custom duty on nickel has been unified at 10% from 5% and 15% irrespective of the class of importer.
(ii)                Custom duty on lead has been reduced from 25% to 20%.
(iii)               Special Additional Duty of Customs (SAD) has been exempted on rock phosphate and sulphur.
(iv)              Excise duty on articles made of mica has been rationalized which will give marginal boost to the crisis ridden mica sector.
(v)                Special Additional duty of Customs (SAD) has been exempted on rock phosphate and sulphur rock phosphate is of low grade and cost of
production and/or beneficiation being higher it will affect the domestic industry by encouraging imports into the country.
(vi)              The major impact on the mining industry would be the rise in fuel cost i.e. diesel as minerals are low value, high volume commodity
where any slight change in the freight would have significant impact.”
16.3              The mining or the mineral industry has not received any boost with the current budget provisions.  The lower custom duty had poised
severe threat on the sustainability of certain minerals like graphite and therefore it was suggested that the customs duty should be revised upwards
to safeguard the Indian industry from cheap imports as the cost of production in India is high because of high power and infrastructure cost. 
However, no relief has been extended to such minerals.
 
16.4                 The representatives of Federation of Indian Mineral Industries in the Committee’s meeting held on 27 th March 2003 and the Ministry
of Mines apprised the Committee through its Pre-budget Papers and expectations of Mining Industry from the budget (2003-04) that the Multi
Disciplinary Committee, constituted by the Ministry of Mines in April 1998 to study the taxation regime in the mining sector,  has given a number of
recommendations for bringing about fiscal priorities between Petroleum and Coal Sectors however, despite the best efforts of the Ministry of Mines
to consider the recommendations for including in the Budget have not received the favorable response of the Ministry of Finance. The major issues
include:-
(i)
      Rate of annual depreciation for mining plant and equipment should be increased to 100 percent.
(ii)    All expenditure incurred prior to commercial production including the expenditure incurred on site and deposit acquisition should be eligible for
amortization over the minimum mining lease period of 20 years or a lesser period at the  option of the lessee.
(iii)   For reclamation of mined out area, the mining companies may be allowed to earmark a percentage of book profits each year to meet
rehabilitation cost in future and set it aside as a special reserve in their books.
(iv)  Import duties on mining equipment may be reduced for equipment used for gold and diamond mining operations nil duty should be applicable
while for to other mining operations the duty should be at par with imports for coal mining.
(v)    Nil levy of excise duty structure for concentrate produced in the leaseholds and low excise duty structure for concentrates produced outside
leaseholds, may be devised.
(vi)  Declaration of ores, minerals and concentrates as “declared goods” under Central Sales Tax Act to limit the Sales Tax rate to 4 percent.
(vii)Abolishing or compounding of local levies, which are not conducive for free flow of goods.
(viii)
           State governments may not insist on equity sharing with investing companies.
16.5                 The Ministry of Mines submitted the recommendations of the Multi Disciplinary Committee to the Ministry of finance for its approval
in July 2000, however, the matter is still pending in the Ministry of Finance

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
