REPORT 
1.1       Small Scale Industry (SSI) sector is one of the most vibrant and dynamic sectors of the Indian 
Economy in terms of low investment, high potential for employment generation and wider dispersal o f 
industries in rural and semi-urban areas preventing migra tion to big cities. This sector offers and ensures a
more equitable distribution of national income and faci litates effective mobilization of resources of capital 
and skill, which might otherwise remain unutilised. It further stimulates the growth of industrial 
entrepreneurship and promotes and diffuses the pattern  of ownership and location. Over 40% of the gross 
turnover in manufacturing activities as also around one-third of our exports are contributed by SSI sector. In 
the area of employment generation, significant contribution is made by SSI sector both modern and 
traditional units which account for employment of over 192.23 lakhs workers and production in rupee terms 
is projected to reach Rs. 7,42,021 crore during financial year (2002-03). 
1.2       The Small Scale Industries sector presents  a wide spectrum consisting of tiny, cottage and village 
industries on the one end and modern small scale industries on the other end. Units engaged in 
manufacturing, processing and preservation of goods with investment in plant and machinery not exceeding 
Rs. 1.00 crore (original cost) are considered SSI units.  Tiny units/enterprises are those whose investment in 
plant and machinery is upto Rs. 25.00 lakh irrespective of location of unit.
 
1.3       Industry related service and business ente rprises with investment upto Rs. 10 lakh in fixed assets 
excluding land and building are also considered for benefi ts of small scale sector. These type of units are 
known as Small Scale Service and Business Enterprises (SSSBEs) e.g. x-ray clinic photographic lab, 
teleprinter/fax stalls and auto repair etc. 
1.4       Indirect finance to Small Scale Industries sector viz. State Financial Corporation (SFC) and SIDC, 
handloom cooperatives, KVIC units, agencies involved in assisting supply of inputs and marketing o f 
outputs of artisans village and cottage industries, subs cription to bonds of SIDBI,  SFS, SIDC, NSIC etc. 
also come under SSI. 
1.5       With the establishment of WTO in 1995, th e SSI sector is beset with the challenges due to (i) 
removal of Quantitative Restriction (QR) on import; (ii)  gradual lowering of tariff; (iii) phasing out of non-
tariff barriers; (iv) withdrawal of preference in  Government purchase policy; and (v) patenting o f 
manufactured products. The removal of last phase of quantitative restriction from April, 2001 is expected to 
pose new challenges to SSI both in terms of meeting international quality standard and valuation. The 
gravity of the situation gets further aggravated by the fact that the items reserved for SSI within India can 
now be freely imported and this has rendered the con cept of reservation less relevant. Heavy inflow o f 
foreign goods pose a great threat in the changed environment for SSI. The issues which need to be 
addressed are innovation and technological upgradation, greater market reach of products adequate state o f 
art infrastructure to carry out activities with certainity  and continuity, access to right type of information, 
improving factor productivity, imbibing self discipline, adhering to time schedule and maintaining 
international quality standards, internationally accepted labour norms, intellectual property rights etc. 
1.6       If SSI has to compete on international scale, reasonable economies of scale and continuous  
investment in technology upgradation become a necessity, besides modification in definition of Small Scale 
Industrial units. However, post-WTO regime also offe rs opportunity for development as well as export o f 
quality goods. 
1.7       Liberalisation process started in 1991 br ought in its wake several changes and posed challenges 
before SSI sector, the important being gradual de-reservation of the items earlier reserved fo r 
production/processing by SSI sector, e.g. as of now 748 items are under reserved category and 64 items 
have been dereserved in recent past. Entry of MNCs and their subsidiary with state-of-art technology is 
another challenge with growing share of entry by MNCs. However, the Government has taken steps to

strengthen and promote SSI sector. The establishment of a separate Ministry of SSI on 14.10.1999 and the 
new policy named "Mission for the Millennium" is a definite roadmap aimed at creating new investment 
avenues strengthening credit delivery system. Thereby promoting modernization and technology 
upgradation, providing support to enhance internati onal competitiveness etc. The Union Budget in recent 
years also contained measures to promote SSI sector  and enhancement in eligibility criteria from Rs. 50 
lakh to Rs. 1 crore in 1999 now to Rs. 25 lakh, increas ing threshold limit from Rs. 2 crore in 1999 to Rs. 5 
crore for computation of working capital limits based on 20% of projected annual turnover, increasing 
project cost limit under the National Equity Fund Sc heme from Rs. 25 lakh to Rs. 50 lakh, granting Rs. 
75000 to each unit for obtaining ISO 9000 certification from 2002 till Tenth Plan. Introduction of Capital 
Subsidy Scheme with 12% backended capital subsidy for investment in technology upgradation in select 
sectors etc. are some of the pointer of the promotional/developmental measures.
 
1.8       The SSI sector has been receiving due a ttention from the Government as well as other extension 
agencies through various policies by way of financia l and fiscal incentives, infrastructural facilities, 
technology, marketing and other simila r support measures. For credit dispensation, SSI sector has been 
accorded status of "priority sector" by banks. Ho wever, with the onset of economic reforms and 
globalisation, a number of challenges and opportunitie s have emerged for the sector. While, on the one 
hand, the process of liberalisation has expanded the sc ope of cross border transactions, on the other, the 
new order has led to different perceptions about the protection and safeguards that the SSI sector has 
hitherto enjoyed. The changed environment has necessitated technology upgradation, quality 
standardization and strengthening of marketing facilities for various products, more particularly, the SSI 
products, to tap the expanded horizons.
 
1.9       During the course of examination of Demand for Grants 2003-04 pertaining to the Ministry of Small 
Scale Industries, the Department-related Parlia mentary Standing Committee on Industry took up the issue 
of credit flow to SSI sector in details. The Committee was informed that the SSI sector, producing a wide 
range of products, accounts for around 95 per cent of the industrial units in the country, contributing to 40 
per cent of the manufacturing sector output and appr oximately one-third of the Nation's exports. As on 
March, 2002, there were 34.42 lakh SSI units providi ng direct employment to around 192.33 lakh persons. 
As per the estimates of the office of the Development Commissioner (SSI), the output of SSI sector at 
current prices aggregated Rs. 6,90,316 crore during th e year 2001-02 and exports at the level of Rs. 69.797 
crore during the 2000-01. During the financial year 2002- 03, the production of SSI sector is projected to 
reach at Rs. 7,42,021 crore. The sector also acts as a nursery for promoting entrepreneurial talents and as a 
catalyst in the industrial growth.
 
1.10     The Ministry has apprised the Committee that the total advance to SSI from the Public Sector Banks 
has gone up in absolute terms from Rs. 48,445 crores in March, 2001 to Rs. 49,743 crores in March, 2002. 
The percentage of SSI advances to Net Bank Credit (NBC) however, has declined from 14.2% as at the end 
of March, 2001 to 12.5% at the end of March, 20 02. The RBI's study of the specialized SSI/general 
branches has revealed that adequate credit is being made available to all viable projects.
 
1.11     Considering the concerns over the trend of  declining share of SSI credit, the Planning Commission

NOIDA
 
3.4       Noida Small Industries Associations
 
3.4.1    The President of the Association informed that the SSI sector is heavily dependent upon external 
financing from the State level financial Institutions a nd the Commercial Banks. Most of the units in this 
sector are run by first generation entrepreneurs w ho are endowed with the know-how and entrepreneurial 
zeal, generally have limited financial resources. Most of the problems faced by the SSI Sector stem from 
this fact. The major problems faced by the SSI sector are briefly recounted below :
 
I.          At the start-up stage, the first problem ar ises from the approach of the lender, who is expected to 
have more financial expertise than the SSI borrower , and who should, therefore, follow a venture capital 
approach of : 
                 (i)  Correctly appraising the needs of the unit for both in term loans and working capital;
 
                (ii)  Keeping the documentation requirements simple and transparent, and to render assistance 
with the documentation as required; 
               (iii)  Ensuring timely disbursement so that the project implementation is not delayed; 
               (iv)  Monitoring the fund utilization process to ensure the implementation is on track and to 
recommend timely corrective action; 
                (v)  Being a mentor and guide to the entrepreneur in financial management, and ensuring that 
fund utilization is in order. 
            Instead of an enlightened approach, what  the SSI entrepreneur often finds is a rigid and mechanistic 
project appraisal system, which often fails to make realistic assessments of need based capital requirements, 
thereby sowing the seeds of sickness at the start-up stage itself. 
II.         Another hurdle faced by SSI units is that  fund disbursement has been made contingent on obtaining 
environmental clearance from the concerned Pollution Control Board. This process is sometimes very 
Page 9 of 25129th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/129threport.htm

protracted, with the result that project implementation ge ts impeded, and cost escalation affects the project 
viability. While meeting environmental concerns, it should be possible to simplify the process, and to 
remove this requirement in the case of non-polluting industries. 
III.       There is a tendency at the stage of pr oject appraisal to squeeze the sanctioned amount. Many SSI 
entrepreneurs, lacking financial and business experience, agree to terms which cause them to start project 
implementation and then find that resources are inadequate to implement the project completely. This 
creates a state of incipient sickness right from the initi al stages of the project, from which the average SSI 
entrepreneur finds it difficult to extricate himself.
 
IV.       There should be a preferential rate of intere st for the SSI sector as was the case earlier. This is 
essential to enable them to compete. It must be remembered that we are now operating in an increasingly 
liberalized and globalised economy, and as such the SSI sector needs to be globally competitive.
 
V.        There are procedural problems in post start-up dealings with the Banks. For example, many SSI
units find it very difficult to obtain Bank guarantees. Such guarantees are required for, inter alia : 
                (a)  Imports
 
                (b)  Central Excise 
                (c)  Trade Tax 
                (d)  Bid bonds for tenders 
                (e)  performance guarantees 
            The procedure for issue of Bank guarantees is very complex, and usually requires high-level 
sanction. The result is that (a) processing of the guarantee takes long time, which sometimes costs the unit 
heavily, for example in terms of not being able to participate in a tender, or through bearing heavy 
demurrage charges on imported consignments, etc., and (b ) heavy collateral security is demanded, which is 
in many cases beyond the capacity of the promoter to provide.
 
VI.       Many of the specialized SSI branches of Banks do not have an arrangement for foreign exchange 
dealings. In an increasingly globalised economy, this  is often a problem. While some of the Banks may 
have the problem of being understaffed for the pur pose, or the volume of Forex dealings may be 
uneconomical, the procedural delays in bill discounting and other transactions should be minimized.
 
VII.      Another problem arises when a unit is sa nctioned term loan and working capital loans by state level 
financial institutions and commercial banks respectively. In such cases, charge registration often becomes a 
problem. There should be a provision in the loan agreements entered into with the state level financial 
institutions for automatic creation of a charge with the bank providing working capital.

of SSI sector is even more serious. This has led to many units incurring heavy losses resulting in thei r 
closure and the consequent loss of employment. Th e enforcement of pollution control laws had furthe r 
aggravated the situation. The small scale sector, which needs some immediate relief to counter various 
threats and to restructure itself. It has been stated that many innovative projects remain only on pape r 
because banks insist on collateral securities. This needs to be relaxed. While the organized sector units have 
options available viz. raising consortium loans, rehabilitation by BIFR etc. Such facilities are not available 
for the SSI units. In case the technology needs upgradation or the small entrepreneur wishes change in his 
line of activity, which is finance viable, then the ba nks should not hesitate to a further exposure of 40-50% 
over and above the existing credit. 
3.7.3    Even in the extreme situations of being declared NPAs, larger borrowers get away with settlements 
ranging from 15 to 30%. Ironically it is the smaller ones who have to pay with their last drop of blood. It is 
only too well known that the losses to Banks from small borrowers are a pittance compared to other sectors. 
Banks should be instructed to follow the same guidelines for small and large borrowers (with or without 
collateral). The Government may consider the following further incentives to improve the financial health 
of the ailing SSI sector.
 
Limit on Investment in Plant and Machinery
 
            The limits which are presently fixed at Rs. 1 crore may be enhanced to Rs. 5 crore as this would 
enable purchase and installation of the latest capital equipment leading not only to improvement in the 
quality of goods produced but also in reducing the cost thereof.
 
Bank Finance
 
            The following suggestions were made :
 
                (a)  Interest rates : Bank finance, both for term loan and working capital be made available at 
concessional rates. 
                (b)  Single window clearance : A single location for clearing proposals for bank finance may

kindly be arranged as this will facilitate expediti ng application for the same. There should be no delays 
between sanction and disbursement. 
                (c)  There should be expeditious need based (additional growth of business/orders) disbursement 
and not piece meal and delayed disbursements as SSI units have no recourse to any alternate 
source of finance. Delays or piecemeal dis bursements negate the efforts and business 
opportunity resulting in losses.
 
                (d)  There should be transparency in processing and disbursal process.
 
Excise/Customs Duties
 
            It is suggested that customs duties levied on import raw materials/components and capital goods fo r 
the SSI sector be reduced by 5%. Similarly the existing excise exemption limit of Rs. 1 crore applicable to 
SSI sector be raised to Rs. 5 crore. 
Exhibition/Trade Fairs
 
            It is requested that at domestic exhi bitions stalls displaying goods manufactured by SSI sector be 
made available free of charge and a subsidy of 55% of the rental charges in case of stalls at Trade 
Fairs/Exhibitions held abroad be provided by the Government. 
Foreign Travel
 
            Foreign travel facilities for travel abroad for participation in international trade fairs and exhibitions 
as well as trade conference in the form of a reduction in air fares made by the national carrier (Air-India) to 
the extent of 50% thereof is requested. This measure combined with point no. 4 above would definitely 
boast the export potential of goods produced by the Small Scale Sector.
 
Power Tariff
 
            A reduction in power tariff would reduce power costs and thereby increase profits. Since powe r 
distribution is privatized in some areas. It is also requested for a subsidy on the same by the Government to 
the extent of 40% thereof. 
Tax Holiday
 
            The Income Tax legislation be amended suitably to provide for Tax Holiday benefits for a period o f 
seven years from the assessment year 2003-04 onwards. 
Sales Tax/Octroi
 
            To exempt SSI product from the levy of Sales Tax and also grant a similar exemption from Octroi 
for a period of years.

RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
5.1       The Committee is of the opinion that the SSIs should be encouraged to have deposits from relatives 
and friends and such investors should be given tax ex emption under section 80 etc. of I.T. Act to enable 
them to have their own financial base. For studying viability of SSI, independent agencies should be 
authorized. Credit rating by an independent agency s hould also be considered. Finance should be available 
at international rates of interest from 7 to 9% to strengthen the competitive strength of SSI's present rates 
which vary from 13 to 16%. The Committee also recommends that 20% of the banks financing ability 
should be utilized for SSI's as per the Government of India's definition i.e. over Rs. 2 lakhs capital 
investment. Delayed Payment Act should be given teeth to control and punish organizations holding and 
delaying payments to SSI. Under the present act  the facilitation committee should be a sub-committee 
nominated by Divisional Udyog Bandhu having full powers to  arbitrate under the provisions of arbitration 
act.
 
5.2       The Committee also feels that BIFR with pr ovisions for SSI sick units should be made applicable 
through divisional Udyog Bandhus by means of an appropr iate detailed scheme to be drawn by the State 
Governments with powers to adjudicate and enforce the decisions/judgements on all the concerned Central 
and State Government departments, Banks, SFC's  Viability study and package for rehabilitation/OTS 
should also be arranged under the supervision of divisional udyog bandhu. For viability study the SISI 
organization of Ministry of SSI Government of  India should provide assistance to udyog bandhu which 
should be made mandatory for financial institutions and banks. The Company Law should have separate 
provisions for small industrial companies as their n eeds and requirements are very different from large 
companies. 
5.3       Income tax department should allow tax exem ption as in the case of individuals upto Rs. 2 lakhs to 
motivate them to show profits in their balance sheets and have enough cash flow to pay instalments of loans 
or to upgrade the plant and machinery. After 2 la khs there should be slabs of 10%, 20% and 25% as

sector. The RBI setup the Nayak Committee in 1991 to advise upon the aspect of adequacy and timeliness 
of Credit to SSI. In its report submitted in Septem ber, 1992, the Committee suggested to implement the 
several recommendations such as granting of working capital credit to SSI units to be computed on basis o f 
a minimum of 20% of their projected annual turnover ; giving preference to village industries, tiny 
industries and other small scale units while meeting credit requirement sector; extension of single Window 
Scheme of SBI to all districts; avoidance of delay in  sanctioning and disbursement of credit to SSI sector; 
non-insistence on compulsory deposit as a quid- pro-quo for sanctioning the credit limit; opening o
f 
specialized branches; identification of sick units a nd urgent action to put them on the nursing programme: 
the standardized loan application forms to be used by SSI units; imparting of necessary training to Ban k 
staff to handle the SSI clients. The Committee reiterates that the recommendations of the Nayak Committee 
should be adhered to by all the Banks. 
5.10     The Committee also feels that another fact calling for attention is the need to provide a linkage 
between term loans and working capital so that there is no duplicity in agencies providing it and thus saving 
the SSIs from caprice of multiple sanctions. The na rrow access to banks finance due to cumbersome 
procedure and the exhaustive regulations prescribed by the Bank warrant that the prevailing narrow access 
to Bank finance affecting the pr oductivity of units engaged in SSI activities be made adequate and 
conducive. 
5.11     Given the mutual need for ensuring repayment of loans, the banks should diversify their role in 
extending non-financial services in the areas of  technology upgradation, management training, skills
Page 21 of 25129th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/129threport.htm

upgradation, quality improvement, environment management, information about market, regulations and 
clients, etc. Commercial banks and SFCs can study th e package of non-financial services offered by the 
SIDBI etc. and adopt them with such modifications as  are considered appropriate. Financial Institutions 
should also facilitate the products for the foreign market and outlining the national logistics such as 
transportation, shipping, insurance and documentation and developing the network of physical distribution 
of the product besides arranging to provide the legal and accounting service in the target market. Not only 
this, financial institution should also provide assistance to small scale entrepreneurs in risk management by 
obtaining credit information on foreign buyers, helping insurance against commercial and political risk o
f 
non-payment, providing assistance when the small busin ess has to issue a bond or performance guarantee. 
This symbiotic relationship will alleviate the malady  of non-repayment of loans and open new vistas fo r 
bank finance. The expertise of an organized institution such as bank shall act as a reliable guardian o r 
mentor for SSIs. The main concern of banks is to ensu re return of loan and with this proactive role o f 
banks, the SSIs would be capable to repay and recoup loans. 
5.12     The Committee strongly feels that the Government should undertake following measures fo r 
enabling SSI units to have access to bank finance :- 
                 (i)  To infuse customer friendly approach, undertaking of orientation course and adequate 
training for staff/officers of commercial banks for a change in the attitude for lending to SSI 
sector;
 
                (ii)  Elimination of plethora of rules and requirements and thereby simplification of procedures 
for obtaining credit from Banks. Arrangement may be made for land mortgage instead o f 
stamp duty for enabling SSI units to obtaining credit from bank against land mortgage; 
               (iii)  Paternalistic Government umbrella for development of services through appropriate policy 
prescription/legislative changes to ease the problems relating to stamp duty, registration; 
               (iv)  Recapitalisation and revamp ing the State Financial Corporation (SFCs) with the help o f 
SIDBI and IDBI enabling SFCs to lend fixed capital to SSI units. 
5.13     The Committee is of the opinion that time limit for declaring a SSI units as a non- performance 
assets should be increased taking in consideration the various factors such as delayed payments, blockage 
of credit flow, corruption, enactment of securitization act etc. which are hindering the growth of small scale 
industries. 
5.14     The age when technology becomes rapidly obsolete, the cost of making state of art technology 
changes and of pioneering areas with the inbuilt axom-high risk, high return, the Committee observes that 
assistance under venture capital funds has assumed unpr ecedented importance. Just as the step at SIDBI, 
being the first financial institutions to set up a Rs. 100 crore National Venture Fund, as a three tier strategy 
for development of SSIs in software/IT industry (NFSIT) in collaboration with Ministry of Information 
Technology and Government of India and the Technology Development and Modernisation Fund (TDMF) 
Scheme in order to assist SSIs. The Committee feels that the Commercial Banks should come forward in 
launching venture capital funds in all its ramifications  so as to effectively integrate and enhance the 
opportunities for Small Scale Industries in domestic a nd International market. The banks should endeavou
r 
to set up more and more venture capital fund not only in software/IT industry but also for high growth 
sectors such as bio-technology and food processing inter-alia. The Committee feels that Government 
should come forward to set up Technology Upgradation and Development Banks to take stock of ground 
realities of sickness of SSI units due to obsolescence of technology and assist the units by ensuring credit 
facilitation at appropriate time and thus save the sick but potentially viable SSI units before dying out.
 
5.15     In order to ensure that there is no let up in the regular flow of funds for SSIs the Committee 
recommends that there should be enhancement in the qua ntum of composite loans; removal of procedural 
difficulties in the path of SSI advances; sorting out issues relating to mortgages of land including removal

of stamp duty and permitting equitable mortgages, allo wing access to low-cost funds to Small Industries 
Development Bank of India (SIDBI) for refinancing SSI loans. 
5.16     The Committee is of the view that the fundamentally vital role played by the Industry in the 
realization process of economic development, employm ent generation, equitable distribution of national 
income, mobilization of capital and entrepreneurial sk ills and contribution to e xport earning of the country 
is undeniable, but SSI sector occupies an equally si gnificant place in the industrial economy of the country 
because of its over bearing advantages in terms of low investment, hi- potential for employment generation 
and wider dispersal of industries in rural and semi urban areas and that make it very suitable to a labou r 
surplus country. By an estimate, more than 40% of the gross turnover in manufacturing activities as also 
around 35% of our export are contributed by SSI sector. Equally appreciable is the contribution of SSI in 
employment generation for over 1.6 crore workers.  Given its potential for employment generation and 
augmenting equitability economic resurgence, Government has appreciated the significance and mooted 
steps to pace the dissemination and flourishing of the SSI economy, the pith is provided by the SSI as small 
is also beautiful. The Government modulates policies so as to provide regular flow of capital to public 
sector banks. An undeclared priority has been infused through Government paternalism that ensures that out 
of total finance available to SSI sector, 40% is granted to units with investment in plant and machinery.

REPORT  
CHAPTER-I 
I.            BACKGROUND OF HIMACHAL PRADESH AS AN INVESTMENT            
DESTINATION 
1.1       The State of Himachal Pradesh represen ts the challenge for the po licy makers because of its
topography and geographical location.  The Committee felt that a diff erent approach would be required
to bring about the process of industrialization in a State like Himachal Prades h.  In this context the
Committee decided to undertake study visit to Shimla so  as to interact with th e representatives of the
State Government of Himachal Prad esh, representatives of various indus trial organizations in the State
and the facilitators in the form of banks who provide the ba sic catalytic factors in  the form of credit,
which is the lifeline of industry.  The Committee undertook its visit   from 19th to 22nd June,  2003. 
1.2       A brief   background of the uniqueness th at Himachal Pradesh  as a State offers is being
highlighted in the following paragraphs. 
1.3    Nestling in the lap of the magnificent Himalayas, the State of  Himachal Pradesh  comprises o f
diverse terrain ranging from plains , sub-mountain areas to higher range s, leading to varied climatic 
zones. This diversity has endowed the State with attractive resource  parameters and production factors
awaiting eco-friendly exploitation thr ough a spirit of enterprise, innovati ve abilities, energy and skills. 
The State has excellent potential fo r setting up industrial projects, wher e it has advantag es like clean
environment, cordial industrial relations,  availability of power and rapidly developing  
infrastructure. Due to its close proximity to the i ndustrialised belts and mark ets in the high per capita
income States like Punjab, Haryan a and Delhi, the State presents attractive and in some ways unique
investment opportunities for industries. 
1.4            Industrialisation is an index of economic pr ogress. Industrialisation in Himachal Pradesh is a
comparatively recent phenomenon. From  relatively backward and pre-dom inantly agricultural State at 
the time of attaining Stat ehood in '1971, it has steadily progresse d  establishing more than 170 medium
and large scale units covering a wide spectrum of industries and about 27000 small scale industrial units
involving a total investment of  Rs.2550 crores and providing direct  employment to 1.40 lakh persons.
The industrialization in the State has now achieved the take off stag e with well diversified base o f
industries ranging from traditional handicrafts and handlooms in cottag e, tiny and small scale sector to
high-tech textile units, te lecommunication equipment, sophisticated electronics gadgets, cement, paper, 
basic chemicals, drugs and pharm aceuticals, food proce ssing, engineering and hi gh quality, precision
tools, besides breweries, distilleries and mineral water units. 
1.5       Today the industrial sector is contribut ing nearly 10 percent to the State Domestic Product
Page 4 of 40130th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/130threport.htm

(SDP). The annual turnover of the industrial sect or is approximately Rs.4000 crores. The per capita
industrial investment of Himachal Pradesh is one of the highest in the country .The sector is consuming
about 60% of the total cons umption of electricity in the State a nd is contributing significantly to the
State exchequer in the form of taxes and levies and more than Rs.500 crores  towards Central Excise
duty.  The total export from the State has steadily grown and now amounts to over Rs.300 crores. 
1.6       The Committee found  that due to geographical factors the industrialization is concentrated in the
border  areas and gateways of Hima chal Pradesh ; Paonta Sahib- Kala  Amb- Parwanoo- IV Barotiwala-
baddi-Nalagarh.  Inspite of the best  efforts, other areas of  the State have been relatively unaffected by 
the process of industrial development. 
1.7       The Committee during the course of its inter action  felt that the existi ng infrastructure facilities
are inadequate to meet the require ment of new investment. Therefore,  it requires signi ficant effort to
improve the  infrastructure. Further lack of social infrastructure has led to the concept of absenteeism o f
proprietors as many of the promoter s of units in the border areas are living in the adjoining States, o r
even in Delhi. 
 1.8      The Committee also felt that non-Gove rnment organisations, wh ich are engaged in the
promotion of industries, will have to play a more significant role in the indus trialization of the State
keeping in mind the socio-economic  policies of the Government. Th eir objectives and functioning will
need to be re-oriented in this direction. The industrial units will have to play an increasing role in proper 
maintenance of the surroundings in  which they work, establishing common services and looking afte r
the social needs of the industrial workers. 
1.9       The Committee also saw that human res ource development f acilities particularly in vocational
and technical education for Him achal Pradesh are not adequate. In this regard both the State
 Government and the industr y will need to join hands for struct uring training  programmes. These will
have to be in relevant areas such as textile i ndustry. If need be, one could also consider setting up
“specialised " institutions in thes e areas if these will help in furt her employment and industrialization of
the State. 
2.0       The Committee observed that the entire Stat e is industrially backward except some development
on the periphery of the State. The State has been classified into two cate gories namely "industrially
developing areas" and "industrially  backward areas". The development blocks of Paonta Sahib and
Nahan in district Sirmour and Nalagarh, Dharampur  Solan in district Solan, excluding backward
panchayats as notified by the Planni ng Department of Government of  Himachal PradeshPradesh from
time to time fall in the categor y of "industrially developing areas".  The Committee was apprised that 
the rest of the State including back ward panchayats in the industria lly developing areas  are in the
category of "industrially backward areas". The Committee found out that there is a need to give an over-
riding incentives in industrially b ackward areas. A special package of  incentives is required for fruit,
vegetable,  maize based uni ts consuming locally ava ilable raw material. In ad dition, emphasis is also to
Page 5 of 40130th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/130threport.htm

be given to thrust areas including 100% EOU's and investment by NRIs, which have been identified and
classified as priority, sector. Relatively higher incentives and support are planned to the units in cottage,
tiny small sector particularly in i ndustrially backward areas and in prio rity sector. For the units in large 
and medium scale sector more emphasi s is laid for providing better infr astructure. In order to accelerate
and facilitate industrialization, clearances required for setting up of units in industrially developed  areas
shall be specially dealt on fast tr ack basis. The Committee also observ ed that Income Tax holiday and
that Central Transport Subsidy Sc heme, the two major central incenti ves have helped the growth o f
industries in the State.  The Commit tee also felt that the Government  of India should be approached to
extend these incentives. The Committee was informed  that it will be the endeavour of the State
Government to continue to request  and persuade the management of  companies to open/transfer thei r
registered offices within the State of Himachal Pradesh.  
2.1       On the basis of the experience that the Co mmittee has had during the course of  its various visits
and interaction  it has come to the conclusion that infrastructure is the most essential requirement fo r
entrepreneurs. The Committee felt th at  the promotion of the existi ng industrial corridors of Baddi,
Barotiwala, Nalagarh, Parwanoo, Solan, Shogi, Paont a Sahib, Kala Amb  etc. would be required and
more industrial areas need to be set up in future to meet the needs of industrialisation in different regions
of the State.  
2.2       The Committee observed that  special empha sis needs to be paid to the Baddi-Barotiwala region 
to develop it into a major industrial township in the State.   The role of the private sector in
infrastructure development and its maintenance needs to be emphasized.  Privatization of industrial areas
for creation of infrastructure including social in frastructure needs to be considered for rapid
industrialization.  
2.3       The Committee was also informed that the State is comm itted to exploiti ng its vast powe r
potential. Besides a number of am bitious schemes are already unde r implementation. Recognising the
importance of this sector for industry the Government has furt her taken note of  two important
requirements i.e. quality of power to sustain high technology industry and a power tariff structure which
is so planned that the entrepreneurs can foresee its impact in the competitive manufacture and marketing
of their products. 
2.4       The Committee observed that Himachal Pradesh due to its location and geo-climatic conditions 
has certain positive assets for certain industries. Th ese are based on considerat ions like available human
resource, natural resources, locally available raw ma terials, fauna and flora.  Agro-horticulture produce 
based industries, including food pro cessing and mineral water bottling c ould be some of the areas. The
Committee felt that  it should be  the endeavour of the State Gove rnment to encourage post harvest
technologies including setting up of cold storages and establishing of  cold chains. The State needs to
identify national and internationa l markets including adva nced technologies in food processing. Herbs
and aromatic based industries because of the geo-climatic zone provide a another unique opportunity for 
Page 6 of 40130th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/130threport.htm

the entrepreneur. Sericulture based activities also have a tremendous scope for further development. 
2.5       The Committee also f eels that Industries in high technology areas where there is a large value
addition with low volumes of raw materials involved, are particularly suited for the State and need to be
included in priority sector. These industries involve smaller trans portation and  volumes of both raw
materials and finished products, which can become a bottleneck in the mountains. With the advancement
of technology today, the Committee was appreciative of the fact that th e State is very fortunate to have
one of the best communication networks. 
2.6              The Committee was of the opinion that the importa nce of the cottage and tiny industrial sectors 
for Himachal Pradesh  needs to be emphasised. It holds the key to large scale employment and
generation of economic activities in  remote areas. It is, therefore, proposed to enhance the opportunities
of employment and income in such activities. The traditional skills and  cultural heritage associated with
production in this sector will need to be preserved. 
2.7              The Committee feels that industr ialisation in Himachal Prades h has been concentrated around 
few districts and a large area of the State rema ins unaffected by industr ialisation. The Committee
recommends that new areas be developed and the process of Industrialisation spread in a manner so as to
benefit the State as a whole. 
2.8              The Committee observed that huma n resource development facilities  particularly in vocational 
technical education are not adequa te in Himachal Pradesh. The Co mmittee recommends that the local
industry and State Government shoul d join hands to restructure trai ning programmes so as to provide
employment to the youth. 
2.9              The Committee observed that the entire State is industrially backward except some development
on the periphery of the State.  The Committee feels that  there is a need to give  over-riding incentives in 
industrially backward areas. A speci al package of incentives is requi red for fruit, vegetable and maize
based units consuming locally available raw material. In  addition, emphasis is also  to be given to thrust
areas including 100% EOU's. For the units in large and medium scale se ctor more emphasis is  required
to be laid for providing better in frastructure. In order to accelerate and facili tate industrialization,
clearances required for setting up of  units in industrially developed areas shall be specially dealt on fast
track basis. The Committee also observed that Inco me Tax holiday and that Central Transport Subsidy
Scheme, the two major cent ral incentives have helped the growth  of industries in the State. The
Committee also felt that the Government of India should be approached to extend these incentives. 
2.10          The Committee was  informed that the State is committed to exploiting its vast power potential. 
Besides a number of ambitious sc hemes are already under implemen tation. The Committee recognizes
the importance of this sector for industry and recommends that the State Government should take note of
two important requirements i.e. qua lity of power to sustain high te chnology industry and a power tarif f
structure which is  so planned  that theentrepreneurs can foresee its impact in the competitive
manufacture and marketing of their products.  
Page 7 of 40130th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/130threport.htm

2.11     The Committee also feels that Himachal Pradesh requires Industrie s in high technology areas
where there is a large value addition with low vol umes of raw materials involved. These industries
involve smaller transportation and  volumes of both raw materials a nd finished products.  With the
advancement of technology today, th e Committee was appreciative of th e fact that the State is very
fortunate to have one of the be st communication networks. The Co mmittee strongly recommends that
the State Government should take every step possible to attract such industries in the State. 
INCENTIVES AND CONCESSIONS: 
2.12     During the course of interaction with the State Government offi cials the Committee was
informed about the incentives and concessions to the industrial units subject to their eligibility as under:
- 
  
SALES TAX CONCESSIONS : 
2.13     Village Industries/Tiny units :  New village industrie s with fixed capital investment upto Rs.l 
lakhs shall be exempted from payment of sales tax for a period of 8 years in industrially backward areas
and in priority sector, a nd for a period of 5 years for units in i ndustrially developing areas. In respect o
f
other new village industries and tiny units, sales tax shall be leviable at a concessional rate of 25% of the
applicable rate on the sale of pr oducts upto Rs.60 lakhs per annum for a period of 8 years in industrially
backward areas and in priority sector; and up to sales turn over of Rs. 45 lakhs per annum for a period of
5 years in industrially developi ng areas. This concession will not be admissible to the produce o f
breweries/distilleries, non-fruit vege table based wineries and bottling   plants (both for Country Liquo r 
and Indian Made Foreign Liquor).  
POWER  CONCESSIONS  
2.14     The Committee was also in formed that  new indus trial unit(s) in prio rity sector shall be
exempted from payment of electricity duty for a period of 8 years in the industrially backward areas and
for 5 years in industrially developi ng areas. The existing unit(s) availi ng this incentive shall continue to
avail the same under the previous rules for the un expired period of its/their eligibility. 
INTEREST SUBSIDY 
2.15     The officials also apprised the Committee that subsi dy in the rate of interest on term loan taken
by tiny and SSI units from financial institution(s) shall be  given @ 4% subject to a ceiling of Rs.2.00
lakh per unit per year for pr iority sector units set up in industria lly backward areas for a period of 6
years provided that the unit pays a minimum of 8% interest after availing interest subsidy. In case rate of
interest after subsidy falls below 8%, the rate of subsidy shall be reduced accordingly. This concession
shall also be admissible on term lo an taken from financial institution for expansion/ diversification. The
subsidy shall be disbursed throug h the concerned financial instit ution. This subsidy shall not be
Page 8 of 40130th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/130threport.htm

admissible on defaulte d/rescheduled installment(s) and the period of default sh all be counted fo r
determining the period of eligibility. 
  
CAPITAL INVESTMENT SUBSIDY 
2.16.    The Committee was also info rmed that tiny units in  priority sector and coming into commercial
production after the appointed date in industrially backward  areas shall be given a capital investment
subsidy @ 10% of fixed cap ital investment subject to a ceiling of Rs.2.5 lakhs per unit. This subsidy
will be admissible on the creation of new assets only. The erstwhil e C.I.S. Manual shall govern the
sanction/ disbursement. 
SCHEME FOR SICK UNITS: 
2.17     The Committee was apprised th at the Department of Industries will provide an interest rebate o
f
4% on any additional loan involved in the reviva l proposal to be administered through financial
institution(s) during the nursing peri od as specified in the rehabilita tion plan. This reimbursement will
be made to the financial institution and subject to a ceiling of Rs.1.00  lakh spread over a period of three
years on a declaration that no penal interest has been charged from the 'unit in question during the period
for which the claims are made.  
2.18     The Committee strongly recommends con cessions to industry in the form of sales tax
concessions, power tariff, in terest subsidy and capital investment subsidy need to be continued over a
long term period. The Committee is of the opinion that once industrial growth takes place the State will
be able to generate revenue and cover up short term losses if any.  
INTERACTION WITH REPRESENTATIVES OF STATE GOVERNMENT 
2.19     The Committee sought to know  the reasons  for the big difference  between the minimum wages
of unskilled labour with those for skilled labour. 
            The representatives of State Governme nt replied that the department  does not agree that there is
a big difference  between the minimum wages of unskilled worker and those of skilled labour.  The State
Government of  Himachal Prades h has fixed minimum  wages  in  24 Scheduled Employments.  The
minimum wages are fixed by the Stat e Government  on the advice of  State  Minimum Wages  Advisory
Board, as per procedure  laid down under Section-5 of the Min imum wages Act, 1948.  The State 
Minimum Wages  Advisory Board represents empl oyers , who are in equa l number and independent
persons and exceeding one third  of the total num ber of members of the Board.  The Government
appoints one of such independent pe rson as Chairman as  per the c onstitution of the board laid down 
under Section 9  of the said Act. 
2.20     The Committee asked that  whether the st ringent labour laws are coming in the way of the
growth of the industrial  sector and what  steps  has been ta ken to make  labour law more or more
Page 9 of 40130th Report of Committee on Industry
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/indus/130threport.htm

simple.    
2.21     The representatives of th e State Government informed the Committee that the labour  laws 
prescribe the  barest  minimum stat utory benefits to the workers and the legal protection to the workers 
necessarily required for ensuring economic and social just ice to maintain the  dignity of labour .  In the
name of  industrial growth , the exploitation of weaker section of working class can not be allowed and  
if  the association of SSI submit  any proposal for any si mplification of the labour laws, this  shall be
considered by Labour and Employment Department  of the State Government. 
2.22     During the course of interaction the Committe e raised a query on the  shortage of power  and the
steps  taken to provide  the required power supply to Small Scale Industries.  
2.23     The Committee  was informed that  the De partment is placing adequate  funds with H.P. State 
Electricity Board (HPSEB) for installing transfor mers, laying transmissions lines exclusively fo r
supplying  a sufficient  power to   the SSI units .  The Department  has   placed an amount of ove r
Rs.10.00 crores to the Board for providing  and augmenting the power supply. 
 2.24    The Committee drew the   attention of the officials to the pr oblems being faced by Industries fo r
easy transit of goods from one place to another. 
 2.25    The representatives of the State Government informed that there were only 4 National High ways
till  1999 in the State. Now th ere are 8 National Highw ays with a length of about 1250 kms. The
Department is regularly providing adequate funds for the mainte nance and improvement of roads within
the Industrial and Estates to developing Agencies like H.P. State Industrial Development Corporation
and Industrial Area Development Ag encies.  An   amount  of Rs .400 lakhs been provided to State
Industrial Development Corporation for the upgradation of road infrastructure  for  exporting units in the
Baddi-Barotiwala region.  Government  of Indi a under its Transport Subs idy Scheme has been 
reimbursing the cost of transportation to and from factory  site to nearest  rail head to  the  extent of 75%
to further offset the locational disadvantages which the industry is facing in H.P. 
2.26     The Committee enquired into the reasons for the  uneven development of industrial clusters in
the State. The Committee was informed that the Small Scale Indus tries in Himachal Pradesh have
developed in almost all the districts of the Stat e where large industries could not come up due to
problem of transportation of  raw material and marketi ng of finished products.  In  certain areas  the
small scale industry is also working  as ancillary units for big  industries  in the  industrial   belts of the
Pradesh.  Small Scale  Industries  units working in local as well as   industrial areas have  provided
employment  opportunities  to the local residents in the State.

CHAPTER–I 
INDUSTRIAL SCENARIO IN THE NORTH EASTERN REGION 
1.0   The entire North East region is very sensitive and has been witnessing troubled socio-political 
disturbances since long.  As a consequence, the economic development has suffered badly, resulting in
poor industrial growth. 
1.1   The main reason for insurgency in the North East was the alienation of the people, which began
immediately after independence. The Government has taken some initiatives and a sizable number o f
insurgents have laid down arms. But immediately after, they have started looking for employment. 
Internal security problems cannot be resolved if such issues cannot be addressed. 
1.2   Every Government that has come to power at the center has been concerned about the developmen t
in the North East but progress has been rather ta rdy, if not stagnant, despite announcement of special
economic packages. In 1995, North East Development Bank with an authorized capital of Rs. 500 crores
was created but how far it has helped expansion and modernization of industrial enterprises is no t
known.  The region still lacks good roads, water and electricity, the basic needs for development. Wha t
can help boost growth is collection of unspent balance of the amounts earmarked for different Union
Ministries and spending of the same in the region with the emphasis on the feasible projects an d
sustaining the existing industries, which are facing diffi culties.  It has two objectives-one is the survival 
of the industry and the second is the generation of employment. The main objective is, however, the
reduction elimination of insurgency.  The existing units should be helped so that they can meet the social
obligation develop the area, generate employment. Everything should not be seen from the revenue poin t
of view. Unless existing industries survive, no investme nt from outside North East is likely to come as is
evident from the fact that after 1997 no new projects have come to the region. The fiscal concessions
along with peace initiative will change the economic climate of North East and bring it in the mainstream
of country and it will not be viewed as a distant territory. 
1.3   The Government of India had granted certain incentives to some specified industries located in the
North East.  These incentives were mainly in the form of excise duty relief and capital investmen t
subsidy. These incentives are applicable only for those started production after 24 th December 1997. The 
transport subsidy scheme 1971 was also included in the above policy. This step is in fact to encourage the
industrial growth in the North East Region. The underlying idea behind extending these incentives was to
provide the much needed impetus to the North Eastern States so that the region could overcome its
backwardness and the difficulties faced by it on account of geographical isolation and provide them a
level playing field.  The ultimate goal was to f acilitate setting up of new industries and sustain those,
which exist already and thus paving the way for all round economic development of the region. Howeve r
due to the incorporation of the cut-off date of 24th December 1997, a large section of the industries in the
area prior to this date were left uncovered by those well intended notification. 
STUDY OF HINDUSTAN PAPER CORPORATION LIMITED BY THE COMMITTEE ON
HEAVY INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES 
1.4   The Committee of Ministry of the Heavy Indus tries and Public Enterprises ( of the Departmen t
Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry ) was constituted in May 2000 which examine d
the performance of Hindustan Paper Corporation Limited and its units viz-Cachar Paper Mills (CPM ) 
and Nagaon Paper Mills (NPM) located in the State of Assam as a case study in the above background. 
1.5   While examining the subject matter, the followi ng points surfaced in the meetings held with the
workers’ unions and the management of the Company on the 9th July, 2000 at Kolkata.

1.6   The Department of Heavy Industry had taken up the issues of transport subsidy, excise duty
exemption of the NE located units as conveyed vide its ATR (45th Report) on the Recommendations / 
Observations Contained in the 36 th report on PSUs of Heavy Industries under Disinvestments, Sickness
and Revival.  However, the persuasive efforts of Department of Heavy Industries were not bearing much
fruit. Besides it was observed by the Committee that these issues needed to be approached through a
coordinated effort and moreover the Committee also felt that there was a lack of appreciation of concerns
expressed by the Department of Heavy Industry in re spect of HPC’s operation by the other ministries.  
The Committee feels that at the strategic level th e problems facing industrial units in the NE,
notwithstanding whether it is private or public sector, are uniform and similar.

3.0    As a result of meeting held on 4 th September, 2003 the Sub-Committee met the officials of the 
Ministry of Railways on the 13 th October, 2003. The Ministry of Railways brought to the notice of the
Committee the following position with regard to the railway network in the North East Region: 
         "(i)    Cachar Paper Mill (CPM) operati ng in the Barak Valley at Panchgram, is connected by the
meter gauge (Lumding – Badarpur Hill section) to the railway network. When the mill was se t
up the understanding was that the by 1990 the broad gauge connectivity would cover Bara k 
Valley also. The conversion from meter gauge to broad gauge has so far taken place only upto 
Lumding. The transshipment at Lumding which is a relatively smaller junction, as compared to 
Guwahati, where earlier transhipments used to take place has caused a lot of problems fo r 
movement of bulk material inputs like coal, Ba mboo, industrial grade salt, etc. and of the 
finished products i.e. paper reels/sheet. 
         (ii)     The Lumding-Badarpur Hill section was completed in 1903. The Railways are not investing
in track renewal or rolling stock with regard to meter gauge sections owing to the fact that 
broad gauge connectivity is envisaged for the entire network.
 
         (iii)    The meter gauge track between Lumding and Badarpur/Silchar rests upon 586 bridges – 73 
major and 151 minor – and goes through 37 tunne ls. The track is vulnerable to breaches an d
landslides, especially during the monsoon period. 
         (iv)    The Lumding – Badarpur/Silchar meter gauge serves as the life line for supply of essential
goods to the people of Mizoram, Manipur and Tripura apart from the inhabitants of Bara k 
Valley in Assam. Movements of materials to CPM receives a much lower priority in view o f 
the freight traffic density.

goods through rake movement – full rake, half rake and even parcel vans, ensuring reverse
loading advantage to the Railways. However, the number of rakes being made available to 
Cachar Paper Mill has dwindled considerably as compared to the previous years. Moreover,

 CHAPTER – V 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
SUBSIDY 
5.0   Under the new industrial policy for the No rth Eastern Region finalized by the Government in
December 1997, the units located in the North East sector are eligible for transport subsidy only for the
first five years of commercial production till 31.3.2007 in addition, all the units in those zones would be
free from income tax, excise duty, for a period of 10 years from the commencement of production. 
5.1   The rationale for transport subsidy is to mitigat e the high cost of transportation of raw material an d
finished products due to location of  units in remote, hilly and inaccessible areas of the country, where
infrastructure is poor. 
5.2   The transportation cost of NPM and CPM for raw materials and finished products from and to the
main land is extremely high and hence needs to be mitigated through extension of subsidy. The grant o
f
transport subsidy should be reviewed in a different light. While units through improved performance may
become economically viable even after tax holiday, the transportation cost does not get mitigated unless
the requisite infrastructure is developed. 
5.3   The southern part of Assam, where the CPM is  situated, is highly monsoon prone area and the roads
are inundated with flood water every years and land slides occur causing disruption of road movement for
about 2-3 months every year. Thus CPM deserves some fiscal concessions from the Government to
become a viable unit. 
5.4   HPC, therefore, appealed to the Government of India to include the existing establishment which are
continuously being affected adversely due to their locational disadvantages, like the CPM, under the new
industrial policy and grant extension of excise duty payment for a period of ten years and to revive the
transport subsidy scheme w.e.f. April 1995 as a special case for CPM.  
5.5   The Department-related Parliamentary Sta nding Committee, while examining the problems of HPC
units located in the North East, felt that at the strategic level the problems facing industrial units in the
North East, notwithstanding whether it was private or public sector, were uniform and similar. The
Committee, after hearing the representatives of HPC, refineries and wood- based industries located in the 
North East recommended in its 58 th report that the facility of transport subsidy and excise concession

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Thirty-second Report on the "MoU performance in respect of PSUs
of Power Sector, Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises)".
2.      The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises was constituted on the 6th January,
2003. This Sub-Committee has been examining the performance of MoU system in the PSUs and this report deals with
the performance of PSUs of the Power Sector.
3.      The report is based on the deliberations of the meetings held with the representatives of various PSUs and the oral
evidence of representatives of various Ministries at New Delhi on 5th August, 2003 and Chennai on 21st September,
2003.
4.      The Committee at its meeting held on 18th December, 2003 considered and adopted the Report..
NEW DELHI
18 December, 2003
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
CHAPTER-I
MoU SYSTEM
1.      The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a negotiated document between the Government, acting as the
owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific PSE. It contains the intentions, obligations and mutual
responsibilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MoU makes an attempt to move the management of PSEs from
management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.
1.2    The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understanding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta
Committee. One of the recommendations of this Committee was for the introduction of the system of MoU for
measurement of performance of public enterprises.
OBJECTIVES OF THE MoU SYSTEM
1.3    The objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy
and accountability of the management; to remove the fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise to pursue
through clearly laid down performance targets in the MoU and to enable the evaluation of managerial performance
through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to
stimulate improved performance.

132nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/132ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:43:05]
1.4    Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the
year. Thus the MoU covers both financial performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this system
performance of the Company is categorized into five categories namely; excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor.
PREPARATION OF MoU
1.5    Based on the guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) in the month of October/November,
the draft MoUs are prepared by PSEs and forwarded to the Administrative Ministry and DPE by December. The draft
MoUs indicate the performance targets on a five point scale as proposed by the PSE for the ensuring financial year for
all crucial parameters like production, sales, profits, etc. The PSEs are also expected to include dynamic parameters of
significance for strengthening the future potential of the enterprise, such as project implementation, R&D, Human
Resource Development, etc. Appropriate weights are assigned to each of these parameters. The draft MoU are discussed
with the PSE Administrative Ministries at the Adhoc Task Force (ATF) negotiation meetings arranged in DPE in the
month of March/April, soon after the presentation of the Union Budget. Since the Budget has implications on the
performance targets, the timing of the negotiation meetings is deliberately scheduled after the budget presentation. The
appropriateness of the parameters and weights and the soundness of the targets as also the commitments of the
Government are examined in detail at the negotiation meetings. The draft MoUs as finalised thereafter are placed before
the High Power Committee (HPC) comprising the Cabinet Secretary as Chairman, Secretary, Finance. Planning
Commission, Programme Implementation, Chairman Public Enterprises Selection Board, Chief Economic Adviser and
Secretary Public Enterprises as Members, for approval. After approval, they are signed by the respective Chief
Executives and Secretaries.
EVALUATION OF MoU
1.6    The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad-hoc Task Force (ATF) on
the basis of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the targets by the pre-
determined stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as ‘excellent’ and when the target is just met, the enterprise is ranked
as ‘very good’. In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either ‘good’ or ‘fair’ or ‘poor’.
Ranking depends on how the performance has been as compared to MoU targets.
1.7    The performance criteria should be assigned appropriate weights corresponding with their stated priorities in the
objectives. It should be ensured that they also reflect the perceived relative importance of the various criteria in the
judgement of the PSE/Ministry. The weight for physical criteria should be kept as low as possible. Instead, Efficiency
and Dynamic criteria should get higher weights. The weight for profit-related financial parameters would be 60% in
case of PSEs operating under free market mechanism. The weight of 60% would be distributed to, Gross Margin, Gross
Profit/Capital Employed and Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20% each. For PSEs operating under
administered prices, PSEs where Government is sole/almost sole customer and Trading, Consultancy, Engineering and
Financial PSEs, the weight would be 40%. The weight of 40% would be distributed to, Gross Margin and Net Profit/Net
Worth, each having a weight of 20% each. The PSEs which have been specially set up for implementing certain
Government policy directives will have no pre-determined financial parameters.
1.8    The targets set should be realistic and growth oriented. It should be insured that the MoU targets flow from the
Corporate Vision/Plans formulated by the PSEs and there is linkage between them. In case there is any variation,
reasons thereof should be clearly specified. For qualitative indicators, the targets for each of the points on the 5-point
scale should be indicated in the performance matrix itself. If these targets are on a time scale, only such target which fall
within the MoU year is included.
1.9    The MOU should contain the past five years performance data on criteria included in the MoU in an appendix. It
should also indicate the projections for the next five years, as far as possible consistent with the corporate plan.
POWER SECTOR
1.10  Power is a critical infrastructure for economic development and for improving the quality of life. The achievement
of increasing installed power capacity from 1362 MW to over 100,000 MW since independence and electrification of
more than 500,00 villages is impressive in absolute terms. However, it is a matter of concern that the annual per capita
consumption of India, at about 350 kwh is among the lowest in the world. Further, people in a large number of villages
have no access to electricity. The end users of electricity like households, farmers, commercial establishments,
industries are confronted with frequent power cuts, both scheduled and unscheduled. Power cuts, erratic voltage and low
or high supply frequency have added to the power woes of the consumer. These problems emanate from:---
         (i)     Inadequate power generation capacity;
         (ii)     Lack of optimum utilization of the existing generation capacity;

132nd Report of Committee on Industry

         (iii)    Inadequate inter-regional transmission links;
         (iv)    Inadequate and ageing sub-transmission and distribution network leading to power cuts and local
failures/faults;
         (v)    Large scale theft and skewed tariff structure;
         (vi)    Slow pace of rural electrification;
         (vii)   Inefficient use of electricity by the end consumer; and
         (viii)  Lack of grid discipline.
1.11  The Committee has been examining the performance of the PSEs in terms of the MoU of various sectors. The
Committee under took this study of MoU performance in respect of PSUs of Power sector and interacted with the
representatives of National Thermal Power Corporation Limited (NTPC) at New Delhi on the 5th August, 2003 and

CHAPTER-II
NATIONAL THERMAL POWER CORPORATION LIMITED (NTPC)
2.0    The National Thermal Power Corporation Limited (NTPC) was incorporated in November, 1975 with the
objective of planning, promoting and organizing integrated development of thermal power in the country and has a
Vision: “To be one of the World’s largest and best power utilities, powering India’s growth”. NTPC is schedule ‘A’
Navratan Company having a total approved investment of Rs.63,242.16 crores. NTPC has an approved capacity of
26,755 MW. The authorized capital of the Corporation is Rs.10,000 crores.
2.1    The Corporation has under operation/implementation coal based super thermal power plants/projects at thirteen
locations namely Singrauli (UP), Rihand (UP), NCTPP Dadri (UP), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Vindhyachal (MP),
Ramagundam (AP), Farakka (WB), Kahalgaon (Bihar), Talcher-Kaniha (Orissa), Talcher (Orissa), Unchahar (UP).
Simhadri (A.P.) and Tanda (UP) and combined cycle gas power projects at seven locations namely Anta (Rajasthan),
Auraiya (UP), Dadri (UP), Kawas (Gujarat), Jhanor-Gandhar (Gujarat), Kayamkulam (Kerala) and Faridabad
(Haryana). In addition NTPC is implementing its first hydro electric power project namely Koldam HEPP (800 MW).
The NTPC has already commissioned 20,935 MW. In addition to this, NTPC has taken over 314 MW of Captive power
Plants at Durgapur, Rourkela and Bhilai Steel Plants of SAIL through formation of 50:50 equity participation Joint
ventures between NTPC and SAIL. Thus, the total installed capacity of NTPC is 21249 MW. Apart from this, Badarpur
Thermal Power Station (705 MW), which is a major source of power supply to Delhi is being managed by NTPC on
behalf of Government of India.

2.30  The Committee was informed that the MoU instrument, which was started with some parameters in the beginning,
over a period of time, it captured various parameters like R&D, ash utilisation, environment, technological improvement
and upgradation, efficiency, technical resources, commercial resources and financial resources, not only gross margin
but also profit as a ratio to the net worth. These performance parameters of the NTPC are brought into focus and they
have been continuously improved upon. Whatever commitments were made NTPC tried to meet the commitments.
Sometimes, it required coordination, sanction and approval of other Ministries and Departments which were
continuously tried to get. After attaining the Navaratna status, the Board of NTPC was also professionalised and reduced
the number of Government Directors on the Board from what it used to be in the past, and brought people from outside,
from the financial side, from the technology side and from the professional management side.
2.31  The Committee observes that the MoU rating in respect of NTPC over the last 16 years have been graded as
excellent this kind of rating needs to be modified in view of the power scenario in the country. i.e. Gross generation of
Power and requirement. It is a fact that NTPC is the bulk power generator in the Country. However, power supply of
country still fall short of the requirement. In view of this, excellent rating seems to be a misnomer. The Committee
therefore recommends that MoU ratio in respect of NTPC should be integrated with the actual need of the power of the
Country and production. Targets should be fixed in the national perspective.
2.32  The Committee observes that although NTPC have taken measures to attain optimum growth of the Company by
taking several measures like reducing the number of Government Directors on the Board, and inducting professional
from finance and technology side to improve its efficiency but there is still scope for improvement although the
Company has a happy experience of working along the MoU instrument. In view of the increasing global
competitiveness MoU parameters for NTPC should be modified to raise it to the status of the global Company that
NTPC needs to attain in the present scenario of liberlisation of economy.
2.33  NTPC, today, is a Company, which has 21.249 megawatts of power-generating capacity. It is almost 19.3 per cent
of the overall capacity in the country. With this, last year, NTPC generated 140 billion units, which was 26 per cent of
the total generation of power in the Country. As regards generation target, compared to 1998-99, currently it has
increased by 31 per cent. The increase in generation is 31 per cent compared to the 18 per cent iincrease in the
generating capacity.
2.34  The Committee observed that the growth criteria for power generation under MoU should be measured year after
year and not from what it was since its inception i.e. 1998-99 if the growth percentage is based from year to year, the
growth trend of this Company is not very encouraging. It is reflected in the gross generation and the total requirement of
the power in the Country. MoU system should be framed in such a way so as to exhibit growth trend year after year and
encourage and invite it. Projects should be completed with in a fixed time frame.

CHAPTER-III
NEYVELI LIGNITE CORPORATION LIMITED, (NLC)
3.0    Neyveli Lignite Corporation was registered as a Company on 14th November, 1956. The mining operations in
Mine-I were formally inaugurated on 20th May, 1957 by the then Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. The main

Tonnes of Lignite per annum) feeds Thermal Power Station-I (600 MW) and Thermal Power Station – I Expansion (420
MW). Mine-II (10.5 Million Tonnes of Lignite per annum) feeds its captive Thermal Power Station-II (1470 MW 7 X
210 MW) Mine – I A (3.0 Million Tonnes of Lignite per annum) meets the Lignite requirement of the Thermal Power
Station (250 MW) set up by M/s. ST-CMS, an independent Power Producer.

and welfare. NLC is continuously making profit from 1976-77 and has earned a profit of Rs.1148.40 crores in 2002-

CHAPTER-IV
POWER GRID CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED (PGCIL)
4.0    PGCIL is the largest and best managed transmission utilities in the world. It was incorporated in October, 1989 for
establishment and operation of regional and national power grids, through transfer of transmission assets and manpower
from the constituent central sector undertakings namely NTPC, NEPC, NFEPCO etc. PGCIL started commercial
operation in 1992-93 and now the Company owns and operates about 46,245 ckt kms of transmission lines at 765 kV,
400 kV, 220 kV & 132 kV levels and 79 sub-stations with transformation capacity of about 44,736 MVA. The
transmission system availability is maintained consistently over 98.5% by deploying best Operation and Maintenance
practices at par with the global standards. About 40% of total power generated in the country, more than 200 billion
units worth Rs.40,000 crore per year, is being transmitted across the country over PGCIL’s transmission network.
PGCIL has been accorded ‘Mini Navratna’ status w.e.f. 14th October, 1998.
4.1    PGCIL has an impressive track record of financial performance as well. The turnover went up from a modest
Rs.634 crore in 1992-93 to Rs.2,533 crore in 2002-03, registering an average annual growth rate of 26%. It registered a
net profit of Rs.643 crore in 2002-03 as against Rs.236 crore in 1992-93 thereby establishing an annual growth rate of
about 16%.
4.2    PGCIL has in-house expertise in all specialised areas of power transmission with systems upto 800 KV EHV AC,
± 500 KV HVDC, Gas Insulated Sub-stations, Static Var Compensation, Series Capacitors, Controlled Shunt Reactors
etc. Towards dovetailing R&D activities into practice, it has tied up with various renowned Academic/Research
institutes like IITs (Indian Institute of Technology), CPRI (Central Power Research Institute), etc. Based upon its
expertise in the areas of Engineering, Contracting, Project Management, Financial management, etc., it has bagged
many national and international consultancy projects.
4.3    PGCIL has adopted one of the highly effective disaster management mechanism through deployment of
Emergency Restoration System (FRS) to minimise the adverse impact on transmission system caused by natural
calamities like flood, cyclone, earthquake etc. The devastation caused by cyclone in Gujarat in June, 1998, Orissa in
October, 1999 and earthquake in Gujarat in January, 2001 were attended by PGCIL on war footing and normalcy was
restored within few days, which otherwise would have taken several months. PGCIL has been recognized as the nodal
agency for disaster management in Indian power sector. It is the first power utility in India to evolve Environmental and
Social Policy & Procedures (ESPP) through public interactions and is implementing the ESPP in its transmission
projects in letter and spirit.
4.4    PGCIL has planned to create a strong and vibrant National Power Grid in a phased manner to ensure optimum
utilization generating resources, conservation of eco sensitive right of way and for having flexibility to accommodate
the uncertainty of generation plans. Commissioning of 500 MW Sasaram HVDC back to back link interconnecting
Eastern Region with Northern Region marked the completion of first phase of the National Grid with 5000 MW inter-
regional power transfer capacity. Under the first phase, all the power regions of the country have been interlinked
mainly through asynchronous HVDC links.
4.5    The commissioning of second phase of the National Grid has already begun with the commissioning of 2000 MW
Talcher-Kolar bi-polar HVDC link, achieved 9 months ahead of schedule and at a cost lower by Rs.700 crore than the
approved cost. Early commissioning of this project enabled transfer of surplus power from Eastern Region to Southern
Region. The 400 KV D/C Raipur-Rourkela line (East- West Interconnector) was commissioned in March 2003, thereby
enhancing the cumulative inter-regional power transfer capacity to 8000 MW. This project has been commissioned one
year ahead of schedule. Early commissioning of this line has facilitated transfer of surplus power of Eastern Region.
This also marks the synchronous operation of regional grids covering North-Eastern, Eastern, and Western Regions with
a combined installed capacity of 50,000 MW stretching from Arunachal Pradesh in North Eastern Region to Goa in
Western Region, i.e. a distance of more than 2500 KM. The second phase of National Grid consisting of a hybrid
system of HVDC & 765 kV systems shall be completed by the year 2007, when the inter-regional power transfer
capacity is envisaged to be about 23,500 MW depending upon completion of planned generation projects.
